Solicitor s. Messrs. SIMPSON at NORTH, Liverpool. Auditors. Messrs. P. Is J. ICEVAN, Bolton, Chartered Accountants. Bankers Messrs. GUN LIFFES BROOKS & Co., Manchester. Messrs. BROOKS k Cu., London. Secretary (pro tem.) M. F. WADDELL. Victoria Mills, Chorley.

This Company is formed to acquire that portion cf the Mills and Property of Messrs. It. and G. Lightoller called the Vic- toria Mills, which were partially destroyed by fire some time since. The Estate consists of 8,612 square yards of freehold land, at the low rental of £lO7 13s. per annum.

The Property has recently been valued in its present state by Mr. John Hoyle, the well-known mill valuer, at £11,840. A Provisional Agreement has been made between Mr. Fred. J. Lightoller on the one part, as representing Messrs. R. &G. Lightener, and the Directors for the Company, by which the whole of this property has been agreed to be sold to the Com- pany at the low price of £7,000, including the right to use the Trade Mark and Tickets of Messrs. R. and G. Lightoller, whose Yarns have for the past century been well known in the Man- chester and Eastern Markets. The Mill when rebuilt will be entirely fireproof, five storeys high, with cel'Ar ; will hold about 69,000 spindles, viz :-32,400 twist and 36,600 weft (with preparation), calculated to produce 51,0001b5. of Yarn per week. The Yarns which the Mill will be laid out to spin are (average) 32's Twist and 38's Weft. Mr. Fred. J. Lightoller has agreed to take £lO,OOO worth of shares in the new Company, and to allow the purchase money to be paid one-third each year, so a.s to complete in three years; also to give his services for three years at least to the Company as Managing Director. Messrs. Platt, of Oldham, and others have given estimates for the Machinery: 36,600 weft spindles. 32,400 twist spindles, 6,272 roving spindles, 1,792 intermediate spindles, 751 slub spindles, 10 drawing frames, 60 double cards; scutehing-room machinery in proportion. Messrs. J. Clayton and Co., of Preston, have given estimates for the rebuilding of the mills, new gearing, eugines, and new boilers, Ac. After carefully going into the estimates of sundry well-known firms,:including the above mentioned, the Directors conclude that a Mill of the most modern proportions, entirely fireproof, 1 and fitted with the best machinery and engines, will be built at a cost (estimated) of 225. per spindle—a lower price than any such Mill has been put up for in Lancashire for many years. These advantageous terms, and tile excellent position of the Mill for obtaining good hands and convenience of carriage Goods Ste- tions), will, (being within 200 yards of the Lancashire and Yorkshire and , London and Nortit-Wes Railway Companies' of the concern. the Directors feel sure, secure a profitable working AS a great portion of the capital is already subscribed for, an early application for shares is desirable. _ For further particulars, apply to M. This Company has been registe,eci with a Capital of £600,000, divided into 60,000 Shares of £lO ea, h. It is not intended in the first instance to issue snore than 36,000 shares, of which 18000 will be „Pieference Shares.' entitling to a first charge upon the profits limited to seven pours per centum per annum. The Company is formed for the purpose of carrying on the manufacture of Alkali by the Ammonia Process on a very ex- teneivel scale, and with this object to purchase and to largely extend the business of Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co., of Win- nington and Sandbach, the only Manufacturers in the United Elngdoni working this process. The pur hese will include two Alkali Works, a valuable Free- hold Estate of 140 acres, very valuable Patent Rights, and other property. The business will be taken to as a going concern as on the lot January. 1881. The vendors will receive and pay all trade debts due to and owing by them on that day, and the profits there- after will belong to the Company, the Venders receiving in- terest at the rate of £5 per cent, per annum thence up to the completion of the purchase. The price to be paid to the Vendors for the several properties enumerated above Is £200,000. from which sum will be deducted the amount of a eel lain mortgage affecting the property (No. 3) for 25,701 k—the liability thereunder being taken over by the Company—and the net amount will be paid by the allotment to the Vs ,dors at par of 12,000 fully paid up £lO Ordinary Snares and the balance in cash.

The Company acquires these properties on very favourable terms, and obtains full value tor the price paid, as will be readily seen from the following statement as to how the main Items have been dealt with. The works have been put down at their cost to the Vendors, the 129 acres at Winnington have been taken at a recent valuation by Messrs. Picton, Chambers and Bradley, of Liverpool, and the sum of £lO,OOO only ha, been added for Patent Bights, Trade Mark, anl Goodwill. No promotion money has been or will be paid, and the Vendors will defray all the expenses up to and including the formation of the Company. Arrangements have been made with Messrs. Brunner and Mand under which they are to act as Managing Directors at salaries of £1,500 per annum each. The Company wpi take over the stocks paying for them the amount at which they stand in the books on the Ist January, 1881. The Company will also have the benefit of advantageous forward contracts for the purchase of raw materials, and for the sale of finished products. The Vendors have during a very few years, developed their business at so rapid a rate that they rank to-day amongst the largest Alkali Manufacturers in the world t—during 1875 their total make was only 2,500 tons, whilst last year it reached 18,800 tons. They have step by step brought their special manufacture to great perfection, and they now prods ss their Pure .411cali for considerably less moldy than the cost of the common Soda Ash made by their competiturs. Their brand stands first in the market, and commands a higher price than any other. The Vendors have decided to convert their business into a Limited Company, for the reason that in their opinion the re- sults achieved and the prospects before them now warrant an enlargement of their operations to an extent beyond the power of private means. Already a large amount of capital has been expended in preparations for extending the Winuington Works, and it is calculated that the first issue of Capital need only be partially called up to enable the Company to complete exten- , slons of then Works sufficient to treble their production. The extraordinary success attained by the Vendors during a prolonged period of severe depression in trade is ample proof of the great dividend-earning power of the business acquired by the Company, and the intended increase of the make will ren- der it still more profitable In the futuie. Tie Directors have no hesitation in expressing their opinion that the Ordinary Share Capital of the Company will for years to come earn a minimum profit of Fifteen per cent per annum, a figure which in every year of fairly good trade will be largely exceeded, and they confidently recommend the Shares as an un- usually sound end profitable investment. The Directors now offer to the public a portion of the Ordin- ary and of the Preference Shares of the Company. Application tor Shares are to be made to the Bankers of the Company. Applications may be made either for Preference Shares alone, —or for Ordinary Shares and Preference Shares together,—but every application for Ordinary Shares is to be coupled with an application for at the least an equal number of Preference Shares. The sum of £1 to be paid on application; £3 on allot- ment ; and £1 on the Ist of July. The Call due in July upon the Preference Shares may be paid up In advance on allot- ment. The Directors do not contemplate making any further Call during the year 1881. THE CONVENTION OF FAIRIES. The fairies dressed in robes of white, Assembled in the pale moonlight; Their place of meeting. a mossy glade. Hid in the midst of a forest shade. " We will go." said they, "to Flora's bowers, And Seetde whisk shall bathe Queen of flowers." They west; and a grave oonvention bad, I Where all rude alarm, and noise was quelled. All the gay flowers were bleoming there, Tilling the air With a fragrance rare. laley watched each flower its charms unfold. Fach one cast perfect in nature's mould.' Proud England's boast is the blooming rose. Majestic it blooms, with gay beauty glows. Rise its perfume, when Zephyrs blows; 0, a regal fLmer is the blushing Rose. • I,a belle hrance claims the Lily fair, What Sewer can boast of its beauty rare. It adorns fair bosonis, it decks their hair, ID, a I..we white flower is the Lily fair. The Forget-me-not, sweet, pensive flower, The levers gift in their parting hour; Who.% e•norfes cling with a strange, sad power, Mound the faded blot= of this treasured flower. By each other flower in than was named, y nations and peas, her bqauty fainted ; 'Vet the fairies, that night, amid the gay scene. eould not decide which should be the Queen. lieddeuly a form appeared in their midst, And each fair flower she fondly kissed; Each flower sent out a fragrance rare, Mu Flora, their goddess and friend, was there. "Hew vain is your task," she kindly said, As a sweet smile o'er her features spread, "Hew hard your task to ettoose a flower, That o'er the others should have regal power. The Father of mercies, who reigns above, ' By these flowers displays His wonderous love; Theierntssion here is to cheer and to bless. To alleviate suffering, soothe pain; and distress. They are silent, yet powerful agents lent, By God in His goodness, to this earth sent; Their beauty and fragrance both are given, Ti raise the mortals' thoughts to heaven. Then leave them to bloom in their beds of green, For they have pot, nor wish to have, a Queen." It. Helena. J. G.. FICLEILSOILL.

• OVER THE SEA. I sit in the fading light, And watch the shadows fall; My day has turned to night, And darkness covers all; The sunlight's gone far over the sea, But the morn vrill bring it back to me. - My summer birds are gone, I cannot hear them sing; I missed them one by one. Till all had taken wing; My summer birds flew over the sea, But the spring will call them back to me. My summer flowers are dead, The jasmine and the rose; The autumn leaves are shed, And buried in the snows; But the flowers are blooming over the sea, And the spring will give them back to be. My darling child has passed • '. Up to the Fromised Land ; . The anchor she has cast Away on the golden strand; But I shall follow over the sea, And Heaven will give her back to me. —Merry Burton, Good Words.'

On the meeting of two friends, the following colloquy ensued:—" Where have you been ?" 'To nay tailor, and I bad hard work makiag him accept a little money." "You astonish me! Why?" "Because he wanted more." When are stockings like dead men ?—When they are men-ded ; when their soles are departed; when they are in holes; when they are past heeling; when they are no longer ea their last legs. A petulant old lady having refused a suitor to her niece, he expostulated with her, aad requested her plainly to com- municate her reasons. "I see the villain in your facet" said she. "That is a personal reflection, madam,' answered the lover. Miss Francis Power Cobbe intimates that women are cowardly chiefly in small things; but that in great con- cerns, where life, honour, or faith is at stake, or where pas- sive fortitude rather than courage is tested, they are'likely to be more heroic than men. In a theatre in this country some time ago a disappoint3cl man in the audience threw a goose's head at an actor 4 The latter came to the footlights with great coolness,-and said, "Gentlemen, I perceive that one of you has lost hie head, but he need have no fear; I am willing to return it to him at the conclusion of the performance." "Can you stay any longer," asked a host of his !clever visitor a few days ago. "I had hoped that you had come to spend the evening." "I thank you, but I must go to the club," was the reply. "I have an essgagement there to- night." " What an interest you take in that club I" said the host, petulantly. 4` It certainly owes very much to you. You have dry-nursed it for years." Oh no," said the visitor; "I have brought it up on the iota& A well-known and very witty Massi.busetts lady :called, on a certain occasion, on a family consiptingof father, mother, and daughter- The father hadvery black hair, and all three were extremely reserved and frigid in manner, so much so that the call proved rather unsatisfactory to the lady. On returning she described it in an epigram worthy of preservation. "I have just made," she said, ",an Alpine visit. I have seen the Mere de Glace, the Tete Noire, and the Jungf ran." A MIntOEABLE Serimotc—Newman described closely some of the incidents of our Lord's passion ; he then paused. For a few moments there was a breathless silence. Then, In a low, clear voice, of which the faintest vibration was audible in the farthest corner of St. Mary's, he said, "Now, I bid you recollect that He to whom these things were done was Almighty God." It was as if an electric stroke had gone through the church, as if every person present under- stood for the first time the meaning of what he had all his life been saying. I suppose it was an epoch in the mental history of more than one of my Oxford contemporaries.— Good Words for March. There are many men who speak of their losses, and when called upon to defail them, can only say that they did not make this or that investment whereby they would have gained large sums. An analogous mode of reasoning would seem in erder as regards profits. At least so thought the brilliant but penniless young "society man" who lately asked a Wall-street magnate to give him his daughter's "But, my dear fellow, you haven't a cent, in the world !" cried the rich man. "What does that matter?" answered the leader of the Germans. "You say that her dot is 500,000 dollars. I will take her with half that sum cash down. We shall come out 250,000 apiece ahead— don't you see ?" From an interesting account in the Scotsman of Carlvle's funeral, we learn that the house at Ecclefechan in Which Carlyle was born is still standing, being inhabited by the village gravedigger. The actual room is described as mea- suring only four or! five feet in width by eight or nine feet in length, with a bed-place formed in the old style of mak- ing a recess in the wall. The house into which his father afterwards moved, and where Carlyle was brought up, situated in a lane known as " Carlyle's Close," has become the village slaambles. The building at the old Secession kirk, to which his father belonged, also exists to this day ; and the parish school, in which Carlyle received his earliest education, is now used as a casual poor-house and soup. kitchen. A CONSIDERATE MAN.—The last joke at the expense of the French Society for the Protection of Animals is to the following effecti—A. countryman, armed with an immense club, presents himself before the president of the society, and c!aims the first He is asked to describe the act of humanity on which ne his claim. " I saved the life of a wolf," replies the countryman. " I might easily have killed him with this bludgeos." sod he swings his weapon in the air, to the intense disc.! tof the president. "But where was this wolf ?" inquires Um latter. " ha,,t, had he done to you ?" "He had just dev. oured my wife, is the reply. The president redects an instant, and then says, "My friend, lam of the opinion that you have been sufficiently rewarded." AN ITALIAN CINDERELLA.—The young wool .n f tone, Italy, say that their grandmothers used to tell them the story-of Cinderella (whom they called Cendrensette) as follows : Once there was a man who had two daughters, one named Catherine and the other Cendreusette, and their mother was aot over fond of Cendreusette. One day she sent her to mind the cow, and gave her a kilo of cotton to spin, which she did not in the least know how to do. She began to cry, and then the cow said to her, Tie the distaff on my horns and the spindle no my tail, and put me where there is good grass and water, and I will spin it.' When she went home her mother was content with what she had done. The sister asked leave to go with the cow the next day, and her mother gave her also thread to spin. When she was on the road she began to cry: then said the cow, Put the dis- taff on my horns and the spindle on my tail, and I will spin it.' The,girl led her where other cows had already refused the grass, and so, instead of s:Onning, that cow gathered cabbages for her. The mother being angry, then said to them to kill and eat the cow. Cendreusette went to warn her, when she told her, ' Take care to eat some of it, and you must then keep the bones and put them in a box; whenever you wish a fine gown take a bone and it will turn into one.' Once her mother was going to High Mass with the sister; they left Cendreusette in the kitchen. When they had gone she took a bone and said, I wish this to turn into a fine gown, and on it a sun shining, and a slipper which walks by itself.' She put them on and went to church, and seated herself on a bench near her mother, who did not know her, but took her for some fine lady. She had a, fan, and on it was pictured the sea ; she let it fall; her mother took it, and she said to her,' You may keep it; I do not wish it any more. She hurried home after Mass to undress, so that her mother should not know. Next day she went again to Mass, now dressed in a gown on which was „the sea, and fishes swimming about it. She put herself again on the bench near her mother. She had a handkerchief with the moon upon it: she let it fall; her mother took it, and she would not take it back. After the High Mass she ran away,losing in her hurry a slipper. The king's son found it, and had it cried everywhere. that she who lost it should come and claim it, and he would make her his wife. All the young women tried it; 1/ht It would not fit. He bade Cendreusette's mother bring her daughters. Cendreusette went, dressed in her gown on which were the fishes, and wearing the other +slipper, and the prince took her for his wife."

AN ANOMALOUS BERD.—I have‘ in my possession a very peculiar fowl, which seems to answer to the description given many years ago of a "hen-cock." Until a short time since, it was supposed to be a Brahma-Dorking pullet, and WAS again and again observed to go to nest. Now he runs after the hens as would any cook ; whilst a cock runs after her as hens are generally pursued; sometimes she is as a hen as to voice, and then he calls the hens as would any cock. In appearance the creature is more feminine, having no sickle tail feathers; the comb hangs over on one side, and, ns well ss the wattles, is of a very bright red. Shall I more rightly describe the bird as he, she, or it `f—Cor. ' Sow CrOOD Som.—Lands Wended to be cropped to oats should be ploughed as soon as the state of the laud will per- mit, evea if not required to be sown just yet, ad old, expe- rienced farmers always prefer, if possible, to put in this cron on "a stale lurrow."rhe chief thing to be regarded, how- ever in cropping land to oats is to sow good seed. There is no kind of produce which is influenced more by the charac- ter of the seed than this—like producing like in the majority of instances. If light long-tailed oats be sown the grower may depend on reaping much tbe same kind of valueless grain; but if a plump, full-bodied berry be deposited and the season prove favourable there are a great many chances in favour of the sample realised being very similar. Owing to inattention to this precautionary measure, we have fre- quently known a difference of 101 b, per bushel in, the weight of samples, although grown in adjoining lands. , HOW CATTLIS DISEASE IS SYRItAD.—A correspOndent writes as follows :—Mr. A. has some cattle poorly, arid he sends for the farrier. He sends them some .titinks, and orders the cattle to be kept warm and sheeted 'np,_ and the farmer then sheets his cattle with provedder sacks irons the mill. In a few days the cattle becoming worse have to he slaughtered (lung disease). The sacks are then returned to the mill. Mr. 8., some miles off, goes to the mill for pro- vender, and gets some of the sacks which Mr. A. has used to "sheet" his cattle.. The disea.,e shortly afterwards breaks out in his place. At this he IS much surprisell, for he says, "Bow is this? I have never bought any cattle this long time." Well, the wise people say the disease comes in the air. 'WHO COULD NAVE TIIOUDHT F!? TILE AMERICAN KITCHEN GARDEN.—From homes Made repulsive, if not by positive squalor; at least, by that utter disregard of domestic comfort which drives men and women to the rum shop and children to the cornparativvluxury of the gutter, the little girls alma in their shabby, homely gar- ments to a bright, airy,room, with its clean, comfortable looking furniture, hung round with pleasing pictures, and dotted here. And there with gay and fragrant flowers. And now we will suppose it is Monday morn- ing, which is washing day in all well-regulated funnies. Our kitchen garden class is certainly well regulated, for here we see four posts, about 18 inches highs stuck into holes, two at each end of the table, ,and, stretched from post to post, a clothes-line of string. This is the laundry and dry- ing-ground all in one, and presently the twenty-four little washerwomen enter the room, with their washing-tubs and boards and bundles of dolls' clothing. After the usual questions and answers, the class proceeds to wash the clothes "with invisible soap and imperceptible water" to a merry tuner— In the tubs so cheerily our little hands must go, Washing all so merrily, and washing white as snow. !cc. 1 More questions follow, be*ing upon the relative treatment , of various articles—the arder in which they should be washed, and the manner in which they ehoold be arranged on the clothes-line; andwhen all have been taken down the class retires with the washing apparatus, and re-appears armed with scrubbing brushes. From washing clothes to scrubbing tables is a natural transition and with the rhythmic accompaniment of their brushes the children sing the "Scrubbing Song" : Scrubbing away at the break of day, To make our homes look neat; For a good hard scrub is the very best way To make all smell so sweet. Chorus—Then scrub away in your very best way, With a face so bright and cheerful, For a cheery face meets much more grace Than one that is always tearful. I —Good Words. TRAVELLED MILK AND BUTTER YIELD.—The Mitch Zei- tuny relates a recent experiment by Fjord :—" A quantity of fresh milk was divided into three portions, one of which was set in ice water at once; the other two were allowed to cool an hour by standing at ordinary temperatures, and one of these was then set in ice water; the third portion was car- ried in a waggon for three hours before being set in ice , water; all the samples were allowed to stand ten hours. Calling the quantity of butter yielded by the first portion of milk ,100 parts, the other two gave 70.3 and 73 parts , respectivelely ; or, in other words, there was a loss of 29.4 I and 27 per cent. of butter in the two cases mentioned, as compared with what should have been obtained if these two portions of milk had, like the first, been put in ice water at once. The loss was not in all cases so great as this; but the 1 fact that it may occur, and may under certain conditions be so serious, is well worthy the attention of creameries; and no less worthy of consideration is the simple. method dis- covered by Fjord of almost entirely avoiding this loss, which consists in heating the milk, as soon as received at its dead= nation, up to about 104 degrees. In the warm season the milk may be cooled as soon as drawn, so as to be delivered in a fresher condition at the creamery, where it may then be warmed as above. These experiments also yielded the im- portant result that with a good centrifugal creamer no not- able loss of butter was caused by this partial cooling of the milk before delivery; so that reheating the milk is unneces- sary when this method of separating the cream is followed." —Quoted in the Monthly Bulletin of the American Jersey Cattle Club. A FRENCH ALDERMAN MECIII.—M. Menier, the well- known chocolate maker and deputy, who is just dead, was a French Alderman Mechi. He devoted a good part of the fortune made in trade to agricultural and economic experi- ments. But he was a larger Mechi in every Way, and above all he was a more fortunate one, for he leaves immense wealth. The fortune he acquired was merely a basis for intellectual enjoyments of a very high order. M. Menier , was a political economist, and he put some of his theories I in practice at Noisiel, where his factory is situated, by forming a model village community among his 1,200 workers. When you went to Noisiel, and had been taken through the factory turning out thirty tons of chocolate a day, you had seen but half of the show, and that the least interesting. You had to walk to the village, which was the perfection of neatness and symmetry. The workmen there bought their goods at co-operative stores under their own management, took their recreation in free clubs provided with every means of rational enjoyment,had medical attend- ance for nothing, and lived in healthy, roomy, detached cottages, with bits of garden in front and rear. All this was, of course, greatly due to the initiative of M. Menier, and he was not a little proud of it. Still other signs of his activity of mind were to be seen in the same neighbourhood. He was an agriculturist, and he had a theory of the value of pulverised stone as manure, which he tested to the full— and, as he always said, with the most striking success—in his own fields. Noisiel was on the Marne. In another part of the country he had a huge manufactory of india-rubber of his own creation, and, in still another, a manufactory of drugs left him by his father. The management of all was centralised in a range of offices in Paris which was like a department of State. Air, to mix with the as supply, is passed through a re- fractory chamber, which is heated by small jets of gas, themselves supplied with hot air. PROFICIENCY IN Wortxmassnik,.—No one who desires to be proficient in his art will rest satisfia_with a knowledge of the mere routine duties required. It is not enough to know that certain results are produced from certain causes; this we may learn from mere experience. But in order to be- come really intelligent, we must go further, and learn why the causes produce results, so that, in an emergency, Other \means may be substituted-to accomplish the desired ends.—

Design and Work.' MICROSCOPY AND ROCES.—The microscopic Structure oi rocks has of late received considerable attention. The first part of a series of beautifully-executed photographs, selected and arranged by E. Cohen and executed by J. Grimm, have just been published at Stattgart, under the title of "Samna- lung von Mikrophotographien znt Veranschaulichung der Mikroscopischen Structur von Mineralien und Gesteinen." These are deserving of the closest study of all who are in- terested in the much-to-be-desired elucidation of this in- teresting subject.--Desion and Work.. To RENDER Ivorty FLExurian.—lvory is readily rendered quite flexible by immersion in a solution of pure phosphoric acid, (specific gravity 113) until- it loses, or partially loses, opacity, when it is washed in clean cold water and dried. In this state it is A flexible-as leather, but gradually hardens by exposure to dry air. Immersion in hot water, however, restores its softness and pliancy. The following method may also be employed: Put the ivory to soak in three ounces nitric acid mixed with fifteen ounces water. In three or four days the ivory will be soft. —Design aud Work. • COPYING DRAWINGS.—By a method patented by M. Jol- train, of Paris, it is olaimed that copies of drawings having nearly black strokes on a white ground can be made by the following sensitising mixture: Gum, 25 grammes; chloride of sodium, 3 grammes perchloride of iron at 45 deg. 10 cubic centimetres; sulphate of peroxide of iron, 5 grammes tartaric acid, 4 grammes; water to fill up to 100 cubic centimeters. The developing bath may be a soluticri of ferrocyanide of potassium, red or yellow, acid or alkaline. The printing is done-in the ordinary way, and the develop- ing in a bath Of red or yellow prussiate of potash. After washing .the proof is put into an acidulated bath, which darkens the lines to an indigo tint, and is then again washed and dried.—Design and Work. . ANOTHER RIVAL TO GAL—lron says that Messrs. Duncan Stewart and Co., of Glasgow, have adopted a system of gas- making from mineral oil, water, and air, and the following is a description of the process :—The furnace contains three retorts, and these are supplied with a combustion of mineral oil, water, and air, which enters through a small pipe car- ried from the back to the front of the retort, and the gas' I finds an exit through a large pipe the back of the retort. The vapour is conducted to the purifier; thence it is carried into the gasholder, and then led through the old pipes M the works to the various machines and benches in the shop, sup- ply Vlg about 200 burners. The gas is said to give a whiter and more pure light than coal gas, or something between coal gas and the electric light. The odour is not offensive,l and it is stated to be freer from deleterious effects on pic- tures and paper than coal gas. The chief advantages claimed are, simplicity of application to public works, country churches, schools, and mansions. The cost is said to be less I than one-half that of coal gas. , AUTOMATIC STENOGRAPHY.—The Daily Telegraph Paris correspondent says—An interesting trial of a new stenograp- hic machine was made in the Chamber on Friday morning' in the presence of M. Gambetta and a number, of other offi-, cials and members. The mechanism, which is an Italian invention, is worked by a kind of keyboard similar to that of a small piano, and the stenographic signs, not unlike those used in the ordinary French shorthand, are automati- cally printed on a continuous ribbon of paper. The signs registered of course represent sounds, irrespective of spelling, and the machine can be used by a person unacquainted with the language spoken. The daughter of the inventor worked the machine this morning successfully, taking down a speech read at average speed in Italian, and one read in French by M. Gambetta, she being ignorant of the latter language. A comparison between the speed of the machine and that of the shorthand writers of the Ohamber proved favourable to the former. Further experiments will be made with a view an a possible adoption of the apparatus, which is already ia use in the Italian Chambers. HEARING SERMONS BY TELEPRONE.—AII invalid member of St. James's-Place U.P. congregation, Edinburgh (Rev. Dr. Andrew Morton) had on Sunday, as on two previous Sundays, the opportunity of listening in his own house to the religious services conducted in the church with which he iiassociated as an elder. The gentleman in question had not been able to attend church for twelve years, and in these circumstances his family resolved to have recourse to tele- phonic communication. The result has proved highly satis- factory, and the invalid had on Sunday the pleasure of hearing his pastor express thankfulness that modern science had succeeded in bringing the preacher in the pulpit into direct communication with the bed-ridden sufferer. "Sound- ing chambers" are placed on either side of the pulpit, through which the voice of the preacher is conveyed; while, by means of another chamber in the gallery, the singing of the choir and congregation is transmitted. It is stated that the sounds, alike of preaching and worship, although travelling over three miles of wire, are distinctly heard, not a word being missed, and other disturbances, such as coughing, being also communicated.—Scotsman. PAPUAN DRILLING MAcßtivs.—Mr. 0. C. Stone, in de- scribing the events of a recent sojourn in New Guinea, found that the natives employed an original apparatus for drilling shells. The drills were tipped with bits of cornelian named vesika. "We discovered, for the first time, that our friends were mechanicians, being the inventors of a rotary drilling machine, having a to-and-fro motion, spindle and fly-wheel. A sharp piece of vesika is bound firmly to the end of a wooden spindlo two feet long, on which is fastened , a piece of heavy wood or some stones, answering the purpose of a fly-wheel. A string is attached to the top of the spindle, and made fast at each end to a horizontal bar or handle, nine inches long, sliding up and down the vertical spindle. Some little dexterity is required to work the machine. The string is first twisted by turning round the spindle, and then by suddenly pressing down the handle, sufficient momentum is established to retwist the string in an opposite direction when the same process is repeated. It is wonderful how quickly they perforate shells in this manner. We have several kinds of fiddle and other small hand drills in England, but I do not remember having seen this particular motion in use. The Polynesians. however, have a very similar drill."

WHAT SHOULD CHILDREN EAT AND DRINK ?—Dinner for children should always be early; and about this let me remark that if beef or mutton be given, it should be cut up very finely, or even minced, and the child should be taught to eat very slowly, and to masticate the food well. Chil- dren's food, like that of grown-up people, ought to be varied; change is always agreeable, and conducive to good digestion. I like to see children sit down to a good dinner, and I de- light to see them enjoy it, but hurrying over meals—and they are greatly prone to this—should always be dis- couraged, while, on the other hand, nothing indigestible should be placed before them. Game of various kinds, as well as fowl, pigeon, and rabbit, make a very nice change, and so does white fish, with the exception of herrings and mackerel, or any other strong-tasted and oily fish. Al- though a little salt should always be sprinkled over a child's food, he should not be permitted to eat salted provisions of any kind, nor any such indigestible food as pork, goose, or even duck, and turkey should be given but sparingly. The stuffing generally used with these latter is very likely to produce a fit of indigestion if given to a child. There are vegetables that a child may eat, and others that he ought not to partake of; potatoes, for example, turnips, and outs generally, are very wholesome, but cabbage and greens are provocative of internal disturbance. Even potatoes, turnips, and parsnips, however, should be mashed. And here let me give a word of warning they ought not to be mashed on the plate with the back of a fork; they will be lumpy if they are. The mashing ought to be complete and thorough. Puddings of sage, rice, or semolina or even corn flour, should always form part of the child's dinner, and suet dumpling, if eaten with syrup, makes a very nice change. What should a child drink ? Milk or water, or milk and water, with meals, or a very little tea or coffee well diluted with milk. Cocoa is most nourishing; I cannot, indeed, speak too highly in its praise. As to beer or wines, I should say never under any circumstances allow a child to partake of them, except under the orders or sanction of a medical man. The supper should be early, say six o'clock, and may be light pudding of any kind, porridge and milk, or bread and butter with milk-diluted tea. Children live fast, and be it remembered that they require more food in comparison to their size than grown-up people do, for they have not only to repair the waste of tissue, but to build and feed bone and nerve and muscle. Even between meals, there- fore, if occasion demands it, do not deny them a crust oi bread. There is little need of physic where children are well cared for, well clothed, and well fed. If a laxativa be needed, either a teaspoonful of magnesia may be mix Id in the pap, or a little fluid magnesia administered, 'nit re- member that magnesia too often given is apt to form con- cretions of a dangerous kind. Castor-oil warmed, so as to make it run easy, is sometimes good, the only objection to its administration being that force is requirzd, and I know by experience that a child will sometimes s+ ruggle so against swallowing medicine as to cause itself , mischief. Syrup of rhubarb is another harmless aperient and one which will not weaken the child; but, after all the less medicine you give, the better, unless the child Oe actually fevered, and then it is time to send for the e.Jetor.—Harper's Weekly

Two of the vacant judgeships have,been conferred on Mr. A. Wills Q.C., and Mr. James Charles Matthew. Theliew line between Walsall and Wolverhampton was opened for traffic on Thursday. At the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, Henry Mor- timer was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude for forging cheques. The parish church of Nevrnhatn,, Gloucestershire, was destroyed by 13re on Sunday night. The edifice wao restored six years ago at a cost of several thonsand pounds. A movement has been commenced for the purpose of cele- brating in a fitting manner the fiftieth anniversary of the passing of the Reform Act of 1832. A Monmouth telegram states that "an attempt has- been made to upset a passenger train o 9 the viaduct over the Wye, by placing stones on the rails. A man was seen run- ning alma. the litre, but he escaped. , • Mr. Bradlaugh, speaking at the Hall of Science, London, on Monday, said his motion for inquiry into perpetual pen- sions was supported by 475 petitions,. with. 154,000 signatures. • [ The annual meeting of the West Bromwich Liberal Asso- ciation paased.a resolution expressing the hope that coer- cive measures in Ireland would be the precuteors of a thorough reformaaen of the Irish Land Ltws. Henry Tolley, a German master tailor, of 33, Chdlrorie, street, Deptford, shot himself through the heart with a MT"- chamber revolver. Deceased was in a good way of business. , At a congress of representatives oftrades unions, held In Manchester, on Saturday resolutions were passed in favour of the Employers' Liability At, expressing a hope that some employers would not be able to evade it. The mayor of Salisbury issued a notice on Saturday stating that as serious breaches of the peace were anticipa- ted on account,of the Salvation Army parading the Weds, in future no such procession wont be permitted. On Monday, W. K. Harris was slued 40s. and costs for disturbing the congregation of St. Agnes* Plytnquth, by throwing firevreths ameng them during divine service. The magistrates remarked that they never heard of such a dis- graceful thing having occurred before in that county. General James Butler, of Holt Lodge, Kintbury, Berks, who was seriously burnt in his bed. on Wednesday through the clothes taking fire, died on Saturday. • The deceased officer had attained the age of 82 years. He carried the colours of his regiment through the battle of Waterloo, and was.present at the capture of Paris. At the adjourned inquest,,on Tuesday, on the man Davis, who was killed by a boiler explosion at Leicester, the evidence showed that the safety valve was over-baled. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, ex- pressing regret that the boiler had been worked without a guage. • In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, before Jus- tice Field and a special jury, Dr. John Brown, physician, Coventry, and having a bone manufactory at Dudley, was awarded £4,000 compensation for Injuries by a railway acci- dent on the London and North-Western at Birmingham, in January, 1880. On Tuesday, the remaining creditors of the late West of England Bank received from the eficial liquidator (Messrs. Turquand and Clark) dividend warrants for the balance of their claims. The entire liabilities which at the time of the suspension were nearly £3,500,000, are now discharging. The election of six Conservative members of the Warwick Town Council was on Monday declared void, otY the ground that the order of election issued by the Town Clerk did not give nine clear days' notice. One of the respondents was also declared disqualified, because he had paid for the use of one cab. On Sunday, the museum at Maidstone was re-opened in the afternoon, having been temporarily shut owing to the action of the Conservative Towle Councillors, but after the large indignation meeting which was held at the b+nning of last week, they thought it advisable for their own interest to open it again to the public. There is now living at Studley, a village three miles from Redditch, a woman aged 91 years, who has four children, 23 grandchildren, 40 great-grandchildren, and three great- .great-grandchildren. One of the last-named has four grandmothers and grandfathers, six great grandfathers, one great-grandmother, and one great-great-grandmother. The farmers of Leicestershire have sustained fearful losses by the ravages of liver-flakes amongst their sheep, and now there are but few sound sheep in the county. The disease has spread to horses, cattle, bares, and rabbits, and even fowls are affected by it. The greatest mor- tality is amongst in-lamb ewes, which are dying weekly in htindreds. The largest vessel in the world, with the exception of the Great Eastern, was launched on Tuesday from the ship- building yard of Messrs. Thomson, Clyde Bank, Glasgow. ThO length of this new vessel, named the Servia, is 530 feet, breadth 52 feet, depth 45 feet, gross tonnage 8,500, and horse-power, 10,500. Her officers andcrew will number

200. A revised army estimate was issued on Saturday. The vote for the number of men of all ranks on the establish- ment of' the regular ariny, exclusive of India; will be in 1881-82, 134,080. In 1880-81 the number was 131,859. The vete shows an excess of 850 ,nen above the numbers stated in the army estimates. The addition is required to provide for the reinforcement proceeding, be Africa. About three o'clock on Sunday morning, Mr. David Bixby, farmer, of Dagenhacn. Essex, left home to catch an early train. Shortly afterwards, three men wearing masks and armed with revolvers entered the house. They presented the revolvers at Mrs. Bixby, and terrified her into giving up £36 in money and three deposit notes, one for £lOO and two for £3OO each. The men got clear away. Mr. Forster, acknowledging a resolution passed by the Bradford Liberal Association, says it is very cheering to him that his Bradford friends do not misinterpret his motives in the performance of a most painful political duty, and their generous sympathy makes him all the more confi- dent that he will have the earnest and helpful aid of his constituents when they come to deal with the remedial measures for Ireland. An ancient custom of playing at football in the public streets WRS observed at Nuneaton on Tuesday. During the morning a number of labourers canvassed the town for sub- scriptions; and between one and two o'clock the ball was started, hundreds of roughs assembling and kicking it through the streets. Tradesmen had to put up their shutters. The police attempted to stop the game, but were somewhat roughly handled. A few days ago, at the annual conversa.zione of the Sheffield Literary and Philosophical Society, a case of dia- monds and precious stones was exhibited by Mr. Bryce Wright, of London. Whilst Mr. Wright's assistants were patting the jewels• into a Bate in London, a cab accident occurred opposite the shop. The assistants went out te see it, and on their retvrn they found that a case of the jewels, worth about £lO,OOO, had been stolen. ' Mr. J. T. Hibbert, M.P., acanowledgieg v.ceipt of a reso- lution passed by the Chadderton Workmen's Liberal Asso- ciation expressing confidence in the Government, says that, though further trials may yet await the Government and the Liberal party, he trusts that with moderation and firm- ness all difficulties may be overcome, and the blessings of a good and substantial land measure be given to Leland. It may be very hard for a time to curtail the liberty of a people and to restrict the liberty of debate, but it would be harder still if the outrages and bad conduct of a few were to stand in the way of a great act of justice to a people. Mary Ann Atkins nurse, was charged at Marylebone Police Court, on Tuesday, with kidnapping a child, 19 months old, the daughter of Dr. Dennis Dowries, divisional surgeon of police, and Robert Gould, traveller, was charged with aiding and abetting Atkins. Dr. Dowries stated that on Saturday afternoon he returned from visiting patients, and was told the nursemaid had gone out with the child, and had not returned. He eventually found the prisoner and the child at Kentish Town police station. Mrs. Downes, when called upon to give evidence, fainted. A long statement by Atkins was read, and the prisoners were re- manded. Eighteen of the tweuty•two passengers on board the disabled Cunard steamer Batavia arrived at Plymoth on Saturday. From their account it appears that the vessel broke her shaft when a week out from New York and about five hundred miles from Fayal. Everyone on board behaved with commendable spirit, and the excellent example set by the officers and crew prevented anything like panic on board during a severe gale which the disabled steamer sub- sequently encountered. While this violent weather lasted the Batavia became completely helpless, her gunwales some- times dipping into the sz.a. Three days after the disaster the tempest-tossed vessel was taken in tow by an Anchor liner and towed into Fayal, whence the above-mentioned passengers proceeded to England viii Lisbon. At Birmingham, on Saturday, Superintendent Birchley and Inspector Latham, froirs"information received," visited some premises at Winson Green, described as a "potted meat and saveloy manufactory," and discovered what they des- cribed as the most perfect manufactory of the kind mentioned they had ever seen, the ovens and steam machinery being of the latest and most improved description, Potted meat, saveloys, "savoury ducks," sausages, and other delicacies in large quantities were in every stage of production. The materials used in the manufacture_ consisted of diseased horseflesh, diseased mutton, dir.Ased pork, red ochre, the. The sausages were coloured wi.th red ochre to give them a " healthy " appearance. S,yeral recently potted cans of potted meat, the meat a'.arist putrid horseflesh, and richly coloured with red ochre, were also seized. The polling for.4.last Cumberland, OR Saturday, readied as follows :—Howard (L), 3,071; Lowther (C), 3041; majority for Roward, 30. After tke declaration of the poll, Mr. George Howard addressed several thousands of the elec ors fnim a window of the County Hotel, aad congratu- lated thr.m on the victory they had won. It had been a hard fioht, and he always knew it would be a hard fight; it was e 2 the more credit to them for having won it. If the Literals had been beaten East Cumberland would have been declared a Tory county—and it was not. He congratulated Ahem on the way in which the contest had been Conducted, and he should like the electors to acknowledge the way in which Mr. Lowther had conducted the contest. Mr. Lowtlser also appeared at the window of the hotel, and thanked the electors for the kind reception they had given him. It was not the first time a Lowther had been defeated in Cum- berland, but previous defeats had not been a bar to future victories.

THE STATE OF IRELAND: - • - MURDER Of A LAND AGINT.—Mr. John Harvey, clerk of petty sessions, Ballinrobe, and agent to the Hon. D. Montmorence, has been shot dead at his residence. No arrests have been made. ArrAcx on A. VILLAGH.--A shocking outrage was per- petrated at the village of Cahernakilly, about six miles from Lougbrea, early on Sunday morning. About a dozen houses, principa.ly occupied by.labourers, were completely wrecked. It seems that at halfpast twelve a.m., about 150 men entm ed the village all armed with guns and revolvers. On arriving ' at the village, the party smashed the doors and windows cif houses, ad fired shots into each house where they thought occupants slept. Some of the labourers were injured, but none were killed. The outrage is attributed to all the labourers having worked for Lord Dunsandle, after he had discharged a number of other men who had joined the Land League. Up to a late hour last evening the police have been unable to find a clue to the effenders. Mr. Mitchell Henry, M.P., makes a strong attack on Mr. Parnell and his policy, He mays it is notorious that Mr. Parnell never took the slightest interest in the land question during the early portion of his parliamentary career, and did not adopt land reform as his cry until the policy of obstruc- tion had failed in the House of Commons anti Michkel Havitt bad Vuggested it to Ifirn as a more telling cry. The stupid, irrational, almost insane policy of the last few month(' bat crippled the Irish vote in Parliament for ever "The money extracted from poor people in America and at home is removed to foreign soil; no accounts are pub.' fished; the leader flies at the very crisis of the fight which he professed, to fight in Parliament; and Parliamentary liberties are destroyed." Such, adds Mr. Mitchell Henry, are the results of Mr. Parnell's policy. At Wednesday's meeting of the Land League Mr., Dillon, M.P., warned the branches, which he stated at "2,000 or 3,000," that the League could not undertake to be responsible for legal expenses in cases not submitted for its advtce. He said that some branches incurred enormous ' expenses with- out consulting the League, under the belief that it had un- limited money at its back; but strict economy was necessary "to meet the stream of writs and persecutions now raised ' upon the farmers of Ireland." Mr. &Inn read reports from several districts professing an intention to adhere to the principles of the League, and he said that if the people could be got to stand firm for the next two months the land- lords would have played their lag card and their power would be broken. Mr. Parnell, in an interview with a Parisian reporter, is reported to have said on hearing of the death of General Colley that reverses made Governments pliable, and that the English army contained 40,000 Irishmen. On surprise being expressed that he, a leader of Irishmen, should be a Protestant, Mr. Parnell is reported to have replied that the question was not a religious but as economic and national one. "The Catholic religion," he said, ." is no longer per- secuted in, Ireland. It is the priests who have had the largest concession's made them, in the absurd hope of mak- ing starving men forget their other grievances. The higher clergy are openly hostile to the Land League. The Pope, who cherishes grand schemes as to England, has been advis- ing the Irish te submit to the powers that be, but his voice, said to he omnipotent in Ireland, has found no echo. I Hunger has spoken louder than creed." A BOYCOTTING PROSECUTION.

At Charleville, County Cork, Petty Sessions, a lawyer's clerk, named Fitzgerald, was charged Inith writing a letter to Mrs. Daly, local trader, threatening her for supplying Mr. Saunders, who was being Boycotted, with necessaries, and for failing to illuminate her hew on the occasion elf the result of the Dublin State trials. The Crown being unable to prove the handwriting, the case was dismissed. IRISH BISHOPS AND THE LAND AGITATIONI The Lenten pastorals of the Irish Roman Catholic bishops, read in the churches on Sunday, all counsel the people to shun secret societies awl to refrain from acts of violence in the present land agitation. Dr. Delany, Bishop of Cork, says that with French revolutionaries Irishmen could have no relations. Dr. MC'ortnack, Bishop of Achonry, enjoins the priests to etpound to their flocks the law of justice, so that they may know their obligations and the consequence of disregarding them. "Every man," he says, "is bound to pay his just debts to the extent of his ability and without unreasonable postponement." ANOTHER -SHOCKIN4 OUTRAGE IN THE ' 'WEST.

At one o'clock on Tuesday morning a most barbarous and wanton attempt at assassination was perpetrated within eight miles of Ballina. county Mayo. It appears that Mr. George Scott, of Stonehall House, high constable, retired to rest at 12 o'clock, his wife still remaining up. Mr. Scott was startled by screams, and on going to the window a shot was fired, and a bullet crashed through the window near his head. He immediately procured a revolver, and with a ser- vant man went to the window, when two more shots were fired through the window. Mr. Scott and the man returned the shots, taking good aim, and wounding one of the would- be assassins, who it is stated, was carried away by his com- rades. Five bullets passed through the window, and it is stated that the attacking party numbered a dozen. One bullet pamsed within an inch of an infant's cot. The shots were fired from the top of a high wall. Mr. Scott has no property in the West of Ireland, but has a small estate in county Westmeath. His brother, who has a large estate in the county, and had large works going On, has stopped them. MR. DILLON, M.P., IN THE NORTH. Mr. Dillon, M.P., was present at a crowded Meeting on Tuesday, in the Land League Hall, Downnatrick ; the Rev. Harold *lett, Unitarian clergyman, presiding. A. Govern- ment shorthand writer was present. .Mr. Dillon spoke for upwards of an hour, urging the people to be true to each other. An address of welcome was presented to Mr. Dillon, in recognition of his own services, and also as the " suc- cessor of the beloved and imprisoned Michael Davitt." Mr. Dillon, in reply, said the tenant farmers should consider now what was their best policy to keep themselves in the land, and to put down the iniquitous system of landlordism which had oppressed the people for over a hundred years. Their policy would be to have every man the owner of his own /arm. It was taken for granted that the system of landlordism must be abolished, and the only question that remained was how this was to be done. In Ulster they had agitated for tenant-right for 35 years, and they had get nothing except the bill of 1870. They were worse off now than they were before. They had nothing to expect from Parliament, and they could only trust to their own organisa- tion, to their own exertions and their own manhood to gain what they wanted. No and Bill could save them now. They should work strictly in accordance with the policy laid down by the Land League, and if they remained fast to the principles of the League every farmer in the country could take his stand on his merits as a man with any lord of the soil.. Resolutions condemning coercion and in favour of the Land League were adopted. ,

THE VOYAGE OF THE Isimons.—On the 9th June they first saw the coast of Novaya Zemlya, a portion of the snow- covered shore of Goose Land. Further north, off Cape Britwin, to their great surprise they saw a small boat bear- ing down upon them, its occupants firing blank charges from their guns to attract attention. The wholly unex- pected appearance of the boat was fruitful of surmises as to what she could possibly contain, the most probable being that it was a shipwrecked crew which had endured the ter- rible hardships of winter upon the ice-bound shores of No- vaya Zemlya. It proved to be a small open boat, about 18ft. in length, containing five Samoyeds—two men, a woman and a couple of children. These Eskimo-like sub- jects of Russia occasionally pass from the mainland to the southern island of Novaya Zemlya; and this party had passed the winter in a hut not far from the spot where they were encountered, and were on their way to visit their friends in a settlement of Samoyeds on the island further south. The party "were 'clad in reindeer-skin coats, with hoods of the same material attached, and sealskin trousers and boots. They appeared very happy and merry, and boarded us in a very unceremonious manner, the two men clambering over our side, leaving the lady to make the boat fast. The latter was, however, handed up by our gallant skipper in true cavalier style, the children being treated with less ceremony, for they were summarily seized by the nape of the collar of their skin habiliments, and thus lifted bodily on board. So similarly were the men and women clothed, that it required a very keen observer to detect the difference of sex. Their appearance and cheerfulness en- tirely set at rest any idea we might have entertained re- garding their being in a semi-famished or distressed condi- tion from the want of food or the hardships incidental to shipwreck." The visitors stated that the Isbjorn was the first vessel they had seen since the preceding year, and prob- ably she was the first of the season, as it was still early. The abundance of certain birds in this region surprised Capt. Markham, who declared that the " loomeries" or breeding. places of the guillemots in Nameless Bay exceeded in populousness anything of kind he had seen elsewhere in the Arctic Regions. Air and water were thick with birds. They could be easily knocked down as they flew over the boats; and many were so unfamiliar with the sight of man that they permitted themselves to be caught by the hand. "Some idea may be formed of the countless numbers of these birds when it is known that in somewhat less than a couple of hours my companion and myself bagged six hull- dred ; and had we required a greater supply, more could undoubtedly have been obtained in the same space of time. On the first discharge of our guns a perfect cloud rose in front of us, completely obscuring the face of the cliff. The sound caused by this sudden flight can only be likened to the fall of water from some gigantic cascade. As they flew outwards they actually struck us in the boats, whilst our victims tumbled about us like • hail. We were, unfortu- nately, a few days too early in the season to supply our- selves plentifully with eggs." On the shores of this bay they first saw reindeer, and Sir Henry Gore succeeded in shooting the herd of four. The contents of the showed that they had been browsing the dwarf willow; and Captain Markham believes this to be their ordinary food, as he never found lichen in the great number of stomachs he examined.—" A Polar Reconnaissance," In/ Captain A. H. 'carkham, F.R.G.S.

In compliance with the request of Mr. Asslieton Smith, the workmen employed at the extensive Dinorwick Ilate quatries. Llanberis, have reconsidered their refusal to contract them- selves out of the Employers' Liability 'Act, anolll not avail themselves of it, preferrinc, to remain under the old system, by which Mr. Assheton Smith dotitinues his support to the quarry hospital, pensions to widows, and other privileges., Nothing has yet been done in the matter.at the PenrLyn quarries, but it is probable, that the men will , adopt the some course as those at Llanberie.

Mr. Wm. Morgan, sculptor, Pontypridd, has hit upon whatis reported to be an ingenious method of preventing gas explosions in collieries. Competent critics speak very ' highly indeed of it. Mr. Morgan went to London to secure the patent. He accomplished this object on Saturday, And in a few hours afterwards he was offered ,£2,500 for the in- vention2-£5OO to be paid at once before any testing; he re= fused the offer. So confident was Mr. Morgan before' lae went to London of the success of his invention that he offered to go into the lOcal gasometer—provided a breach was made—and stop there twelve hours with his apparatus, tbe gas being destroyed as quickly as it is generated. The matter has engaged the assiduous attention of Mr. Morgan for the last three years. THE IRONWORKERS AND THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILIIT 'ACT.

An official communication appears in the 'organ of the National Association of Ironworkers for March, issued on Saturday, strongly condemning contracting out of the Em- ployers' Liability Act by the workmen in the coal trade. The action of the coalownsrs in Lancashire is condemned ; but while the miners there "had fought se nobly for thai which is their legal right, and the coalowners have failed in thar object, the employers in other districts have been More successful in their efforts, and have succeeded by promises of contributions to a mutual insurance fund, in inducing their woikmen to give up that which has cost the labour of years to obtain.' The address urges that this action will affect fuTure questions in workingmen's interests intro- duced into Parliament, and weaken -the power, not only of the leaders of Trades' Unions, but of the Trades Congrev Parliamentary Committee. The Government, on the repre- sentation of the Trades''Congress Committee, Messre. Bras- say, Morley, Macdonald, Burt, Broadhurst, and other mem- bers of Parliament, and a large and influential deputation representing a very large majority of the workmen of all trades who had waited upon the head of ,the Government believing the deputation was:thoroughly representative of the working classes, rejected the mutual insurance clause which had been proposed at the instance of the employers. Under those circumstances, it is urged the men ought not to contract out of the Act. So far as the iron and cOal
trades of the North of England are concerned,it is believed that the Act will be adhered to.

• THE SOUTHPORT AND WEST LANCASHIRE BANK. In calling the extraordinary general meeting of share- holders for the 7th inst., the directors give the following further explanations with respeet to the proposals which will be laid before them in the event of its beibg decided that a new company should be formed :--" That the new company takes over all the assets and liabilities of this company (including the costs of the winding up of thisl company), and that each shareholder in this company is entitled to one unpaid £5 ordinary share in the new com- pany, and to his proportion of the surplus (if any) of the assets of this company over its liabilities and costs of winding up as ant when such surplus is realised. The capital of the new company is to be £440,000, divided into 88,000 shares of £5 each, of which 38.000 are to be or- dinary shares and 50,000 are to be preference shares. The preference shares are to be entitled to 5 per cent. per an- num before the ordinary shares receive any dividend, and both preference and ordinaryshares are then to rank equally for further dividend in proportion to the • amount paid upon them. In the event of the new company being wound up, the preference shares are further to be entitled to a preference in repayment of capital and in pay- ment of the arrears (if any) of their preferential dividend of i 5 per cent. One pound per share s to be payable at a short date on the ordinary shares, aud £2 on the preference shares. In case further calls are necessary, the ordinary shares are to be called in full before farther calls are made on the preference shares." The notice convening the meeting, and which contains the above proposals, is signed by the liquidators, Mr. Frederick Whinney and Mr. T. Walton Stead.

Scarlet fever is prevalent in Oldham. The sani- tary department attribute the outbreak to a want of proper isolation. The Lord Mayor of London has received a telegram in Greek from the governor of Gythion, in Laconia, stating— The assembled neighbours have been distressed by the aid news of the accident to your distinguished and Hellenophil fellow-citizen Gladstone, and are praying to the Most High at church for his speedy recovery." Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P., in a lecture at Leicester on the land question advocated the repeal of the law of settlement and entail, and a system of registration of titles and easy sale. At present three-fourths of the holders of the land were crippled, and agriculture was consequently in a poor condition. Lord Cairns' bill, lie argued, was utterly incom- petent to deal with the question. Job Warner, of West Derby, who in October contracted to supply the Toxteth workhouse with pure milk, has been fined £l.O and costs for adulteration. The analyst certified that of the skimmed milk 64 parts water had been added to 100 parts of the poorest milk; and that to the new milk 33 parts of water had been added to every 100 parts of the poorest milk. The master of the workhouse said the milk was not fit for the sick and the children for whom it was intended. Although up to the present no authenticated case of trichina in American pork has been reported to the Local Government Board, that department has determined to issue a circular warning consumers of hams and bacon to cook those viands well before eating, in order that no unpleasant consequences, such as those resulting sometimes from their consumption abroad in a raw state, may ensue. At Stafford station, a young farmer, named Landers, on his way home one night, attempted to cross the line after he had taken to much drink in the refreshment room. He was knocked down by a passing engine, and died the next morn- ing. His widow sued the Railway Passengers' Assurance Company in the Exchequer, for the amount of hisinsurance, £l,OOO, but the judge decided against her on the ground that deceased wilfully exposed himself to unnecessary danger. Tun HEREFORD HIGHWAY BOARD are closely watching the timber merchants, who have not yet, in their dealings with timber sellers, contracted themselves out of the High- ways Act. One firm of timber merchants who make exten- sive use of the roads in the Board's district had been' com- municated with touching the "extraordinary traffic" for which they were responsible, the usual certificate having been given by the Board's surveyor. The firm agreed at once to pay a fixed sum for all claims up to the date of the cprtificate, and proposed that thereafter they should pay to the Board is. per load for long and short distances, instead of, as had been suggested, 2s. in winter and is. in summer. The proposition ha e just been discussed by the Board, and it was resolved that the firm should be asked to pay ls. fid• • per load in winter, and 9d. per load from March to October. • Road surveyors would do wen to note what is being done in • Herefordshire; and if a load of 120 feet has been agreed upon, they should resolutely object to such lengths as 300 feet —Land.

_ GERMANY. The religious ceremony connected with the marriage of Prince William and the Princess Augusta was performed on Sunday evening in the Chapel of the Castle at Berlin, and and afterwards a grand reception and state ban9uet were I held.

THE BASUTO DIFFICULTY. CAP TOWN, March I.—ln at( official minute published to-day, Sir Hercules Robinson, the Governor and High CommissiOner, and the Colonial Minister protest against the public expression of disapprobation of the terms of peace offered to the Basutos, as tending to encourage their re- sistance.
The Colonial Government has received no information of the resumption of hostilities with the Basutos or of the pro- longation of the armistice.

- CAPE TOWN, March 2.—No reply has been received from Lerothodi or the other Basuto chiefs, and the armistice has come to an end. Owing to the heavy rains military. opera- tions have not been resumed. OUTBREAK OF THE PLAGUE IN THE EAST. ST, PETERSBURG, March 2.—The Gobs of to-day pub- t lishes a despatch from Odessa, stating that the Russian Am')assadof at Constantinoplejms received a communica- tion from the Russian Consul at Bagdad announcing that I the plague had broken out at Djaffar, Mesopotamia, and that four deaths had already occurred. Am imperial decree declaring Batoum to be a free port is officially published to-day.

div.head: CANDAHAR.
div.p: CANDAHAR.

A telegram from Candahar states that two personages of sonsiderdble importance have arrived in that citywith letters or messages from Ayoub Khan at Herat td the British Government. At the time the telegram was sent off the nature of their mission was unknown, and the wires through Persia have since been interrupted. All was tram:lllH in Candahar, and caravans were regularly !allaying from Herat.
THE TURCO-GREEK QUESTION. SERIOUS ASPECT OF AFFAIRS.

• CONSTANTINOPLE, March 2.—The Council Of Ministers sat from ten o'clock last night until ten this morning with- out arriving at any decision with regard to the Greek fron- tier question. It is understood that there are two strongly divergent currents of opinion in the Council. The Porte has not vet made any communication to the ambassadors. Munitions of war were despatched to Prevesa, and to-morrow a detachment of troops proceeds to Volo. The following telegram is announced from Berlin of Tuesday nigLt's date :—R.:gording war as unavoidable, in consequence of the action of England, Austria, and Russia, Turkey is endeavouring to prolong negotiations until large supplies of American military stores arrive. The Porte is taking its last military measure—the Anatolian reserves are called in. Greece is engaging numerous German surgeons. There has been an interesting debate in the Greek Cham- ber of Deputies on the enforced truce. Ths Premier stated that the Government, complying with the wishes of Europe, would not commence hostilities, but hoped that the decision of the Berlin Conference would be speetfily executed. The leader of the Opposition agreed to support the Government, bat only on condition that the Ambassadors at Con- stantinople did not contemplate a revision of the Berlin award.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCFI ‘5, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCFI ‘5, 1881.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS:---MONDAr.

Tau PROTECTION Bill was read a first time. ; THE DISASTER IN THE TRANSTAAL.--Th reply to the Eirl of Cadogan, the Earl of KIMBERLEY said he was afraid there could be no doubt of the death of the Governor• General of Natal. He bore his testimony to the very efficient and satisfattory way in which the gallant officer had discharged his duttes as Governer of Natal. No one could doubt that Sir George Colley was an able, energetic officer, and the country would not forget that he had fallen in its service and in the performance of a most arduous duty. THZ BANKRUPTCY Buz.—The Bankruptcy Law !mend- ment Bill, introduced by Earl Cairns, was read a second time.

1 HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Moimmi. Local. P ' nryxru BILLS.—The Cheshire Lines Committee Bill, the London and North-Western (Additional Powers) Bill, and the London and North• Western (New Railway) Bill were read a second time, and referred to a Select Com- & mittee. URGENCY.—The SPEAKER announced that, as the Protec- tion of Parson and Property (Ireland) Bill was read a third time and passed on Friday, the state of public business was no longer urgent. THE TELEGRAPHS AND POST OFFICES.—IE reply to Mr. Macliver, Mr. FewcrT said, with the object of securing greater administrative efficiency, it was proposed to amalga- mate the postal and telegraph staffs at certain local post offices, and those who had been in the service of the tele- graph companies, but had never passed a civil service ex- amination, were required to pass a very simple one in diete- tical and the first four rules of arithmetic. The result had been of benefit to the public and to the service, but he did not in- tend to extend it until he completed his inquiries into the pay and position of telegraphists. No steps had been taken to inquire into what number of telegraphists the railways could supply on SE emergency. He believed the report arose from Ids inqniries into the rates of pay by the railway companies and others for similar work to that of the tele- graphists in the post office. Sours AMERICAN WAR.—In reply to a question Sir CHARLES DILLE stated that the Peruvian Governmenehad, through their representatives to the Powers, applied to the Governments of England and France for mediation. THE DISASTER IN THE TRANSTAAL.—MI. CHILDERS an- nounced that Sir George Colley would be succeeded by Sir Evelyn Wood.

Tin BUSINESS OF THE HOI7SE.—LORD HARTINGTON, in the absence of Mr. Gladstone, who, though progressing favourably, was still unable to resume his Parliamentary duties, made a statement on public business. He referred to the extreme anxiety of the Government to introduce the Land Bill, Mr. Gladstone having never concealed his opinion that "this measure, more than to any temporary repressive legislation, must be rooked to for a permanent improvement in the condition of Ireland." At the same time, Mr. Glad- stone is of opinion that it would not conduce to the calm and deliberate considerations of the proposals of the Govern- ment that discussions should concurrently be going On as to measures of a repressive character and as to measures of a remedial character. The Government, therefore, proposed to interpose the business of Supply in the consideration of the second Peace Preservation Bill. The Home Secretary, in the absence of the Chief Secretary for Ireland, would the next day introduce the Peace Preservation Bill. It would further be necessary to appeal to private members to waive their privileges for the purpose of permitting progress to be made with public business.—This statement of course, gave rise to considerable discussion.—Sir R. A. CROSS had "great pleasure" in postponing a notice which he had on the order paper, but declined any further to pledge the op- position until he bad consulted his friends.—Mr. O'Dommum boldly suggested that the Land Bill was not to be introduced yet because it was not ready, and Mr. SULLIVAN asked whether urgency would be declared on that measure also.— Lord HARTINGTON replied that the last question had better be deferred.—The Spnenna stated, in answer to an inquiry, that the rules relating to urgency would not be applicable to Committee of Supply unless Supply were distinctly voted urgent._

A WASTED NIGHT. After IMO conversation, Mr. O'DowNELL, upon the motion that the Speaker should leave the chair for Committee of Supply, rained a discussion on the Irish magistracy, and moved a resolution thereon.— When this was rejected, another motion on the same subject was brought forward by Mr. M`Coax ; and the debate was continued in a very thin House.—The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to one o'clock without the War Esti- mates being brought before it. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY. AFGHANISTA/C—Lord ENFIELD. replying to the Marquis of Lansdowne, said it was the desire and intention of the Government to withdraw from Peshin as well as from Candahar. As to Quettalr, it WAS not intended at present to make any change with regard to the occupation by British troops.

Tits Puonterrox BILL.—Lord SPENCER moved the I second reading of the Protection of Person and Property (Ireland) Bill, and in doing so re-stated the arguments with which the measure had been supported in the Commons, adding that the danger of an actual rebellion in Ireland could not be regarded as altogether averted.—The Earl of BEACONSFIELD supported the bill, and reviewed the legisla- tion during the preseat reign in order to show its failure in achieving the pacification of Ireland. He traced the cause of the agitation in Ireland to the failure of the harvests, the inflammatory speeches of "accomplished orators," and the machinations of the Fenian Brotherhood.—Earl Gaorvxma replied, and after some discussion the bill was read a second time.

his seat amid lend cheers.—ln a speech of ,an hour I THE REV. HENRY VALENTINE. OF and a quarter's duration, delivered in the hearing of I about a score of members, Mr. O'DoNsuna, moved the rejec- • , RUNCORN, ON THOMAS CARLYLE. tion ef the Bill. He was followed by other Irish members, 1 including Mr. HEALY, Who excelled him in the matter of i On Sunday evening the Rev. Henry Valentine preached length.
