div.head: ALLEGED FENIANISM AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED FENIANISM AT WIDNES.
IMPORTANT SEIZURE, OF ARMS AND AMMUNITION.

As well known, a great proportion of the inhabitants of Widnes, are Irish, or of Irish extraction, and when trade is brisk, they earn good wages in the chemical works, of which the town can, probably, boast a larger number than any spot on the face of the globe. Of course, amidst such a. large body of the Celtic race, it can hardly be otherwise than expected that there are a somewhat large number of sympathisers with Home Rule, the Land League, and, some say, with Fenianism. The fierce struggles which have for some years been going on in Parliament between the Parnelites and whatever Governme,nt may have been in power, have been watched with the keenest interest by the members of a nationality who pride themselves as much on their love of race, as they do upon the fact that their country has produced an O'Connell, a Burke, and a Shiel. - As the battle for supposed national rights ban been pressed closer and closer to the gate, and deteloped the great movement carried on by the Land League, It can hardly be supposed that amongst the large body of men in Widnes who have either been born in the green isle, or descended from some family who formerly had a home there, some have not been influenced by the seductive offers made by the. members eat the Feaian brotherhood. We believe we are correct in stating that for some time past the police have been in pos- session'of informatimref a pretty conclusive character as to Fenian lodges having been held in the town. We under- stand that they have ever said that they knew the very houses where these meetings were held, but owing to the cleverness shown by the members of the order in guarding against a surprise, or the difficulty of proving that the gatherings were of a treasonable nature, nothing definite has been done. It will be remembered that when the unfortunate man Delaney was murdered whilst pursuing his lawful call- ing during the night time, at the Pbcenix Alkali works, it was broadly hinted hr the police, and the fact Was given publicity in some of the journals circulating in the district, that the crime bad been committed at the instigation of a secret organiza- tion, whose emissaries were in the midst of the population, but not known, and able to inflict a terrible penalty upon any who proved faithless to the oath they were alleged to have taken. It will be remeanbered that at the several in- quiries held before the Coroner to fathom the mystery sur- rounding the crime, many of the witnesses underwent protracted cross-examinations, with the object of eli±iting some admission which might prove a thread by which the suspicion entertained might be rendered a certainty that the deceased had met his death at the hand of some of the mem- bers of the Fenian brotherhood. However, whether through fear, Or from the clannishness which causes an Irishman to stand by another of the same race when in a difficulty, the indefatigable efforts of the police to discover the murderer proved utterly unavailing; and the mystery surrounding this Widnes midnight tragedy is about as great to-day as it was within a few days of its perpetration. Of course such outrages as those committed at Salford barracks within the last few weeks, and the course of matters in the sister isle, have made the Widnes police snore careful and industrious than ever in pushing their enquiries. It is stated—but we are not able to vouch for the accuracy of such a startling report—that for some time past it has been known that bodies of men have been drilled at nights in the neighbourhood of Ditton. This statement seems to carry its own refutation upon the face of it, as it looks utterly impossible that any drilling could be carred on even at night time in such a neighbourhood, where people are constantly going to and from their work at the chemical manufactories, and the police are traversing their long and wearying beats. Another assertion his been made, which seems to have far more of the air of probability-about it, viz., that for some time past, notwithstanding the dulness of trade, very large sums have been sent over to Ireland in support if the Land League movement, and that many of the shopkeepers know this to be true to their cost. Some little excitement was caused on the last Sunday in January, as people were coming from the various chapels and churches, en it being discovered that a small placard, printed on very'thin paper, and professedly issued by the National Irish Directory, had been posted on the walls of the town of Widnes, and a copy of which was inserted in The Examiner. By order of those in authority, the bills were either torn down or defaced within a few hours, and though some little excitement was caused upon the fact of their publication becoming generally known, it was allayed and very little more thought was given to the matter by sensible people, on it being stated in the morning journals that similar bats had been posted in several towns in the kingdom.

_ Thus matters went on until Saturday, when the police received some private information which led the inspector in charge of the Widnes division which is under Superinten- dent Brindle (of Prescot) to visit a house in Market-street, occupied by a man named Michael Campbell, a labourer employed at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co's chemical works, The Inspector surrounded the dwelling with a dozen of his best men, and sent, as a kind of avant coiffeur, Sergeant Eastham, one of the most daring spirits in the force, to the door, dressed in the garb of a railway porter. The Sergeant succeeded in gaining admittance, and was followed by the inspector. On entering the kitchen, the latter officer asked Campbell and his wife whether they had received a box, but they appear to have at first pleaded ignorance. Whilst the conversation was in progress, the Inspector saw Campbell's wife turn the key of the parlour door and put it in her bosom. He demanded that the key should be given to him, and amidst mpch trepidation on the part of Mrs. Campbell, she handed it to him, at the same time giving him a glance supplicating mercy. The officer at once guessed he was on the right track, and entered the front room, where he discovered a strongly made box aboat 3 feet long, about 1 feet wide, and 18 inches deep. The box was addressed to "Michael Camp- bell, 26 Market-street, Widnes," and the Inspector asked Campbell if it was his, and he answered that it was, but he did not know what it contained as he had only just received it. Under these circumstances, Campbell, and a lodger named Patrick Shea, also a chemical werks labourer, who came into the house at the time, were taken to the police station with the box. On the latter being opened it uas found to contain 18 eight•bore pin-fire six. chamber revolvers, on which was the name "11/isset, Liver- pool." In the bottom of the box were 1,500 ball pin-fire cartridges of a corresponding bore to the revolvers, which are all new ones. Immediately afterwards telegrams were sent to the head quarters at Preston, and early on Sunday morning the Widnes force was augmented by a large num- ber of men from Prescot. The pame afternoon between 20 and 30 constables arrived in the town by special train from Ilaydock, and Captain Moorsom, chief constable of the county of Lancaster, and Captain Alison, deputy chief con- stable, put in an appearance. It was also stated that a num- ber of detectives visited the neighbourhood, but we are not able to vouch for the accuracy of this statement.

PRISONER § BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. On Monday the two men, Michael Campbell and Patrick Shea, were brought up at the Prescot Police Court, before ir Captain Willis, charged, on suspicion, with having stolen from some person or persons unknown 18 revolvers and 1,450 cartridges. Mr. Swift, of St. Helens, prosecuted, and in opening, the case said the proceedings originated from :- information received by the police, and it would not be , necessary for him to say whence that information was , derived. It would be enough for him to tell the magistrate A that the police had reason to suspect the house where the ,2" prisoners lived, and that the property was found there. On ' being questioned as to the box containing the revolvers and 1' cartridges, Campbell denied any knowledge of it, and he had not since given any satisfactory account of it. It was not lat all likely that any man would come into possession of 4 property of that kind without being able to give some account of it. He asked for a remand for eight days, in order that the case might be fully investigated.—lnspector Barnett said he visited the house where the prisoners lived about eight o'clock on Saturday last. He sent Sergeant Eastham to the door in the garb of a railway official. On gaining an entrance he (witness) noticed the prisoner Camp- ,\ bell's wife turning the key in the lock of the parlour door. She concealed the key in her bosom, and went into the kitchen. He followed, and asked whe-e the box was. The husband Campbell said, "What box ?" He said, " Have You no box here ?" and then turning to Mrs. Campbell, in- • quired for the ker of the front parlour door. Sha said she •:k knew nothing about it. He sail, "You have just locked it," on which she said, in a supplicating tone, "Now, in- Spector ;" and, after manifesting considerable reluctance, gave him the parlour key. He unlocked the parlour door and t found the box, which was addressed to Campbell. He asked Campbell if the box was his, and he aUnitted that it was. , revolvers al:trhsena takennd catrot, cartridges s he foundpolice station,ini tin n searched,— aawr tm eandltihre Swift, Mr. Barnett said he had reasons to believe' that if the t prisoners were remanded further material evidence might be '1 obtained.—Campbell asked for bail, but Shea said he had nothing to say.—Bail was refused, and the prisoners were remanded for eight days. 4

The two men, Michael Campbell and Patrick Shea, appre- hended on Saturday last, on suspicion of stealing 18 re- volvers and 1,400 cartridges, were brought up, on remand, at the Prescot Police Station, on Thursday morning, before Mr. W. L. Evans, when it was stated on the part of the police that the investigation which had taken place during the interval since the remand had led to the conclusion nat other persons who had absconded were more deeply impli- cated in reference to the possession of the arms in question than the prisoners were, and that until such persons were apprehended it was not thought desirable to proceed against the two prisoners separately. The police, therefore, did not Purpose to offer any further evidence against the prisonersat present, but would ask his worship to set them at large upon their entering into recognizances to appear and answer fur- ther to the charge when called upon. Upon being dis- charged, the prisoners asked whether they made any claim to the property, and they each answered in the negative. It was stated that the arms had been removed from Widnes to a safe place of deposit, and the magistrate said they woul remain in the hands of the comity police authorities unt;l investigation showed the ownership.

Men and their systems and their compliments were to him but sweet hells jingled out of tune." The greatness which sprang from union with Christ was trle only form of greatness which would command divine commendation. This was a great- ness which all of them could possess. Only a few were bele to rule. When Carlyle met the question, "What are the people of England?" he made answer, "Thirty millions, chieil fools." The answer by many had been deemed un- just. Perhaps it was. Still the thought held good that there were not many wise, not many noble, dot many des- tined to have sway over the minds of men. The Carlyles, the Lathers, the Cromwells, the Gladstones, were the excep- tion, not the rule. But moral greatness was possible to all, and it was the only form of greatness which could survive the stroke of death. , Said Carlyle, "The literature of Europe will pass away. Europe itself--Lthe earth itself— will passaway. This little lifeboat of an earth, with all its noisy crew of mankind and all their troubled history, will one day have vanithed, faded like a cloud-speck from the azure of the all. Yet in the being and doing of. a faithful man there is a something that pertains not to this wild death element of time; that triumphs over time, and is, and will be when time shall be no more." The Christian was the highes style of man, and true nobility was to be good. BY a hearty consecration of themselves to God they could make the present moment a etepping-stone to a heaven of count- less magnificence and im-xpressible bliss, and b, "Patient continuance in well doing" seek for honour, glory, immor- tality, and eternal life.

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Dr. Twyford, Mr. T. and R. Pilkington. 1 A VIOLENT FELLOW.—John Wareing, Eccleston, pleaded "guilty to being intoxicated with drink," on Saturday ' night in Parr. He was also charged with assaulting P.C. Peebles and damaging the policeman's clothes.—lt sppeared from i.C. Peebles's evidence that be took the prisoner Into custody because he was creating a disturbance in the street. Prisoner got hold of him, placed his head be- tween his legs, and attempted to throw him over his head, 1 but they fell together on the ground. A violent struggle ensued, and the policeman's coat was very much torn, pri- soner doing damage to the amount of 7s. 6d. During the struggle prisoner` succeeded in wresting the staff from the constable, and with this he dealt the officer a violent blow on the head, and in consequence of the injury thus inflicted the officer had been under the care of the doctor. Prisoner was taken to the police station by the officer with assistance. —Prisoner was also charged with assaulting a young man named Thomas Kilsbaw, on the 7th September of last year. To this charge he pleaded guilty.—Kilshaw stated that on the date in question he was walking along Liverpool-road when the prisoner walked up to him, commenced to pick a a quarrel, and then struck him two violent blows on the face, breaking his jaw bone.—lnspector Wood said Kilshaw was in a very bad state for a long time.—Superintendent Johnston said the prisoner had 16 convictions recorded against him —He was fined IN. and costs, or 14 days, for being drunk; £5 and costs for the assault on the police, or two months' imprisonment; and £2 and costs for the assault on Kilshaw, or one month's imprisonment—altogether £9 2s. Bd., or the terms of imprisonment, which will take effect one after the other. THEFT OF IRON AND FOULTRY.—JohnGaskeil, Ecclesten- street, was charged with stealing a quantity of old iron in December, 1880.—Charles Sutherland, 51, Cropper's Hill, foreman joiner, in the employ of Mr. E. A. Pemberton, said that about let December he saw the iron produced in Tal- bot-street, a portion of the iron being sunk in the ground. He knew the prisoner, who came to him about that date, and asked if M. Pemberton would sell him the iron. Wit- ness said that very likely he would, and nothing more passed betwee/them.—Alice Ward, wife of Ellen Ward, marine store dealer, deposed to buying the iron for 4s.— PriSoner was sent to prison for a month. Prisoner was then charged with stealing two hens and two cocks, value 10s., the property of George Houghton, beerseller, Liverpool- road, Eccleston, on the 4th January.—Prosecutor deposed to seeing the poultry safe on the night in question, but on the following morning four out of the eleven were missing. Prisoner had two glasses of beer with some friends in the kitchen, and two or times during the night went outside into the back yard.—John Crane, a carter, residing next door to the beerhouse said he heard the screaming of poultry, and he put his head out of the window and saw prisoner with a hen in his hands. Prisoner offered it to bim, but witness refused to take it. Prisoner then went away.—On this charge prisoner was sent to prisbn for a month. THREATENING TO THROW A. BEERSELLER INTO THE CANAL.—James Sutton and John Kennedy, Eccleston, were charged with using threats towards Joseph Giles, beer- seller.—Complainant said that defendants were in the habit of annoying him and obstructing his doorway, because he, a short time ago, refused to supply them with beer. They also threatened to throw him into the canal, and he was afraid of them.—Defendants, not appearing, warrants were issued for their apprehension.

VACCINATION CASES.—John Slowey, Rainford, was sum- moned by Martin Tunstall, vaccination officer, for neglect- ing to have his child, which was over 12 months old, vaccinated. Fined is. and costs.—Hugh Sephton, Eccles- ton, summoned for a similar offence. Mr.- Kirkman said he did not know that the child was not vaccinated until that morning, as no certificate had been sent to him. Defen- dant said she did not receive, the certificate from the doctor (Dr. Ricketts) until that morning. Withdrawn.— Michael McGhee was also summoned for a like offence. Defendant's wife said the child had been in a delicate state of health, but no medical certificate having been obtained, a fine of Is. and costs was inflicted.—John Jones, Vilndle, was summoned for a like offence. Mr. Kirkman said that the defendant (who did not appear) had conscientious objec- tions against his child being vaccinated, and he asked for a fine and costs in this case. Fined Is. and costs.—James Hayes, Sutton, fined Is. and costs.—Benjamin Sutton, was also summoned. Defendant said the child had been vaccinated twice but not successfully, and he intended taking the child that afternoon. The case was adjourned.— Similar summonses were taken out against Henry Kells, Patrick Dunlevy, and Mathias Rostock, Windle, but these were withdrawn.

COST OF RESISTING THE POLICR.—Wii iatn ThOMASOII, of Warrington, was charged with resisting the police on the 22nd January, at Bold. P.C. Wilson said a disturbance was going on near a public-house at Bold and he was taking one of the men into custody when the prisoner endeavoured to prevent him: He had some drink in him but was not drunk. He received prison( r from the Warrington police on Monday night. Superintendent Johnston read a list, which he had received from the Warrington police, of 13 convictions against the prisoner.—He was fined £2 and costs or one month's imprisonment.

RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIRCUIT TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. On Monday a meeting in connection with the Halton- road branch of this society was held in the Mill Brow school-room. The Rev. 11. Valentine presided, and amongst these present were Messrs. John Simpson, T. Simister, and C. Garnett. The CHAIRMAN thought it needed no argument to con- vince them that intemperance was still in their midst. He referred to the opinion of several judges and doctors, who stated that a great proportion of the crime and distress in the country was due to intemperance. They had, however, no need to go to anyone to learn that fact, for the blighting effects of intemperance were to be found everywhere. He meilioned several cases which had come under hi a own notice of families who hid been ruined through the use of alcoholic liquors, and said he thought the drinks he evil bad to b a s seuvme erd y such gigantic proportions as to demand the attention of everyone ;goG si :RhNorr T caredbelfioery believed s in country.intoxicating pernicious, and it was impossible to exaggerate the evils arising from the use of them. When they considered that about 60,000 of their countrymen died every year from the effects of drink, he thought they were not to be blamed for trying to suppress the traffic in it. He argued that tie effect of alcohol was to weaken the will ; and anyone in the habit of taking it, however moderately, could not be con- sidered entirely safe. It was a popular delusion that alcoholic drinks were good in nearly every complaint flesh was heir to; but almost all the leading medical authorities agreed that in many cases it was hurtful. He thought the facilities for drinking were far too great. Many women bad acquired the habit of drinking through the medium of the grocer; and it was the duty of all to to exert their strongest efforts for the suppression of such a traffic. He did not wish to do away with the public-house. but to convert it into a place for the entertainment of travellers, and one ' where the working man could spend a profitable evening. If this were done, a large portion of the evil would be swept away. Mr. JOHN SIMPsoN spoke of the important duties which devolved upon parents in the training of their children. It was very likely that a child who had been brought up in the principles of total alistinence would coutinue an abstainer when he becamp a man, while, on the other hand, it was possible that the habit would grow upon the man who had been accustomed to the use of drink in childhood. div.head: 'WARRINGTON POLICE CASES.
div.p: 'WARRINGTON POLICE CASES.
MoNtavr.—Before Councillor John Croakld and Councillor Fairclough.

7Wet END DRINEING.—Martha 'Corns, charged wiala being drunk in Bridge-street on Saturday night, was tens tenced to 14 days' imprisonment —Andrew Duffy was fined 10s. and costs.—Martin Leonard was ordered to pay the ewes of the court, 4s. 61, for similar conduct.—A fine of 10s. was imposed on Richard Weaver fov a like offence.— Jane Ford was mulcted in the sum of Ss. for being drunk in Orford-lane on Sunday night. She was found laid un- conscioas in a pool of water by Sergeant Spinks, who stated that she would soon have died had he not found her.—Wm. Lloyd was charged with being drunk in Carta-right-street at one o'clock on Sunday morning, and also 'with assaulting his wife, Sarah Jane. P.C. Hennessy paaved the charge of drunicennesa—Prisoner's wife did not wiah to be bard with prisoner, but he "teemed mad " when he had "drink in him."—la sister of last witness said the prisoner had Mused his wife shamefully and had struck her on the face with a utensil so hard that she " thought she was killed, for a few minutes." (Langhter.) The Bench considered this a bad case and fined the prisoner :Ws. and costs or, in default, a month's imprisonment. He was also bound over to keep the peace for six months.—Richmd -Jackson pleaded guilty to a charge of drunkenness in Crcrssley-street on the lith ult., and was fined bs. and costs. Pnovarez LANCITAAN.—Thomts Wilson, a -young man, was summoned for using obscene and profane language at Market-gate, on the previous Wednesday. ;P.C. Hitchon gave evidence in seaport of the charge amd.defendant was tined 2s. 6d. A VarmanT.--John Smith, a saddler, was charged with beiag a vagrant and sleeping in a closet in Litton's-row, on Saturday night—P.C. Chantler said there had been frequeraa complaints from the inhabitants of Litton-street about the prisoner sleeping on their premises.--;Prisoner was die- charged to give him a chance to reform. linnamt (N, THN FACTORY Act.—Thomas Robinton, fustian cutter, was summoned for having, on the 10th empleved a young person beyond the hour of seven o'clock in the evening, and also with employing a young person under the age ef 16 years for more than four days without having obtained a certificate.— Captain W. 0. Meade-Kieg, Her Majeety's inspector of factories, said the regulations as to the employment of women and young per- sons in non-textile factories applied to fustian mattes, and the hours of employment must be between the hours of six and six, or seven and seven, but, whichever period was selected, it mutt :be stated on the abstract of the Act re- quired to be hung up on the premises. In defendant's workshop the times of employment were fixed from seven to seven, but the evidence would show that work was con- tinned on the night of the 10thcs late as midnight. It was not for him to anticipate the defence that would be set up, but if it was contended that work was continued during pro- hibited hours without the knowledge or order of the defen- dant, it was his duty to submit that such a defence was of no value. It was stated in the 91st section of the Act that workers in A factory or workshop, whether for wages or not, are deemed to be employes as those who are working for daily wage.—Patrick Mullen, occupier of the Star and Garter Inn, Friars Green, said defendant's shop was over his house. On the night of the 10th inst., at about eleven o'clock, he was disturbed by a noise in the workshop, and his wife went to ask the reason of it, and see if they were working. A boy came to the door, but as they got no satis- factory answer he went for A policeman. Inspector ,Proffit said that, from infbrmation received from the last witness, he went to the shop, but found the room in darkness, and the door locked. He received no answer to his inquiries, add he left telling last witness he would call again in about an hour. At 12-25 he paid another visit withT.C. Powell, and heaaw alight. A young man named John Buckley was working, and on searching the premises he found a young girl hiding under a frame.—By Mr. Moore: Mr. Robinson was not there.— Caroline Bradford stated that all thr hands, about 16, walked on the night in question until 10-20. Butterworth was cut- ting when the inspector was heard ascending the stairs, but the light was put out, and she hid herself under a frame. The gas was re-lighted.—By Mr. Moore: Defendant lets us work after hours every Thursday night. He didn't tell us to work. I orITI 14 years of eige, and have been employed there over twelve months.-atdr. Moore saioke• of the excellent character of the defendant, who, he said,did not know the gir was in the shop. He pleaded guilty to employing the girl without a certificate, but had been under Om impression that 14 years was the age.—Mary Parry, daughter of the defen- dant, said she locked the shop up at seven 'clock, and took , the key to the house of Mrs. Roach, where it was usually left. Her father left the shop about a quarter to seven. All the hands left at seven o'clock, and she did not know that anybody was left behind. The two who were found in must have been,hiding under the steps. She never went back to the premises.—The Beach thought the evidence given by the girl te be true, and they were also of opinion that late hours had been worked on other nights besides the one in dispute. It was theird-aty to make an example of the case and defendant would he fined £2 and costs in each case. Mr. Moore asked that defendant should be allowed time to pay the fine; it was a very heavy one.—Mr.Crosfield: These cases are difficult to find out and to prove, and we think it our duty to visit them severely.—Mr. Moore: It is more difficult to disprove than to prove. (Laug:iter.)—Defendant was allowed a month to pay the money. TuEsnax.—Before Councillor ,Eroadbent.

CIARGE OF VAGRAFTCY.—James Babbitt (16) and Geore McKenna (16) were brought up charged-under the Vagrancy Act with being on a siding of the London and North- Western Railway Company, at Bank Quay, at 8-45 ori the previous night, withlntent to commit a felony. Prisoners were seen by Detective-inspector John Cleaver walking round and under the trucks at the goods station. He went to them, bat es they could-not give a satisfactory explanation as lo why they were therete gave them in costody.—Mr. Hunt remarked that the poisoners had been charged with steal- ing some cakes from the cocoa rooms, in Parker-street, but the occupier declined to take out a warrant. There had been some goods stolen fromithe Central Station in a very glaring manner. The inspector observed that theiprisoner Babbitt had been found eleepirtgdu carriages very often.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoners were ripe for anything, and had done much damage to empty property in Parker-qtreet. Babbitt was a very daring youth.—Mr. Broadbent remarked that public property must be,protected, and committed the pri- sonerkto prison for 14 days. DANGEROI7B PHAWACTHR.—Joe Joe, nooloured man, was charged with being in the dwelling-housoof Peter Letcham, brashmaker, 30, Orford-street, at 12-10 thismorning, for the purpose of committing afelony.—The prosecutor left home at 11-10 on Monday night to meet his wife, fastening the door with a drop latch and the lamp burning. In the street he met the prisoner who eaid he had nowhere to sleep; and prosecutor gave him a halfpenny. When prosecutor returned home about 12 o'clock the icloor was locked and the light extinguished, and after trying.to gain an entrance for sometime the prisoner came and opened the door. "Beg,your pardon" said the black apparition. "let me go and I will give you all tbe,meney I have." Prosecutor bad missed no property.— P.C. Cbantler deposed to opprehending the 'prisoner. He found tisl. in his pocket, le., in his clogs, and did. in the lining of his trousers. He also found a kind of begging letter upon him. He threatened to take the life ,of the pro- secutor, who he said he should know again.--FPrisoner had it appeared tried to get into another house about an hour previously, giving the woman ..of the house a severe fright. —Mm :Broadbent considered it a suspicious case, and sen- tenced prisoner to 14 days' imprisonment.
RUNCORZ Scnoot, BOARD.--The monthly meetr:ng was not held on Wednesday, haviug*,been postponed oneweek.

MATCH 1313 TWEEN WARRINGTON ATI:METRE. —OR Saturday afternoon, a foot racelor £5O took place at the Abbey Hey 'ark, Gorton, near 'Manchester, between T. Dagnall and L. Harrison, both ,af Warrington. ,A large number of Warrington and Liverpool men pot in an ;appear- ance to witness the race, the distauce being one mile. CONaanT AT LATCHFORD.—Itt aid .of the funds of !ice Latchford cricket club, a concert wal given in the National school 'room, Wastelane, Latchford, on3donday evening, at which there was a good attendance. The programme wag el a miseeillaneous aaracter, and the vocalists and instru- mentalists acquitted themselves in a n3anner which showed they were possessed ef ability of no sneanorder. The follow- ing took past :—Miss ,Riley, Miss Wallington, Messrs. J. ,Reynolds, E. Reynolds, F. Reynolds, John White, Rev. T. P. Williamson, Jenkins, Price, and Cooper. Readings were given by the Mayor and Mr. Due. The usual votes of tlyinke were accorded, and the concert was concluded 16 the singing of the National Anthem.

SER'ICE OF &ONG AT •VALTOEL—Despite of the weather being bitterly colt!, a capital audience muetered Id the pretty chapel beeonging o the Wetleyan Methodists deaomination, at Halton, for the ,purpose of hearing a capital service of song known as " T,he Mayflower." The Bev. Bateman gave the connective readings, in a tone which Ivo rather moriotonious. The children belonging to the SuodaY school, who formed the choir, mustered about 80, and went through their difficult task very well, with the exception of a slight break down in "They werc weak and craven headed, and the singing of " Home," sweet home," which was .only indifferently given. Much credit is due to Mr. Davies for the manner in which he discharged the duties of conductor, and the labour which had evidentlyibeen bestowed upon HA littie ones. The solo parts were given very fairly by Miss Edwards and Mr. Roe. Mr. Pilling, as organist. The dramatic and spiried of anner Bolton in, whichac e d some of the pieces, Eueh as "Hoping on," "Land ahead,' awl "On to the field," were given by the children, was worthy of much praise. Of course it was hardly to be expected that the youthful choir would be quite equal to dealiag with a piece like that where the approach of the Indiaus is described, but, on the whole, they managed it very well. In describing the persecution of the Pilgrims before their departure in the good vessel Speedwell, Mr. Bateman said, "We live in happier times, when the Church of England holds out the hand of fellowship to sill who love our Lord Jesus Christ." Some of our readees may be a little inclined to differ with this wide sweeping Statement. No charge was made for admission, but at the close a collection was made.

div.p: THE , EXAMINER, SATURDAY IVIARCH 5, 1881.
FRODSHAM AND FRODSITAM LORD-
SHIP SEWERAGE SCHEME. LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.

A Local Government Inquiry was held in the 'Down Hall, Frodsham l yesterday, by Mr. Samuel Joseph Smith, to receive evidence of any person interested in the appor- tionment of expense of constructing sewerage works between the townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship, which had been appealed against by the overseers of the said townships. There were zresent, besides the Inspector, Messrs. H. Linaker (clerk to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority), IV. H. Linaker (assistant clerk), H. Bancroft (engineer), Dr. Bride (tnedicul officer of health), James Farrington (in- spector of nuisances), James Andrews and Thomas Davies (overseers cf Frodshain), Robert Andrews (assistant over- seer), Ralph Bate (overseer of Frodsham Lordship), Samuel Aston (assistant overseer), Charles Reynolds, J.P., Rev. F. F. Edmunds; Messrs. John Ashton, James Rigby, C. E. Linaker, :John Challoner, Thomas Andrews, S. Spencer, F. Rigby, Henry Tiley, Thomas Riley, Joseph -Cunnah, G. Gorst, Thomas Roberts, William Youd, Thomas Cooper, Henry IT °rater, Peter Warburton, Thomas Jones; Thomas Hough, James Peicival, Thomas Lewis, R. E. Walford, Thomas Wright, J. W. Bothwell, GreorgeWarburton, Samuel Walker, J. E. Bat e. John Wilkinson, Sprouse, Peter Riley, Henry Davies, Sm. The Clerk to the Authority (Mr. H. Linaker) read the notice of inquiry froni the Local Government Board, and also the apportionment made by the Authority, and which had been served on the overseers of the townships of Frodsham and Frodsharn Lordship, from which it appeared that the sum of £3,294 16s. 4d. had been charged to Frodsham, and £585 18s. 86. to Frodsham Lord- ship, the total cost being £3,880 15s. Ocl. The proportion chargeable to Frodsham for land and outfall works being four-fifths, and one-fifth -to Frodsham Lordship, each township being charged with the actual cost of sewers to be constructed in the respective townships. Mr. Bancroft stated, in answer to the Inspector, that cer- tain sewers in the township of Frodsham bad been increased in size to provide for the sewage from sewers to he con- structed in Frodsham Lordship, and stated that, in his opinion, the township of Frodsharn Lordship shonld be charged with the increased cost, which be estimated at £176. It subsequently transpired that certain sewers in Frodsham Lordship would receive the sewage from certain parts of Frodsham Township, when Mr. Lewis and other Frodsham Lordship ratepayers contended that a portion of the ccst of such sewers should be borne by Frodsham. The Inspector sad that it was only fair, if Frodsham Lordship contributed towards sewers used in Frodsham, that the same principle should apply on the opposite side, and remarked that it was the old story of "get as much out of each other as you Tan." Mr. Challoner suggested another route for sewers in Fred- sham Lordship, and pointed the suggested line on the map, when it was decided that the matter be left for a subsequent conference with the engineer. Mr. Robert Andrea's, assistant overseer, explained, on be- half of the Frodsham Overseers, that in their appeal they applied for the ,cost of the outfall works to be divided equally between Frodsham and Frodshain Lordship. Mr. Bancroft stated that theapportionment had been made on the population, and not on the rateable value. Mr. Ashton asked if the Inspector would make a note of the rateable value of the respective townships. The Inspector made a note of the point raised, and the proceedings terminated.
WIDNES PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. —There was no meeting of the members of this society on Wednes- day, owing to there not being sufficient members in atten- dance to form a ,quorum.

EVAY Ott IVIVSIC AT ItnncortN..—On Monday night Mr. John HuHord delivered an essay on " Music," at the weekly meeting of the Ellesmere-street Mutual Improvement Class. There was a large number of members present. Mr. E. Gandy presided. A discussion followed the reading of ,the paper, which was taken part in by the Rev. J. Billingtoo, Messrs. 'Cordon Jones, T. Morres, and F. Clarke. YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION, RIINCOR-V.— On Thursday, the annual soiree of this association took place in Bethesda Schoolroom. The proceedings com- menced with tea, tables for which had been kindly given by Mesdatnee T. Hazlehurst, G. S. Hazlellurst, R. Shaw, and C. Garnett, and Messrs. C. W. Hazlehurst, T. Norman, J. Johnson, and Z. Dobson. The tea was got up under the superintendence of Mr. William Shaw, of the Mersey Mis- sion, and was assisted by an efficient staff of lady workers. After tea, Mr. Robert Shaw, president of the association, took the-chair; and a good programme was creditably gone through, comprising glees by the Brunswick Glee Party, (with Miss Norman as accompanist), songs, instrumental music, and recitations. The glees sung were, "Softly falls the moonlight," "Come, celebrate the May," and "Wight, lovely night." Miss Wright sang "Caller Herrin'" and "We met:" She also took part in the duet, "Matrimony," with Mr. Moil is, which created great amusement. Miss Jones was very successful in her song, "The blue Alsatian mountains"; and Miss Horton sang" Hope's fairy belle "in a charming manner. Mr. Dean, a new "basso," gave "Rocked in the cradle of the deep." Mr. John Pownall was hardly his . usual self in "Tne white squall," hut was in much better fosm in "-Simon, the cellarer," and well de- I served the encore he received. Mr. R. W. Pierpoint played two cornet solos with his usual skill, being accompanied on the opipnotoite by Miss A. Pierpoint. The first,solu -was selected/from Donizetti's "La title du regiment," and -was a fine effort. The second was Nicholson's "Hurricane," and the" triple-tonguing" it introduced was wonder/0y well executed, and reeeived an encore. Mr. Pierpoint responded with-" When other lips," from "Maritana." Besides accom- panying the songs with her accustomed ability, Miss Jukes Performed a solo on the pianoforte. The account of the proceedings would be incomplete without a reference to the fine rendering of the recitations, "John Maynard" and "The wreck of the Hesperus," by Mr. Edward Rhodes. He was recalled after the latter piece, and gave Mrs. 'Hemans' "Casablanca" in response.

RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.—The weekly sitting of this society took place on Tautlay, in Bethesda schoolroom. The Speaker (Mr. Thos. Handley) took .hiseeat at-S O'clock, and there was a fair attendance of members and strangers.—The member for Birkenhead asked the Foreign Secret..ry, in the absence of the ,Colonial Secretary, whether it was true that her Majesty'c Govern- ment had offered terms of peace to the Boers in the Trans- vaal.—The `Foreign Becretary replied that the British were not in the habit of offering terms of peace, but of receiving them.; and they would he willing to listen to any reason- able proposal in the direction of peace.—The Leader of the Opposition asked the Indian Secretary if it was the inten- tion of thet Government to give up Candahar.—The Indian Secretary saw no reason to alter the course laid down in his speech during the debate on the address.—The Leader of theeOppositisn in a vigorous manner moved the adjourn- ment of the House, and complained of the unsatisfactory mannerin which it was the habit of responsible officers of the Crown to answer questions put to them from the 'Oppo- sition. He .then opened up the whole question of the Liberal policy with regard to the retention or otherwise of Candahar,and quoted the authority of the military officers in favour of its retention.—The Foreign Secretary elo- quently defended the action a the Government.—The member for Nottingham and the member for Bir- kenhead -spoke on the Opposition, and the Prime Minister, Home Secretary, and Irish Secre- tary on the Ministerial side. In, with- drawing the motion, the Leader of the Opposition announced his intention of raising the quection at some future time.— The member for Halifax moved the following resolution— " That it is expedient that all legal restrictions which at present debar females, otherwise legally qualified by law, from serving as members of Parliament and engaging in professional pursuits, or any other employment whatever, be removed.—The motion was introduced in a neat speech, which was well received.—The member for Nottingham seconded the resolution.—The member for Stoke spoke in favour of the motion, theugla his remarks were of a some- what satirical character.—The member for Dudley (Liberal whip) spoke against, and the Colonial Secretary in favour.— The debate was adjourned en the motion of the member for Carlisle.—The Leader of the Opposition gave notice to ask the Foreign Secretary whether he could harmonise his extra- parliamentary utterances with his continuance in office as 'Chief Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs ?—The Prime Minister asked the'right hon..questioner if he was prepared to lay before the House the extra-parliamentary utteranoes upon which he based his interpellation.—The Leader of the Opposition said he was quite prepared to do so.—The House then adjourned. BEWSEY ROM) WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WARRINGTON. A gathering of a social nature was held en Saturday, the 2fithinst. By the kindness of a few gentlemen, the mem- bers of the choir were invited to meet a few guests at supperdn the large room adjoining the above chapel, when ample jsstice was done to•the good things provided. After supper, in the absence of the superintendent, the Rev. J. Agar Beet presided, and interesting addresses wore delivered Ly the chairman, the Rev. T. E. Brackenbury, Messrs. Hayward, Biddle, and Horton. The very efficient and practical services rendered by the choirduring the past year were heartily acknowledged, and the hope was expressed that the kinctiy relation existing between the choir, minis- ters, and congregation might long he sustained. ne desire of the choir to ,promote the work of God is fully testified by the fact that several of them have evinced their willingness to help the mission at Wesley Hall, Silver-street, every Sunday evening at the close of the public services in the sanctuary. Nothing attracts the masses so much as really good singing, and he service rendered to God and the church by an active willing choir in this way cannot be estimated. In the ,course of the evening the followieg anthems, under the leadership of Mr. Wood, the organist. were very creditably siting:—" In Jewry is God known," "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills' "" Praise the Lord, 0 Jerusalem," "Call to remembrance, 0 Lord," "Sing unto the Lord a new song." After the passing of the usual votes of thanks, which were responded to by Messrs. Wood, Bal- low, Houghton, and Mercer, a very enjoyable evening was brought to a close.

The weekly meeting of the House was held in the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday evening, when the right hon. member for Montrose presided. There was a very fair attendance of members on both aides of the House, and also of "strangers," the latter including a number of ladicq.

THE ORDER OF TT:MINERS. • The ri4/t hon. member for Noaveics, in the absence of the Leader of the Opposition, asked the Prime Minister if the Government could and would give the order of business for the remaining nights of the session. The PRIME Almsnaireplied that the bill for that night was the one to be brought forward by the hon. member for WoodstoCk—the bill to abolish actions far breach of promise of marriage. When that bill had beet disposed of, the hon. member for Sheffield would bring forward his bill to abolish flinging in the army and navy. The Goverment bill to close public-houses on Sundays would follow, and then there was a motion to abolish hereditary peerages. Those were four subjects for the five nights, and he did not think it was likely they would be able to do more than that this session. The Government would take their stand on the Licensing •Bill they would themselves bring in, or lithe House passed a resolution for the abolition of the House of Peers, the 'Government would have to resign.

div.head: HON AND METAL TRADES.
div.p: HON AND METAL TRADES.

BIRMINGHAM, Thursday.—The iron market continues de- pressed, except in the case of common sheets for galvanising and conStructive ironwork, and in the latter competition is so severe that prices approach an unremunerative point. Prices generally are weaker than a week ago. Common bars, angles, and tees are changing hands to a limited ex- tent for manufacturers' immediate requirements. Stocks of pig are accumulating, and production is again curtailed. ' The secretary to the operatives' section of the Wage, Board has given notice to re-open the question of wages, in which' the men seek an alteration in their favour upon the ground that the sliding scale as at iiresent fixed compares unLivour- ably with the wages scale of the northern district. The application will doubtless be strenuously resisted by the ironmasters, many of whom have as much as they can do to contend with circumstances as they now.exist.

• LONDON, Thursday.—Copper easier; good ordinary Chili, £6O 10i. to £BO 7s. 6d. cash; closing £do 7s. 61 to £6O 12s. 6d. cash. Tin weaker; fine foreign 'sold at £B7 10s. down to £B7 cash, and £B7 10s. to £.BB 10s. forward. Spelter, £l5 15s. to £l6. Lead, English, £l5 to £l5 7s. 66. Scotch pig iron, 48s. 96. to 495. cash. MANCHESTEII.—Extreme dulness still characterises the iron trade of this district. Not only is there little or no de- mand in the market for pig iron, but there is considerable difficulty in getting consumers who have bought to take their deliveries. The, recent stoppage of operations at a large number of the finished iron works in the district has also thrown a considerable quantity of iron upon the hands of makers, and sales are being pressed in the market at very low prices. For Lancashire pig iron the inquiry continues exceedingly small, and the iron going away from the works is almost entirely on account of old contracts. Nominally the quotations for delivery into the Manchester district re- main at 475. 61 for foundry aad 465. 6d. for forge, less 21, but local iron could be bought at per ton under these figures. Lincolnshire, Derbyshire, and Middlesborough irons are all being offered in this district at under makers quota- tions, which are now purely nominal. In the finished iron trade there is no material change, except that; if anything, prices are not quite so stiff, transactions in bars being re- ported at under £6 per ton for delivery into the Manchester district. In the engineering and machine making branches of the trade there is still an absence of any general activity, the only department in which any large amount of work has recently been given oat being amongst locomotive builders and makers of railway plant.

WIDNES PARISH CHDRCH.-011 Ash Wednesday, there was a service at this churkh in the morning, when the Rev. J. Wright Williams preacled. In the evening the Rev. W, R. Worthington, Brombio' Pool, and late of Runcorn Pari3h Church, conducted service.

Mn. J. G. Moblnman M.P. for Warrington, Col. Blackburn, and Sir R. Cross, voted with the Govern- ment on Tuesday on the motion to declare the Peace Pres- ervation Bill (Ireland) Bill " urgent " and also afterwards with the majority for granting leave to bring in the Arms Bill.

THE WIGAN PETITION.—The Mayor of Wigan has been officially informed that the petition presented against the return of Mr. F. S. Powell for that borough will be heard on the 23rd of this month. The petition alleges that the elec- tion should be voided on the ground of briber', undue in- fluence, and treating; but doas not claim the seat on behalf of the Liberal candidate.

HILTON MUTUAL LLPBOTB.MENT SOCINTIL—On Mon- day, Mr. G. Leathwood read a paper entitled, "Man's free agency," to a large attendance of members. Mr-Leathwood tried to prove by means of the Bible that man is a free agent. The members seemed to fully endorse the opinions of the essayist. The following gentlemen spoke :—Messrs. R. Hughes, W. H. I mdbury, S. Barrow, and A. D. Davies. The Rev. L Bateman presided.—Com.

Tan EMPRESS •Orr AIISTRIA. WITH THE CHESHIRE Hooxps.--The Empress of Austria had a grand day's sport with the Cheshire hounds on Wednesday, and the country gone over was sufficient to try the mettle of the stoutest hunters. Soon after three, the hounds brought her into Whitchurch, and having called at the Victoria Hotel, she got with the dogs again, and finished about five o'clock. Some of the runs were remarkable ones, the foxes going with great gameness. WESTON POINT GLEE CLUB—The members of this club, asslst4 by other friends, gave their third entertainment of the season in the Weaver schoolroom. Mr. L. Rosenberg, the hon. sec. of the Glee Club, presided. The room was filled in every available spot, and numbers were unable to gain admission. The programme was creditably sustained by the various performers, and gave entire satisfaction.

..,„ 11,13NOONN AND THE ARIAN NoventiorT.—There is at present no ammunition at the Drill Hall, Runcorn, wherel about 150 rifles belonging to the volunteers are usually kept. The arms have, during the past few days been at Birming- ham, for the purpose of being browned, and it was expected that they would arrive in the town yesterday. We under- stand that the rifles will be placed in the armoury until to- (lay , Saturday). when each man will take charge of the arm belonging to him. fast night a guard was on duty at the hall, as some strange reports affecting Feoianism have been circulated in the town ciliate. THU PAILISH CHIJIICE ENTERTAINMFCNTS AT WIDNES.— The eleventh of this series of entertainments was given in the Waterloo-road schoolroom, on Tuesday evening, and I well attended. The Vicar, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, presided. With the exception of a humorous reading from "Andy Andy" given I?.y Mr. W. Treacy, jun., the entertain- ment was entirely =mica. Three es were given by the choir The performances of the Runcorn Handbell Singers Was a decided feature of the entertainment. Songs were given by Mr. Cross, Mrs. White, and Mr. .1. B. Imison, and a piano- forte solo by Mrs. Rumsey. Mr. and Mrs. Rumsey also gave a pianoforte duet. Messrs. Wilkinson and Imisou also Bangs duet. , A WOMAN BURNED-TO BEATE AT WIDNES.—OR Monday afternoon, an inquest was held at Whiston workhouse, by . Mr. Barker, deputy coroner, on the body of a married woman named Ellen Rehoe, the wife of a chemical labourer, named John Kehoe, of 18 Tra,vis-street, Widnes. On Wednesday week, whilst deceased was attending to some potatoes on the fire at home, herclothescaught lire. Her screams attracted two neighbours who went into the house and put out the 'flames. The woman was attended by Dr. Cooper, but after- wards conveyed to the Workhouse, where she died on the following Friday. Miss Leatham' nurse at the Workhouse, deceased's husband, and two neighbours having given evi- dence, the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUN. oonx.—The weekly meeting, of this society was held on Wednesday, in the Brunswick Schoolroom. Mr. T. Simister, president of the society, occupied the Chair, and there Was a good attendance of members. A most interesting and instructive paper was read by Mr. Keohler, of Higher Run- corn, with the title "How to spoil a Mutual Improvement Society—a tplayfuL paper addressed to all unconscious spoilers of such societies." The following rules were laid down, and the way they might be made to work was huntourously set forth by the essayist. 1. Attend seldom, and when you do, come in late. 2. If you consent to write a paper, select old and well-worn sub- lents, and carefully 'avoid all new topics. 3. When you stand up to make any remarks on a paper, speak very long. 4. Leave everything to be done by 'abler men' than your- selves. The paper was very well received, and at the close a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Keohler. RUNCORN lIQLT TRINITY TOUNG Max's CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—Under the auspices of the above association an interesting and instructive lecture on "The chemistry of flame; its bearings on respiration and ventilation," was delivered by Mr. J. H. Annett (certificated teacher in ex- perimental physics), in Holy Trinity Schoolroom, on the 25th ult. The Rev. W. Robinson presided. Mr. Annett first took the candle as the most primitive and common of all sources of flame. Its flame, he said, might-be considered as the type of all same, being analogous to that obtained from an oil lamp, gas, or a piece of coal. The lecturer then experimented with carbonic acid gas in many different and interesting ways, for the purpose of showing its weight and irrespirable nature, and pointed out the close connection be- tween burning and respiration, and iustanced many deadly effects atising from the inhalation of carbonic acid gas. He showed, by experiments with candles, in varions ways and arrangements and under various conditions, the effects of ventilation and non-ventilation. A cordial vote of thanks to the lecturer brought the proceedings to a close. INQUESTS AT NVIDNEEL—On Tuesday afternoon. Mr. j irker, deputy coroner for the county, held two inquests at j the Mersey Rotel, Widnes. The first was on the body of 1 Edwin °swirl., labourer, of Cholmondley-street, who died suddenly on Saturday morning, whilst in bed. The evi- dence showed that deceased was skilled in herbs, and on the ; previous day he was engaged hawking medicine of his own composition, at Xorthwich. On his return home, he had a hearty supper and went to bed. On Saturday morning, about seven o'clock, as his wife was getting up, she heard him making a gurgling sound in his throat, and a doctor was sent for, but before his arrival ,deceased was dead. He had complained of a cough ' for seine abort time.—The next inquiry was as to the death , of a man named Isaac Hatton, aged 64 years, captain and owner of the at Lynx, of Winsford, who was found dead J ma boat, which was drifting down the river, by Joseph • Hignett, a,Widnes flatman. On the previous Friday the j vessel, of iirhich deceased was captain, was lying off Widnes, and about six o'clock in the evening he went ashore to Duke's-pier. Runcorn. Some time later he was seen sculling the boat to his own vessel by a man named Thomas Holland, and when observed he was at some distance from his Own flat. He was not seen again until he wit; found lying in Vae bottom of the boat by ffignett. The oar which de- ceused had been using was missing.— The jury returned a veract of "Death from natural causes" in each case.

The How SECRETARY, replying to the member for Evesham, said he had not been able to ascertain the truth of the allegatiorkthat the rectors of Falmouth had the privilege of levying it rate upon all rateable property in the town. If it were true, he would like to know how it was done, because he would like to try it on himself. (Laughter.) He fancied the hon. gentleman must be the victim of a hoax—(laugh- ter)—and that there must be some Conservative in disguise upon that side of the House 'who had put the hon. member up to ask the question. (Laughter.) The right hon. member for Nonwicrt, in .the absence of the right hon. member for Northampton, asked whether the Prime Minister was prepared to introduce a bill disfranchis- ing the Staffordshire and Irish voters of Warrington in con- sequence of their voting against Sir Gilbert Greenell at the last election—(loud laughter) '•—whether he *as prepared to make a statement to the House respecting the large amount of bribery and corruption carried on in various cathedral and university cities; and also respecting the purity of the Northampton elettion ? The PRIME MINISTER was sorry to find this joking pro- pensity was spreading to such an alarming extent amongst gentlemen opposite. He had certainly no intention to bring in a bill to disfranchise the Staffordshire and Irish voters Of Warrington—(hear, hear)—who, he had no doubt, would come to a better mind some day. (Applause, and loud laughter.) He would be glad to do his very best to conduct them and he had no doubt when they had lived among the people of Warrington long enough they would be converted. (Ironical cheers.) He did not know anything about the Purity ef the Northampton election; but as to the bribery and corruption carried on in various university cities he had not heard yet that MaccleAeld or Warrington were uni- versity cities. (Hear, hear.) ' He thought the bribery and corruption in Macclesfield and Warrington—{The member for Sheffield: No corruption in Warringtoni—were quite equal to what took place in university cities. The HOME SECRETARY in reply to the right lion. member for Drogheda, said it would be admitted that the Artizans' Dwellings Act was a step in the right direction, inasmuch as there was no attempt on the part of the Liberal Government to repel the Act. As to defining the "reasonable amount of satisfaction" the Act had given, he should say a reason- able amount of satisfaction vase reasonable amount of satis- faction. (Loud laughter.) The member for NEWCASTLE-11PON-TYNE asked when the Government proposed to introduce the four measures pro- mised in the Queen's Speech, and whether they had forgotten that according to the rules of the Society the House could ()sly sit five more nights during the session. The PREMIER, having referred to his previous announce- anent of the order of business, said the Government had not forgotten there were only five nights in the session, but they would not be able to bring in all the measures mentioned in ' the Queen's Speech. The measures were mentioned not with a view to introducing them, but because the Govern- ment thought they were subjects which really required legislating upon.._ _

div.head: BREACH_OF PROMI,E or MARRIAGE.
div.p: BREACH_OF PROMI,E or MARRIAGE.

The member for WOODSTOCK, in introducing the "Abolition of Contract to Marry Bill," said in bringing before the notice of the House the most Important subject that had yet engaged their attentien—(laughter)—he was desirous of removing one or two misconceptions which he found prejedicing the minds of many. It was so unusual for an action of breach of promise bf marriage to be brought by a man against a woman that his position might very naturally be misunderstood; and he might be regarded as engaged in a sort of crusade against a supposed privilege peculiar to woman. On the other hand he regarded t• e Bill as one which should be welcomed by the female population of the United Kingdom as a measure of relief and justice. (Hear, bear.) As a matter of law, women were just as liable to be sued for damages as were men ; and as a matter of fact they laid themselves open to litigation more frequently than men did—(laughter)—though consequent upon the generosity of the nobler creation—(laughter)—they did not so frequently suffer the penalty of their breach. (Laughter.) It would be superfluous to point out those facinatitig viva- Cities of temperament, that fond clinging tendency which prompted them to worship all their worshippers with be- wildering promiscuousness; or that sprightly airiness of affection which deceived at once so gaily and so fatally. That was only too apparent, and these circumstances tended to prove that relief would be given by the Bill to women as well asto men and probably to women more than men. He claimed, therefore, to be acquitted from all accusations of eingallantry. He fancied that front some of the clearer- minded—he wis confident that from the most modest and retiring—portion of the gentler sex, they would receive some measure of gratitude for their effort to deliver women from a false position, repulsive to them and galling to men. At the same time he was prepared to admit that consequent upon the proverbial blindness of love—and as the ladies were always loving, blindness must be presumed to be their normal state—women might regard the present state of the law as the proper state, and fear change would affect them prejudicially. It might be, therefore, that the hon. member who intended to mote the rejection of the Bill might be fondled in the soft dalliance of favouritism—(laughter)— but he invited that 'member to imagine for one moment the prospect which the passing ef the Bill would open before him. Freed from all the conventionalities of custom, he might without let or hindrance "prove all things, and hold fast that which was best." In 18711, when the Bill was be- fore Parliament, only one petition was presented against the Bill. and that had only received nine signatures, those of nine ladies. (Laughter.) Its main allegation was "that matrimony was woman's profession, and that therefore they had a right to be compensated for being prevented entering upon it." But this argument was erroneous, and the assumption illogical. A profession ! Vhat a cold-blooded and calculating phrase! If matrimony was nothing better or holier than a profession, then an engagement might be a business con- tract, and its breach cause for damage. But he thought the House would repudiate any such mercantile valuation of an institution designed by Divinity for the good of humanity. (Hear, hear.) Then the assumptiorathat women "have a right to be compensated for being prevented entering upon matri- mony" was fallacious. No one prevented them. The fact that they:were prevented marrying one particular person did did not prevent them entering into matrimony. The world is wide, opportunities were many, and man was still the poor weak fool he ever was. (Laughter.) He contended that a contract which compelled two persons to live to- gether, however incompatible their natures, and however much their former love might be turned to hatred, ought not to be treated like other contracts. He was old-fashioned enough—(laughter)--to believe that love was reason suffi- cient for marriage. (Hear, hear.) When love was absent I no persuasion of friends, no influence of parents, no splendid temptation of fortune, constituted cause enough for the degradation of the holiest ef alliances. (Hear, hear.) When it was discovered that love—the only justification of marriage—was absent, or had been transferred to another, the man or the woman who still strove to drag a reluctant one-time lover to the altar, invoked the retribution of a badly planned life. (Hear, hear.) The change proposed would bring the law of the country into harmony with that of the principal European states. On this question England was behind the times. Nobody would lose by the change except eloquent counsel, speculative attorneys, and news- paper proprietors. (Laughter.) By this BM damages for specific losses might still be claimed in the County Court. It would exhibit very much higher spirit if those who were deserted would follow the spirit of the advice given by Hamlet to Ophelia, "Get thee to a nunnery, go. Or if thou wilt needs marry, marry a fool ; for wise men know well enoegh what monsters you make of them." (Laughter.) It was most ridiculous to invite a jury to estimate the value of wounded feelings. The amounts awarded were materially affected by the eloquence or stupidity of counsel, or by the beauty or the unattractiveness of the plaintiff. (Laughter.) As the law stood, no woman of delicate mind and refined sensibilities would avail herself of it. Wounded feelin 8 outraged affections, and broken hearts did not love to gb'e dragged into the light of day. (Hear, hear.) If need be, the deserted woman would suffer and make no show of her loss; but it was to guard such from tho stigma which pro- claimed to Europe that British beauty needed the inters position of the law to chain her laggard lovers by .her side. (Applause.)

, The right hon. member for KENDAL moved that the bill be reed that day six months. He thought the House would agree with him that the member for Woodstock was entitled to get credit for the courage of his opinions—(hear, hear)_ and for expressing them so publicly and baldly as he bad done. The hon. member informed them he had never had the experience of being "jilted." He was net going to argue that question with him—(loud laughter)—but he would ask the hon. member whether he was expecting an action for breach of premise. (Renewed laughter.) The lion, member did not inform the House on that point. He thought the time bad not yet arrived for legislation on the subject. Were they to disregard the com- pensation that was due to wounded feelings, blighted affec- , tions, and blasted hopes for ever? He said no, most ikcidenly not. The hon. member for Woodstock mentioned

that a petition had been presented to the House of Commons, which was signed by nine women. It would be interesting to know whether those women were of inaependent means. He should imagine they were, and therefore it was a matte) of no moment to them whether those adtions were susiained or abolished. He hoped the House would pause before pass- ing that bill. (Applause.) The member for Srogn-ost-Tranarr thought they would be doing an injustice to the women if the House did not get one or two of them to give their opinion upon the subject. (Hear, hear.) He thought the bill was nothing more or less than free trade in affection. Women had As much right to be considered as men in this matter, and he,thought the bill was a needless interference with legislation. The bill was an unmanly and illegitimate attempt to coerce the female sex. (Laughter.) It was bad policy for any Government to interfere with one of the great powers, and if love was not a great power he did not know what was. (Laughter.) ' If the bill became law a young man would have to sign in- denture.; before apprenticing himself as suitor, or deposit his watch as security for his good behaviour. (Laughter.) He seconded the amendment, and trusted if the bill passed the hon. member for Woodstock would die a withered and lonely bachelor. (Laughter.) The member for Werantattrroar supported the bill. (Oh, and laughter.) He thought it wrong that any woman who had received damages from a man should be allowed to marry another. (Laughter.) It was not reasonable a she had got that which was awarded to her by law as being equal to a husband. (Loud laughter.) The member for Yarixotrrir thought actions for broach of promise of marriage were unjust and undesirable. They mast remember that a bill like the one before the House would have a very great effect epon the country, for it would affect a ver7 large number of people at a very important period of their lives. If the bill was passed it would cause people to look upon ladies with more respect, and to realise the fact that compensation for wounded feelings and that sort of thing, was not to be paid in cash. The bill would tend to do away with matrimonial alliances for money, and cause ladies to look lets upon marriage as it profession. The member for NEWCASTLE-ON-TYNE said the speech of the member.for Woodstock indicated a want of morality. The only strong point was in the last few words from one of our great poets—a new one. How many women the hon. mem- , ber for Woodstock had jilted he did not tell the House, but how many he might jilt on the principle of a new one they could not imagine. He looked upon men who would blight the affections of a woman and cast them to the winds just as caprice might dictate, as men utterly unworthy of the name of men. (Hear, hear.) If a man for the sake of self aggrardisement (as was too often case), would throw a woman overboard and marty another with money, then that man ought to part with some of that money. He did not care whether the lawyers got it, but the man ought to be punished. (Hear, hear.) He would go further and give him corporal punishment. ("Hear," and laughter.) He considered the affection of a true woman was the purest and noblest thing upon earth, and ought to be so revered by every man. He had heard some strange things from the quarter where the hon. member for Warrington sat —(laughter)—but he bad never beard anything so strange before as the statement that pecuniary compensation was equal to a husband. (Laughter.) He entered his protest against the bill.

'The member for SHEFFIELD having spoken in favour of ths amendment, The right hon. member for Nonwrcw supported the bill. as he thought it would take more than golden rivets to heal a broken heart.' As there were two kinds of morality so it seemed there were two kinds of love, and he supported the bill as it would do away with the commercial phase of the question and leave untouched that which could not be bought with gold.

The member for BIRKENHEAD supported, and the member for CARLISLE opposed the bill, as did also the member for NORTHAMPTPNi- who thought all the statutes on the rela- tions between man and woman ought to be repealed. The PREMIER spoke in favour of the bill, and stated that .he thought these actions were really not the proper way to settle these breaches.

The member for Woopsroc'x briefly replied, and on a division being taken the amendment was rejected I;y a majority of 3, the voting bsing-23 for and 31 against. The bill was then put and carried, and the House adjourned.

THE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION. A meeting of the General Committee of the National Liberal Federation was held on Thursday evening in Bir- mingham, Mr. Powell Williams presiding. The recommend- ations of the sub-CoMmittee on the Ballot Act were Con- sidered. They included various arrangements for ensuring secrecy of vote, the omission of the ;provision for taking the votes of illiterates, the omission of a distinctive num- ber on counterfoil, and the prohibition of picketting or stationing agents outside the booths to check the names of those who voted. These recommendations were approved. The meeting then procceeded to consider the Ballot Con- tinuance Act now before oParliament. Resolutions were passed recommending the extension of the hours of polling till eight p.m, and limiting the number of personation agents to one for each candidate at each polling station. A letter was read from Mr. Ashton Dilke expressing con- fidence that thiz wi.! receive full consideration, and pointng to the onmt,* IN't7,an election as an instance of the advantage wlifEe would result tr,.ioihis nlan being adopted. MANCHESTER COMMERCIAL, THURSDAY .—We have had a day of ahnost unmitigated dulness. Sellers have been easier to deal with in Cloth and Yarn. The only market for which we hoar of anything doing is China, and for it the demand is neither general or very large. We have now lost all or more than all we had recovered since last Friday, and the tendency is still against sellers. The main cause is certainly increasing faith in Cotton being abundant. LIVERPOOL COTTON, THURSDAY. Spot: The market has been very feeble all day. Buyers have been very indifferent about purchasing, while holders have shown more desire to sell. Prices have, consequently, been weak and somewhat irregular, and only a limited amount of business has transpired. Official• quotations for American are reduced 1-16 d. Brazils are par- tially 1-ltd easier on the week. The imports and sales for the. week have, so far, about balanced each other; but as a good quantity of Cotton is being forwarded from the quay, the stock has probably been reduced.

SATIIRDAT.—Bpfore Captain Birley and Mr. John Person

ASSAULT ON THE Ilionwer.—William Travis was sum- moned for unlawfully assaulting J. Lythgoo.—Complaintnt was walking on the road from Earlestown to Newton on Saturday night, the 12th inst., when, without any provoca- tion wh tever, he was set upon by the defendant, who knocked him to the ground watt his fist and then. kicked him twice.—Defendant made no defence, and he was fined 40s. and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment. Capt. Birley observed that the Bench were determined to stop these kind of assaults.

A GRIEVOES ASSAULT: EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT.— Edward Jones, a young man, was summoned by Jane Har- rison for unlawfully assaulting her at Newton.—At half- past nine on Tuesday night, the 22ad ult., complainant, who appeared to be about 18 years of age, was on her way home from the print works, accompanied by another girl, when prisoner was obsetved to be following them. He began to tread on the heels of the complainant, who becoming alarmed, commenced to walk quicker, but defendant also quickened his pace. They then' crossed the road, but defendant still followed, at laskseizing the complainant by the throat and e.sking for a kiss. Her companion requested him to desist, as " he was strangling her,' but he paid no heed to her expostulations, threw the complainant to the ground, and got on her chest. The girls then commenced to scream loudly, and the defendant ran away.—lt was elicited by the Bench that the defendant Wag not quite sober. —Defendant remarked that he had nothing to say; and he w'as fined 60s. and costs, or one month's imprisontnent.— The Bench considered this a grievous assault.

TRANSFER.—Mr. Moore' orf. Warrington. applied for the Vmporary transfer of the license of the Hand and Banner public-house from the executors of Ann Unsworth to Mr. Rd. Walmsley,of the Legh Arms.—The application was granted. MOLYNEUX'S ANNUAL PARTY AT EARLESTOWN. This annhal party in connection with the Earlestown Household Stores came off on Monday, at the Earlestown District School, when about 580 partook of an excellent tea. After tea a conctrt was given by the members of the Earlestown Church choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Dorman. The programme which 'was well executed, included a choice selection of songs, duets, trios, glees, part songs, dm. The proceedings closed with a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Moly neux. LECTURE AT EABLEsTow,N.—On Monday, a lecture was delivered on "Hero worshi, p,' in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, by the Rev. J. Travis, of Liverpool. Mr. Hall pres,ided. The lecturer in an instructive and elevat- ing discourse, dealt with the following features :—Hero worship universal—factor in human progress—Greeks, French, and Jingoes—reality wrinkles--.individuality counts one—Beaconsfield, Gladstone, Cobden, Peel—manly pur- poses—candour—religion, politics, and unsel fish nese— Napoleon—self-sacrifice—a great fool—daring—socialism— Garibaldi—nothing succeeds like success—failuro—W. Scott, W. Lawson, Wolsey, Livingstone/Tom Thumb— sensation—hero worship illustrated in the common walks of life, dx. The lecture was listened to with the greatest attention, and at the close a 'warty rote of thanks was given to the rev, gentleman, on the motion of the Rev. Mr. Vaughan, seconded by Mr. Ball, which was humourously acknowledged by the Rev. J. Travis, and the meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman. The proceeds were devoted to the Trust Fund.

NEWTON CHORLL SOCIETY —This society, which num- bers about 50 voices, gave a miscellaneous concert in the Town Hall. Newton-le-Willows, on Tuesday. The room was neatly decorated, and was well filled; the reserved seats containing many of the leading families of the district. The following was the programwm:—Glee, "The cuckoo sings," &c.; song, "If doughty deeds," Mr. S. Swann ; song, Kathleen's answer," Miss S. Rose; glee, "The sands of Dee"; pianoforte selection, "Scotch airs," Mr. W. H. Davies ' • song, "The lady of the lea," Miss A. Appleton; duct, "Mountain streams," Miss Ball and Miss Grac ; song, "The return of the lifeboat," Mr. T. Howard; part song, " Semno,r eve," female voices; song, "Out on the rocks," Miss Wood; glee, " Hunting song." Interval. Glee, "Stay, prithee stay ;" song, "In the gloaming," Mr. Has. kell ; song, "The hay is in the mow," Miss Ball; part song, " A little farm well tilled," Messrs. Howard, Liptrof, Has- kell, Dudgeon, Sephton, and Fairclough ; pianoforte duet, "Chant du Bracconler," Mr. W. H. Davies and Mr. P. Fair- dough; song, "The castle by the sea," Miss Grace; glee, "Come, Dorothy, come ;" part song, "The bird at sea," Misses Grace, M. Ball, E. Fairclough, S. Rose, E. Ball, and A. Wood; song, "A wet sheet and a flowing sea," Mr. T. Hughes; part song, "Night! lovely night ;" fin.,le, " God save the Queen." The songs by the female members of thesociety were undoubtedly rendered with good effect, elicit . • ing hearty encores. Mr. Swann, Mr. Haskell, Mr. Howard, II and Mr. Hughes were also encored. The glees and ,partt songs were fairly rendered, but in the soft passages a II aD of blending was observable. Mr. W. H. Davies as accom- panist, and Mr. P. Fairclougb, conductor, acquitted them- selves with ability.
