POISONING BY GAS BALI-HEATERS. Sir,—A paragraph has recently appeared in your journal respecting the death of Mr. C. E. Deacon, of Anerley, Sur- rey, who was poisoned by the noxious vapours arising from the gas apparatus by which his bath was heated. A Dr. Turner is reported to have stated at the inquest that gas hewers were highly dangerous, and he advised that the use at them should be discortinued. To this sweeping eondem- station wide publicity has been given. I have already received numerous letters from persons who have been aLsemed by it, and I trust therefore you will permit me the sight of a public reply. It is perfectly true that some of the unsOods now in use of heating water for baths by means of gas are not safe. None of the class known as instantaneous water-heaters for baths should be used in any room unless the products of combustion can be perfectly carried away at once by a flue although smalnizes may be safely used in sanlleries and lavatories for heating small quantities of water quickly. They are especially dangerous in bath rooms, which are, as a rule, small and close, and the danger increases with the power of the heater. Although lam a patentee and manufacturer of these instantaneous heaters, I have never used them or recommended their use for baths. This, however, does not warrant a condemnation of all systems, and the one I have adopted for heating baths is such that no danger or unpleasantness can arise from its use. Even in the smallest and most confined bath room without ventilation, the fumes given off by the burner used stein exceedingly small in quantity as to be incapable of musing the slightest harm. I cannot therefore permit Dr. Turner's remarks to pass without protest. It is evident that be has formed his opinion mithout possessing a full know- ledge of his subject, and intending only to condemn the system he knew, has at the same time condemned others which, his remarks prove, he can never have seen.—l am yours respectfully,

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. - The monthly meeting of the Town Council was held in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Present :—The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) in the chair, Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Kean, Harrison, Davies, Chand- ley ; Councillors Broadbent, Sutton, Platt, Barker, Woollen, Woods, Litton, Francomb, Jeans, Bargees, Fairclough, Brown, Greening, Whittle, Greenall. Dixon, Crosfield ; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Charles Cborley (borough treasurer), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). THE REPRESENTATION OP THE RATEPAYIIRS IN TRH COVECIL. Councillor PLATT proposed :"That a petition be _Tem- pered in favour of the 'Municipal Corporation Act .1.18 ts_9) Amendment' Bill, and that the petition be sealed yeah he corporate seal of the borough, ant forvrarded to with mem- ber for the borough for presentation to the House f Com- mons." He said it would last he submitted a motion to the Council—and that motionhe be remembered that in September was confirmed by a majority of about two to one—that t representation of the borough in the Council was at present very unequally distributed, and that it was desirable the same should at the earliest opportunity be readjusted. The matter had to rest there at that time for the reason that, ' there was no adequate means of carrying it out. It could only be carried out by means of a special Act of Parliament which was an expensive proceeding it was not thought ad- visable to take. It was true there was an alternative for effecting a reform of that nature, and that was by means of the Municipal Corporation Act, 1859. But under that Act , action could only be taken that the concurrence of two- thirds of the members of the Council for the time being, and besides that some of the provisions of the Act were open to objection. The consequence was that that Act had been very little made use of since it was passed. Only four boroughs had, taken advantage of it in about 22 years, so that it had been almost a dead letter. Still the necessity arose, as boroughs increased in size, for a revision of the wards, and also the number of councillors apportioned to each ward, because as time went on an arrangement, which might be just and fair at the time a borough was incor- porated, might become very unfair. It was evident then that the means which they had at present for readjusting the matter and effecting a reform in the redistribution of the seats in the Council were not readily available, inasmuch as 'be had shown the Act had been very little made use of since it I was passed. But a Bill had been introduced in the present session of Parliament to amend the Municipal Corporation Act, 1859, with a view to making a re-arrangement of the wards and an alteration in the representation of the borough more easy and less costly, and his pa position was that the Council should present a petition in favour of that Bill. The first clause of the bill was as follows:—" It shall be lawful for Her Majesty from time to time, if to Her Majesty It seems fit, upon application made in manner hereinafter I mentioned, and after such local inquiry, as to Her Mayesty may seem requisite, by Order in Council to do-all or any of the followidg things: namely, to divide any borough into wards; to alter the number of the wards into which any borough is divided; to alter the boundaries of any wards into which any borough is divided, and to determine the boundaries of any new wards created by an order under this Act; to alter the number of councillors of a borough; to alter the number of councillors assigned to any ward, and to fix the namber of councillors for any new ward crested by any order under the Act • to alter the Dumber of alder- men so as to correspond to the altered number of councillors; to make regulations as to the retiring from or continuance in office of the existing councillors and aldermen, or any of them, and such other incidental' provisions as to Her Majesty may seem necessary for carrying the order into effect; and to revoke or alter 'any order previously made under this Act." An alteration might be made in the number of the councillors, and arrangements made to more fairly represent the various wards. The Bill also provided for an alteration in the number of alder- men to correspond with the number of councillors. The application might be made by the Council of the borough, or by individuals being either any number notless than one-thira of the persons who were at the time of the application members of the Council or of the borough, or any number not less tkan one-third of the persons whose names were at the time of the application on the burgess roll of the borough, Sr if such third exceeded two thousand, not less than two thousand. The application might be made by means of a petition to Her Majesty sent to or left at the Privy Council office. The Privy Council would cause hotice of the petition, if made by individuals, to be given forthwith to the Council of the borough. and if it was thought fit to proceed with the case, not less than one month before the local enquiry was held, cause it notice of the time at which the local enquiry ,would be held, to be given to the Council of the borough, and to be published in such a manner as the Privy Council might direct. To pre- vent a petition being presented on insufficient grounds, the Act provided that the Privy Council might, if they thought' that if no fit, require the petitioners to give security to their satisfac- tion for the costs incurred—(hear, hear)—so order in Council was made to carry out the wish of the petitioners the costs would be thrown upon the pld prevent etitioners. He thought that was a good clause, as it wou petitions being got up where there was no necessity for them. If the order in Council was made, the cost would fall on the borough; but it would be very small indeed. If a borough was found to be unequally divided in the matter of wards, and the wards themselves were unequally repre- sented in the Council, the earliest opportunity should be taken to put the matter right by havinF, an election. The number oaaldermen would be increased in proportion to the number of councillors—one alderman for every three coun- cillors. The Bill provided that the additional aldermen might be appointed on the first 9th day of November, after the provisional order came into force, and that the existing. aldermen should remain undisturbed till their natural term of office bad expired. It appeared to him that the Bill was a very simple way of effecting the necessary reform. It was evident, under the existing Act, they had no power to effect it without considerable expense and trouble, whereas under this Bill a provisional order might be made, andithere would be no need to expend more than £l5 or £2O. The bill was a private one brought in by Mr. William Fowler, Mr. Peter Rylands, Mr. Walter James, and Mr. Henry Fowler. Alderman Heaussag: All staunch Conservatives ? Councillor Piave: I don't know their politics; but I know Mr. Rylands is not. I don't think there is anything in the Bill that wilt make it a party question. (Hear, hear.) Being a private Bill and one which is so applicable to the exigencies of this boroughal think it only fair we should give it what support we can by petitioning in its favour. AN APPEAL FOR THE IRISH. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to say a word or two in favour of the poor Irishman. It seems to me that what with Tory Gavernments that will do nothing but govern through the aid of stringent repressive laws, and Liberal Governments ruling through coercive measures, the poor Irishman is likely to be a great sufferer. Those of your readers who have tried honestly to make themselves acquainted with the bistory of Irelandnaust have noticed that a systematic course of repression, rather than one of love and encouragement, has been the treatment meted *tit to the sister isle. We have had it impressed upon us very strongly by members of the late Government that had they continued in office they would have asked for power to continue to continue the Peace Preservation Act. I believe they would. ' Ill,lso believe that in so doing they would have been likethe man sitting on the safety valve, the result of which foolish action was a blow up. True, we should very likely have had no open Land League, but would secret societies have become less? I think I may challenge our Conservative friends to point to one solitary act of theirs whereby Ireland has benefited. Mr. Gladstone's measure of 1870 was spoiled by Whig andTcry landlords in the upper House, the Bright clause being the only portion, or nearly so, that was allowed to remain in its original state, the 'unit of which has been that a considerable addition has been made to the number of peasant proprietors. But, sir, my intention or put pose at the present time is not to praiss Mr. Gladstone or Mr. Bright, but to say most distinctly that I think they have missed their way. Sir, the Coercion Bill is just about be- coyling law, and who are the parties that are bringing this great crime about? We shall be told next election—the Liberals. Never yet in past history did the Tories do a good political action without being forced by public opinion— now they have coalesced with the Liberal party with the • base view of drawing the latter into a mess and reaping profit out of it. Mr. Editor, the Tories have another reason beside the one oaroed. They desire to protect the landed inteeesrl ,they care not one jot about the Irish, not if they were to kill each other until no more remained than did of the Kilkenny cats. I have sa:d the Tories' desire is to pro- tect the landed interest. I might have added this is also the great aim of the Whigs, and the sooner the people are brought to see that between them and the Whig and Tory portion of the community there is a great gulf stretched the better. It is a simple question of selfishness on the one side and self-preservation on the other. To whom does the land belong? Shall the majority answer, and say the people? or shall it be the select few, who seem to be here amongstus for no other purpose than crying out like thiehorse leech, "Give, give?" Sir, to have a settlement of the land qnes- ticn, we must consult no individual wishes. The question must be, What is good for the State? What method shall be adopted whereby the great majority shall be lees at the mercy of a comparative few greedy and selfish landlords? The questions we should seriously ask ourselves before we turn round and blame the Irish are, What do we know of their state? and what has been done to alleviate their sufferings? In answer to the first, the Press has teemed with accounts of Irish distress of such a character that, had such occurred in England, I don't hesitate to say no landlord or agent's life would have been safe. The true and unmistakeable signs of a country's deciy are seen when the population decreases. In the year 1841 the population of Ireland was 8,175,124. In the year 1846, by n 'rural in- crease, the population would have grown to 8 750.000 ; and in 1851 that population ought to have been 9,000 000. The population of Ireland in 1851 was 6,552,385, which means 2,500,000 of the Irish race blotted eat of existence. In the year 1847 no less than 300,000 people died of famine and disease: and in the same year no less than 300,000 were evicted from their homes by the landlords. In the year 1849 there were 50,000 evictions. Between 1849 and 1852 there were no less than 221,845 evictions. In 1876 the potato crop was worth upwards of £12,000,000; but in 1879 it was worth only £3,341,025; and in proportion as the value of the crop decreased the number of evictions in- creased. If any of your readers are wishful to know what death through starvation means, let them r-ad the able letters written some years ao.c. by Lord S. G. Osborne, and let them bear in mind also that it is only in conse- quence of the Irish Land League being formed that we have been spared similar horrors during the past winter. Mr. A. M. Sullivan, in his defence of the Irish patriots, said : "I; in my own parish, when a boy, stood at the workhouse gate and saw the heap of dead humanity go by, and I paid my penny to the bearer of the trap-bottom coffin, whereby I had seen put into one vast charnel pit 200 human bodies." Irish landlords pronouncing the famine a blessing sent by heaven to clear oil a redundant population! So much for what we know of Ireland in the pat, and let not those who wish to turn a deaf ear to Ireland's cry say this state of things exists no longer. Colonel Gordon, the great traveller, states that such misery as at present exists in Ireland is to be found in no other part of the globe. Gus, ave de Beaumont, writing on Ireland, says: "I have visited the negro and the pariah in his forest; I thought I bad witnessed the lowest stage of human misfortune, but the misery of the Irieh people is a special sight of which nothing seen in any other part of the world can give an idea." Now, sir, what has been done to alleviate all this? Very little; I may eay almost nothing. In 1819 a committee appointed to enquire into the condition of Ireland repor'ed to the House: "That the state of things was calamitous to the last degree, and called for immediate legislation." Nothing was done. In 1823 the same farce was gone through. Its 1825 the same. In 1829 again the -same. In 1830 still the same; and so we have gone on until the present time appointing select committees. Within the last few years the Liberals have tried to do something; but, heavily burdened by the dead weight of the House of Lords, they have not dared as yet to grip the land question thoroughly, for that is at the root of all this evil. I should like to have given my views of the land question, but I dare -not trespass further on your space at present. With your permission I will refer to it next week.—Yours, H. W. Warrington

Ikeep selling at a loss, it would be a poor argument to say , that trade was bad, and that in sonsequence all the employed I • shopmen in the town should have their wages reduced. Cowley says "'Unhappy they to whom God has not re- vealed, by a strong light which must their sense control, that half a great estate's more than the whole." A large estate to one who cannot manage it is impoverishing, the veriest tyro in political economy will tell us. And don't we find• that some collieries in the neighbourhood have offered the advance while larger firms, may be, obstinately refuse not only the advance but weekly pays. This is a sufficient evidence that trade is better than the Rev. Mr. Ward will have us believe. As to there being a sorrowful suggestiveness in the word "strike" I think there is also another light in which we might look at the word; but without going into history to prove the beneficial results of it is only fair to say that those who unjustly and stringdishonestlyik act in such a manner as to cause a strike, which the masters in sour usstances have been guilty of, ought to bear the responsibility for driving away the fair angel of peace and brotherhocd.—l am, yours, dr.c., BLACK DIAMOND.
S. Helens, February 25, 1851.

strong part of Councillor Sutton's speech, and that which he evidently thought would have the most weight with the Council, was the expense of going to Parliament for a pri- vate bill in order to rearrange the wards in any particular borough. If tkep had a prospect of such an expeaditure as Councillor Sutton had stated, they would not on any con- sideration incur it. But Councillor Platt wicked the Coun- cil to support the bill, so thtt, when it passed, these altera- tions could be effected in a manner that would entail little expense. Therefore the alarming part of Councillor Sut- ton's speech could have no weight whatever. Alderman Kiwi said there was too much of the elements of politics in the motion. He had had a seat in that Council for many years, but he had never seen so much of the political element as in Councillor Platt's speech. Councillor FLAT?: I have never said a word about

politics. Alderman KEAN found Councillor Platt WAS determined to make himself very conspicuous in putting the Corporation to expense, and at the same time trying to throw dust in their eyes. "Talk about a commissioner being sent down to make enquiry (when ,a petition had been presented) at a cost to the Corporaten of Al 9 ! Surely he meant £1,900 I It would almost cat £l9 to go up to London, if he wished to enjoy himself. (Laughter.) 1101 was totally opposed to the motion, and he should give it all the opposition he possibly could, both in and outside the Council Chamber. He be- lieved things had gone on in Warrington for many years as they ought to, and whatever political fighting there might be outside, there had been no attempt to introduce politics into the Council Chamber. (Hear, hear.) He never saw a member of the Council more anxious for the interests of the particular ratepayers he represented than he was for those of the borough, and therefore Councillor Platt's motion was totally uncalled for. Even it they got a Bill without a penny of expense, what would the subsequent expenditure be? If the wards and the number of representatives were increased, could they be contested at the same expense, and was the Council Chamber sufficiently large to hold more members? What would be the end of the expenditure? He trusted the Council would pause before listening to Councillor Platt's proposition, as it was utterly at variance with common sense. . Councillor BURGESS did not know the proper order of the business at the meetings of the Council, but it seemed to him that some specified rule should be followed, and that if on one occasion the motions were placed upon the agenda paper after the proceedings of the committees, thus afford- ing those who were not prepared to support a particular motion an opportunity of shelving it without interfering with the confirmation of the minutes of committee, the same should be followed on all occasions. Since they were not allowed to express their disapproval of the motion by walk- ing out of the room, and leaving Councillor Platt and his friends without a sufficient number of members to conduct business, they must discuss the motion, and, he hoped, most of them, vote against it. When Counc lloriPlatt got up and said he had no political motive in bringing forward his motion, and when he remembered Councillor Platt was sent there by the members of one party and be by another, he (Councillor Burgess) naturally looked carefully at the Bill. He found that it bad been brought in by Mr. William Fowler the member for Cambridge; Mr. Peter Rylands, Mr. Walter James, the member for Gateshead, and Mr. Henry Fowler, the member for WolverharePton, all of them, no doubt, very 'estimable members of Parliament, but there was one pecu- liarity about them—they were all out-and-out Radicals. (Laughter.) That looked rather inauspicious, especially, 'after Councillor Platt's virtuous disclaimer, "I come not • friends, to steal away your hearts from any political motive." At present, as they were doubtless aware, when it was thought desirable to alter the boundaries of a borough, or of wards in a borough, it was necessary that a petition asking for such alteration to be made should be presented to the Queen in Council by two-thirds of the members of the Town Council. But by the Bill they wereasked to approve it would be competent for the memorial to be presented by either one-third of the members of the Town Council or one-third of the burgesses; if such one-third ex- ceeded 2,000, by 2,000 burgesses. An important feature in this proposal was that a minority of the Council or of the ratepayers might ask for the change, and that if the could persuade the Commissioners that for some reason the change was desirable, the boundaries and wards might be altered in opposition to the wishes of the majority of the ratepayers. lie bad thought that it was an axiom of modern politicians of a certain,school that majorities must rule, and he was certainly surprised to find the gentlemen, whose names were printed on the back of the bill, advocating an opposite theory. As the law stood at present, the majority ruled, and he failed to see what advantage was to be gained by allowing one-third of the ratepayers or their representatives, in opposition to the wishes of the other two-thirds, to put the town to the expense of an enquiry, and, possibly, in spite of the wishes of the majority, to have the whole electoral arrangements of the town disturbed. Taken as a whole, the Bill was not a good one. He did not see that any advantage could ;possibly arise from the changes it pro- posed to make in the existing law. Its leading principle kwas undoubtedly bad, and even if thd Bill would do no harm, he did not think it could do any good. Before memorializing Parliament in its favour, he hoped they would reflect upon words which were written long ago, and which were as true now as when they were first written :—" It is well not to try experiments in states, except the necessity that it is the reformation that draweth on the change, and be urgent and the utility evident; and it is well to beware not the desire of chan (Hear, hear.) that pretendeth the reformation." Alderman Houxes had listened to the gentlemen who had been opposing the scheme, and confessed he was surprised at the fears they had entertained, and the strong expressions they had made. From what he had heard of the Bill all that it sought to do was to simplify the mode of altering the boundaries of municipal boroughs. It had at various times been thought to be desirable to include the outlying portions of Orford in the municipal borough, as well as Sankey Bridges and Wilderspool, to make the municipal borough co-extensive with the parliamentary borough. If the Bill would enable the Corporation to do this in the simple way Councillor Platt had described, what harm it would do he failed to see. The Bill was entirely outside party politics. It was simply a Bill for the better government of the town, and therefore be supported it. I Alderman Davies did not rise to speak as to the merits or demerits of tbe Bill from any party view, but there were several reasons why he should vote against it. HO would ask, was Warrington now suffering from the want of the Bill? ("No.") It was not so suffering. There was an Associatioe of Corporations in England, established for the express purpose of watching the proceedings in Parliament bearing on their own interests, and of promoting Bills in the interests of Corporations. But he had not heard a word from that Association to show that the Bill in question was required. During the past month a deputation from the Council had waited on that Association; but the matter was not mentioned, and as it did not come before them the' Council might depend upon it the Bill was pot of any vital Importance to corporations generally. There was another strong reason why he should oppose the Bill, namely, that there were several stages at which they brought in what they called the centralization powers—powers as to the way in which corporations should conduct their business. He should at all times set his foot against intrusion in that respect. In six or seven stages, application would have to be made to the Privy Council for some officer who would be sent down to them. He thought it was desirable indeed in the interests of all corporations, that they should be deter- mined as far as possible bisat the central power in London should not interfere with the independence of corporations. (Hear, hear.) If they went into details they would find it was a very weak Bill, and he objected to it entirely. Councillor JEANS thought the object of the Bill, as stated in the first clause, was a good one, if carried out in a prac- tical and proper way. But he totally objected to the mode in which the machinery was to be put into operation. lie thought it would be monstrous for any 12 members of the Council who might meet in the parlour of a member's house, to send a petition to alter the.boundaries of the borough or to alter in any way the representation of the borough. For that reason alone he should object to the Bill. He thought any action taken by the Council should be as a body, and not by 12 members, constituting only a portion of the body. He proposed as an amendment that the Council petition against the Bill. Councillor Sorrow: I don't think it is necessary to bother with it at all. Alderman BURGESS Imving read what appeared on the first page of the agenda paper, said they all knew that it was the Mayor and the Town Clerk who arranged the procedure of the business of the Council, and it was unfair to the Mayor to be sneeringly called to account as he had been that even- ing. He bad never seen such a thing before in his 30 years' experience, and be sincerely trusted he should never hear a repetition of the same offensive remarks. He was sure after a little more experience there would not he a repetition of that kind of thing.. (Hear, hear.) If the Mayor was allowed to be spoken to in that way they were parties to the degradation of the office he held; and be should never be one to allow that. Councillor BURGESS rose o make an explanation. He certainly did not make any observations with regard to what the Mayor had done; he only said that he thought it would he advisable that the business should be taken in regular order. He did not think there was anything irregular in that.

Alderman BURGESS said he should have no hesitation in voting for Councillor Platt's motion. As to the staternent that the motion had been introduced with political motives, he thought that observation should have been kept backas there was no necessity for it at all. The Bill appeared to him to meet the requirements of the case, as far as Warrington was concerned, and while he objected as much as anyone to centraliz Ilion, he failed to see where in the Bill there was that extensive interference to which reference had bem made. They could not even make an application for a charter for incorporation without going through very much the same process. (Hear, hear.) He could not sea why there should be any serious difficulty in supporting the motion of Coun- cillor Platt. If he thought it was going to bring power to a political party, he certainly would not support it. (Laughter and hear, hear.). Ile was surprised that Aldermam Harrison should laugh, the Alderman knew that he never did it— (renewed laughter)—and never should. Alderman HARRISON said on the last occasion when Councillor Platt introduced a kindred question to this he was free to admit he voted for it, as an abstract proposition, but not with the slightest idea of supporting it if the ques- tion came up for adoption by the Council at anything like this early period. He did not think for a moment there was any real necessity for taking the action Councillor Platt had suggested. As some of the previous speakers had asked did any anomaly exist? (Cries of "Yes" and "No.") Was there any portion of the municipal machinery that was in a state of dislocation on account of that? ("None at all.") Councillor Platt had not ventured to say there was. tie had disclaimed altogether that he was influenced by any political feeling in moving the resolution.

Councillor PLATT: I did not say so. Alderman HARRISON said he was rather afraid there was political feeling involved, and if Councillor Platt admitted that he thought there was the strongest reason why the political party opposed to him should oppose him tooth and nail. He believed with Alderman Davies that a spirit of centralisation pervaded a considezbie portion of the Bill, and to permit minorities to rule ins' trl of majorities was reversing the order of things in oe i e that surprised him; and he could not wonder that Coune,:lor Burgess should have been surprised. Coutacill..w Platt had failed to show the necessity for the change which he contemplated, and there- fore he *should certainly feel it his ditty to vote against the
motion. Councillor CROSFIELD : I am rather amused at Alderman Harrison. He of ten amuses me. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He objects to minorities ruling, and yet that is exactly what
I objet to. Alderman HARRISON: No. I did not say so. Councillor CROSFIELD: I understood you to say that. Alderman HARRISOX : No, I was only quoting the dictum

of your own party. Councillor Crrosruatm said the simple question was this— whether the representation should go with the greatest num- ber of electors or not. That was how it appeared to him. ' The fact was that the whole of England wanted going over —(laughter)—aud dividing into electoral districts—("'"Oh,") —and that there should be a member for so many thousand electors, and, in each borough, each councillor should, as far as practicable, represent an equal number of the electors. (Hear, hear.) He had not the advantage of hearing Coun- cillor 'Platt's speech, but be expected that gentleman ob- jected to the two north wards in Warrington having too few representatives. Alderman DA.TIES: He never said anything about it Councillor CROSFIELD said that was what he had under- stood. He was as much opposed to centralisation as Alder-

man Davies, and would not lift a finger to encourage any- thing in that direction. He failed to see anything in the Bill that would lead to zentralisation. [Alderman Harrison: The spirit pervades it.] There had been more said about expense than was necessary. He did not think it would cost the Council anything. Councillor PLATT, in reply, said the Bill bad not been pre- pared to meet the wants or wishes of Warrington particu- larly, but it was intended to apply to the whole of the coun- try. The whole scope of the Bill seemed to be to save expense. Action taken under this Bill would save the ex- pense, trouble, and annoyance experienced in Liverpool, and instead of spending £3,000, what was required might easily be done for about £2O. All that had been said about expense was simply throwing dust in the eyes of the members of the Council.

Alderman DAVIES : I take it that what a man says in this Council Chamber is what he honestly thinks, and that no one wishes to throw dust in the eyes of any member. Councillor CROSFIELD : But somfone charged Councillor Platt with it. It has been said to-night before by someone. Councillor PLATT said on the ground of expense the argu- ment was very much in his favour. As to the necessity of a re-arrangement, that question was well diseased on the last occasion and it was decided there was a necessity for it. He could quite understand the members of the minority wishing to rule as they at present did in the Council Chamber. (Laughter.) He objected to minorities ruling, and said at the present moment the minority of the borough did rule in the Council. One- third of the borough was in a position to over-rule the other two-thirds. He hoped when the bill was carried, as he hoped it would be, that they would take such steps as would pre- vent minorities ruling. He had been taxed with having said he had no political motive in bringing the matter for- ward. What he said was that he did not think there was anything in the bill which could make it a politic.' question, and he did not think there was. How it could be said that the Bill itself was a political measure he did not know. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry to say the Bill did not provide for an extension of the boundaries of the borough. He should have liked Alderman Davies to have pointed out where in the Bill centralization was carried one jot further than in Bills of the same character. It went no further than

the Act of 1859. Alderman DAVIES : I quite agree it does not go further, but it is another link strengthening the power of the Central Board over us. Councillor PLATT said Councillor Jeans thought it a mon- strous thing that 12 members of the Council should be allowed to petition for anything. Councillor JEANS: As individuals, I said. Councillor PLATT: Put it as you like; but I think the meanest subject in the kingdom is allowed to petition the Queen, if he likes, let alone 12 respectable members of a Council. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It is one of the birth- lights of Englishmen that we should be allowed to petition without interference. Councillor JI4ANS : I submit outside:this chamber any 12 members are simply ratepayers. Councillor PLATT said the arguments and justice of the case were for him—(oh)—but the Council, which ruled the majority in the borough, were against him. (Laughter.) Councillor SUTTON: The intelligence is against you. The votes were then taken, with the following result:— For the motion, Aldermen Holmes and Burgess, and Coun- cillors Crosfield, Broadbent, Greening, Platt, Brown Barker, and Dixon-9. Against, Aldermen Kean, Davies, Brown, Harrison; Councillors Fairclough, Litton, Sutton, Greeenall, Whittle, Woolfall, Woods, Francomb, Jeans, and Burgess- -14. The motion was, therefore, lost. WATCH COMMIT'TBIL At a meeting of the Watch Committee, held on the 27th January, it was resolved that the Mayor, Mr. Alderman Chandley, and Councillors Platt and Woolfall be appointed a sub-committee to select the material for police and other officers' clothing, and that Mr. John Harrison be requested to assist the sub-committee. It was recommended that John Smith, the town crier, be allowed a new coat similar to the last supplied to him, and that a new bell be purchased for his use.—At a meeting held on the 3rd February, it was recommended that the tender of Mr. John Dolan for the supply of clothing for the members of the police force and fire brigade be accepted.— At a meeting held on the 10th February, the Visiting Com- mittee reported that they had visited the Bride.vell, and that the roof required certain repairs. It was recommended that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to get the repairs done.—On the 17th February, a letter was submitted by the Borough Surveyor from the Secretary of the Waterworks Company, together with a draft of a proposed agreement for the use of hydrants upon the mains of the company laid for trade puruoses, which were referred to the Town Clerk for his opinion thereon.—lt Was recommended that Mr. Ashton and other inhabitants of Latchford be allowed the use of one of the manual engines, for the purpose of pumping water out of their cellars, they bearing all expenses and paying for the cleansing of the engise and hose after use. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor WOODS sconded, the the adoption of the minutes, which were passed. THB NAMING OF STREETS AND NUMBERING OF HOUSES. At a meeting of the Street Improvement Committee on the 3rd ult., an order far payment of an account was made for gas for street lamps for half year amounting to £924 88.— On the 17th February, a letter from the Census Office was read requesting the committee to name all new streets and to number all houses in the borough, which was referred to the Borough Surveyor.—The following plans were ap- proved :—Plan for new streets in a plot of building land in Orford-lane, for Mr. Robert Davies. Plans for four cottages at Sankey Green, for Mr. John Longshavi. Plan of two cellars under the end house, proposed to be built in Percy - street by Mr. James Beswick. Plan of detached cottage on land adjoining Orford-lane, for the Right Rev. T. 0. Bury. Plan of workshop, for Mr. James Morris in Church-street. Councillor BROADBENT, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, called attention to the desirability of as soon as possible naming the streets and numbering the houses for the census, which was to take place on the 4th of April. Councillor PLATT seconded the motion. He said the Council would observe an item of £924 Sc. for street lamps. It was a very large amount, but on behalf of the Lighting Sub-Committee be wished to say they would have proceeded with the erection of new lamps and the improvement of the lighting of the borough if it had not been that the rates were so very high. They did not wish to incur additional expense, and the inhabitants of those parts of the borough which were badly lighted nfust bear with them until the finances were in a better condition. Alderman CMANDLNY asked whether there was not some byelaw compelling owners of property to number their houses themselves. Alderman HoLafEs thought it far better that the num- bering of the houses should be left to the Corporation. It was the greatest economy to have the town well lighted and thus protect the public against violence and crime, and he hoped the committee would not allow the expenditure of a few pounds to stand in the way of carrying out the lighting of the town. Alderman BURGESS said it had come under his notice that a communication had been sent from the Registrar-General on the subject, the object being to get such a numbering of houses and naming of streets as would facilitate the taking of the census. He hoped the ch.irman of the committee would explain how, if the work was town work, it had been left undone. If the numbering did not obtain, it would scarcely be brought about by such a recommendation. It should be rectified by a house-to-house canvass. Councillor SUTTON thought the most effective and simple method would be for the Borough Surveyor to communicate with the two political agents in the borough, who knew every street not named and every house not numbered. After some further discussion, Councillor BROADBENT said the Borough Surveyor had put himself in communication with the political agents, and had received valuable information. The Council should understand there had been no, neglect, and no arrears. In the natural growth of the town, there were streets not yet named; and it was important the inhabitame should give special assistance to the Borough Surveyor at the present time. He did not know of any bylaw, but the matter had been left in the hands of the Corporation for some time. The Town CLBRIC sal it was the duty of the Corporation to see that it was done. The Corporation could call upon, the occupiers to do it themselves, though it had not been the practice in Warrington to do so. Any occupier, after a week's notice, failing to number his house was liable to a penalty. That only applied to the numbering of houses. The minutes were confirmed. THE SANITARY CONDITION OF HOWLEY. The minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committe con- tained recommendations that an order for 10,000 Buckley tiles be given to Messrs. Pendlebnry and Son; that a cart- road crossing be made to the pith works of Messrs. Preston and Co. at Bank Quay, Liverpool-road, at the cost of the company ; that a new pipe sewer be laid in New-street, off Battersby-lane, and that tie attention of the Street Improve- ment Committee be called to the condition of the houses

adjoining certain private streets in Howley, such houses waste, iatntede what tshtaetpscothmemyititneteetbide qinugesbteud to iltonincflo'ermmicthail being to take with those houses, as this committee was anxious to proceed with the paving of those streets. Alderman Knew, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the last recommendation was passed in consequence of a request from the property owners to have the streets paved. The Committee could pave and form the streets without adopting them. He did not think it would be wise to adopt the streets if the Corporation paved them inasmuch as there was a great question whether houses built OR chemical waste were not liable to be closed as unfit for habitation. The Committee hoped the owners would not have to sacrifice them, and that they would not prove so unhealthy as was imagined. But for the safety of the occupiers it was neces- sary something should be done to the streets, and the com- mittee were instructed by the Deputy Town Clerk that the Street Improvement Committee had power to inform the Paving and Sewerage Committee as to what was to be done in the matter. Councillor WOOLFAEL seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor CROSFIELD eslled attention to the way in which the paving of the streets was taken up and re-set by the gas and water people. The other day when driving along Sankey-street he WAS nearly thrown out of his machine by the wheel going down one of the holes. Alderman HARRISON: It is disgraceful. Councillor :SUTTON said the attention of the Sanitary Committee, and not the Street Improvemt Committee, should be called to the streets at Howley. The Street Im- provement Committee simply passed the plans on condition that they complied with the bye-laws. As building on chemical waste was not prohibited by the bye-laws, the Street Improvement Committee could not refuse to pass plans on that account. Whenever that committee had passed the plans of houses to be erected on chemical waste, they had made a note on the plan that if the houses were built, the builders would be subject to any action which might be taken by the Sanitary Committee. Alderman CRANDLEY said the matter was one of great importance. He thought it desirable they should refer it to the Sanitary and Street Improvement Committees, as it would resolve itself into a very serious sanitary question. The MAYOR had always understood that the Street Im- provement Committee could refuse any plans brought be- fore them on certain grounds. Councillor PLATT said where the committee knew the houses were to be built on chemical waste, as they had no power to refuse to pass the plans, in each case a note was added stating that the plans were approved of, but that the owner must be prepared for any action taken by the Cor- poration with regard to the chemical waste. When plans were in accordance with the by-laws, the Street Improve- ment Committee had no alternative but to pass them as plans, subject to any subsequent action by the Corporation. He corroborated what Councillor Crosficld had said as to taking up of the streets, and said the matter had become very much worse recently. In many cases the sets were replaced in a very slovenly manner, which showed that it was not the work of a pavior. The EX-MAYOR was glad to see that the Council were • taking steps to do something in Howley, the sanitary condition of which was something disgeaceful. During the time the plans were passed the Street Improvement Com- mittee had not the power to prevent houses being built on ! chemical waste, and for that reason the committee put the note on the plans. It was only after the new Improvement Act was passed that the committee got the power to prevent houses being built on chemical waste, and since that time no houses had been built upon it. He hoped now the matter was taken in hand something would be done to put Howley in a proper condition. Councillor JEANS said he took it that the resolution re- ' ferred to houses already built. He asked whether the Cor- poration had power to pull the houses down: Councillor DIXON said it was a question whether the paving of the streets would not make the houses stilt more unhealthy, because if any gas was generated by the waste, how was it to escape? The TOWN CLARK could quite understand the importance attached to this matter by the committee, as a report was made upon the subject some time ago by the medical officer of health. The question as to which committee the matter was to be referred to depended on what it was intended to do. If it was intended to close a house and declare it unfit for human habitation, Jecause it was not sufficiently healthy, that was a matter for the Sanitary Committee. With refe- rence to the passing of plans, it was perfectly true they could not prevent a man building a house or occupying it if the plans.submitted were in accordance with the by-laws. It was nevertheless not incumbent upon the committee to pass plans, although they were entirely in accordance with the by-laws, if there were other reasons why the houses should not be • built. But if in spite of their refusal to pass the plans the houses were built, the Corporation was free to act and give a decision that they should not be inhabited. The difficulty could not arise in future, because before a house could be occupied, the builder had to get a certificate from the Borough Surveyor. It had been his advice never to pass any plans, as long as they were of the same opinion, for building on chemical waste. There was a difficulty with regard to houses already built. If the houses core not fit to be inhabited, the Sanitary Committee had the power to have them closed. Councillor BROWN said he was told the houses had been well built. The only question was whether the streets were to be put in a sanitary condition. Alderman KEAN trusted the Street Improvement Com- mittees would send the committee all the information they required. Councillor Crosfield had referred to a very vexed question. They had constant trouble with the Water Works people taking up the streets for their own purposes. But they must allow that the extraordinary state of the weather had made matters worse. The committee thought their own men ought to be left to pave the streets and put them in proper condition. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were adopted. TIIR CARPENTER MEMORIAL IN TIIII PARK. The minutes of the Town Hall, Park, and Bsths Commit- tee comprised recommendations that a water-pipe be laid to the " Carpenter Memorial," and the fountain supplied with water at the expense of the Corporation ; that the sum of £2O be paid to the widow of the late Mr. James Wood, for studio and buildings now standing upon the land behind the Baths, in Legh-street, according to the tetint of the reso- lution of this committee of the 14th May, 18 ; that the attention of the Sanitary Committee be called to the report of the gardener as to the damage done to the shrubs and trees in the grounds by noxious gases, and that a copy of such report be sent to the coaunittoe ; also, the scale of charges for the use of the Baths, until the 31st December,

1881. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor PLATT seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman BURGESS, referring to the recommendation as to the Carpenter Memorial, said he could not help thinking it was a mistake that memorial was ever placed where it was. It appeared to be an obtrusive obstruction upmi the footpath. Thepark was intended for We living, and not for the dead,—(hear, hear,)—but if they went on for the next few years erecting niemorials of that character for those who had passed away, there would be no place for the living. The time would come when the generation would insist upon the removal of the memorial. They all revered the memory of Dr. Carpenter, who had done a great work in Warrington, but he was not sure that those who were desirous of bon( ur- ing his memory had taken the most judicious step they might have done in the course they had adopted. He should be glad if no further step was taken by the committee for giving the memorial a permanent position where it now stood, as he thought it should be removed to some more suitable place. Alderman HOLMES presumed before the memorial was erected the consent of the Council was obtained. [The Mayor: It was.] The memorial was a drinking fountain and as it could be of no use without water, he therefore hoped the water would be allowed. • Alderman CHANDLEY said thecommittee scarcely thought the projection would be as much as it was. Hut having granted permission he thought it would be more graceful to cause a deviation in the footpath than remove the memorial. The MAYOR said it was quite true the plans came before the committee, but he must say the memorial Was larger than he expected it would be. But as a walk was made round it for the public, there would be more room than before. Considering the thousands who visited the gardens in summer and in hot weather, he thought the fountain well supplied with water would be very bendcial. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS only ohjected to the memorial being permanently in its present position. The MAYOR said the memorial was given with the best intentions, and ho thought the Council ought to take it as it was. The minutes were then confirmed without dissent. MUSEUM LIBRARY AND ARTS COMISITTED.

The minutes of this committee contained the report of the curator for the month of January :--Visitors to the Museum, 2.018, a decrease of 1,406; volumes issued to sub- scribers, 2,542, a decrease of 247; volumes issued to readers, 903, a decrease of 377; compared with January, 1880.— The thanks of the committee were ordered to be sent to the following donors:—Mr. Powlson, a curlew; Mr. Stubs, a young Hooper swan; Mr. T. Fletcher, his "Practical dental metallurgy," and four directories; the Author, " Cries in a crisis," by Macfie ; Dr. Kendrick, four boeks for the local collection; the Local Books Fund, two volumes; the Rev. J. Whitley, 70 volumes of books. On the motion of Councillor GREENING, seconded by Councillor Dixotir, the minutes were adopted. CEMETERY COMMITTER. The minutes of the Cemetery Committee comprised the report of the registrar that the interments for the past 4 weeks were—adults 45, minors 54, stillborn 10; and for the corresponding period last year—adults 40, minors 46, and stillborn 5. The Cemetery Sub-Committtee reported that they had visited the cemetery, and after inspecting the chapels and buildings sida grounds generally, they recom- mended several alterations. The receipts for the past four weeks were .£67 ss. This committee recommended that an additional sum of 2s. 6d. per ton be allowed to Mr. J. H. Nichols for all cannel supplied by him during the present strike, and that the tender of Messrs. Wm. Jones and Sons for a second-hand upright steam boiler (4 horse power) at £23 105. he accepted. —Orders for payment of accounts entered in "the accounts presented book," were made as under For two weeks ended 4th,February, amounting to £4OB 10s. 41. For two weeks ended 18th February, amounting to £1,409 18s. 4d. ; total. £l,BlB Bs. 84. And for accounts on gas extension ac- count :—For two weeks en 'ed 4th February, amounting to £759 108. 4d., for two weeks ending 18th February, amount- I big to £339 4s. 104. • total, £1.098 15s. 21—The average illuminating power of the gas for the fortnight ended 4th February, was equal to 18.20 candles, and for the fertnight ended 18th February, 18.31 candles. Alderman HOLMES, who moved the adoption of the mintites, said he was glad the colliers' strike was over, and that they had got through their, difficulties as ta the supply of .coal. (Hear, hear.) At one time during the strike the town was within a few hours of being in darkness, by reason of the great difficulty of getting coals. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion, which was carried.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. A meeting of the above committee was held on the 7th February. It was resolved that the Mayor, Alderman Davies, Alderman Holmes, the Town Clerk, the Borough Treasurer, attend the meeting of the Municipal Corporations Associations on the 10th February, and that the member.of the borough be requested to attend the meeting of the Municipal Corporations Association—On the 21st Felawary, It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Alderman Thewlis, se- conded by Mr. Councillor Crosfield. That this committee have heard with the greatest regret of the death of Mrs. Charles Chorley, and that they desire to express to Mr. Chorley their most heartfelt sympathy in his great bereavement." It was recommended that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to get the tower of the Trinity clock painted. The Minutes were confirmed on the motion of the Ex- MAYOR (Councillor Fairclough), seconded by Alderman HARRISON.

Hurmrs LIBERALS.—A meeting of the Liberals of the St. Helens polling district was held on Friday at the Liberal club, for the purpose of electing two delegates to the executive committee and five delegates to the council of the South West Lancashire Association. Mr. A. Sinclair pre- sided, and there were also present Councillors Brook and Hanson, Messrs. H. L. Riley, J. B. Leach, H. Martin J. Boydell, J. Pennington, and J. Cotton. Colonel Gamble, president of the Liberal club, and Mr. Sinclair were unani- mously elected members of the executive committee; and the five delegates appointed were Messrs. J. B. Leach, Amos Harmon, 11. Martin, J. Boyden, and R. G. Brook.

TURSDAT.—Before Sir Thomas Earle and Captain Willis. AN IND:um/4; CASH—Mary Rimmer, was charged with creating a nuisance contrary to the provisions of the Public Health Act—Mr. Swift prosecuted.—nomas:Evans, watch- pinion maker, said he lived at Burrows lane, Eccleston. He lived in the second house of six belonging to Mrs. Lord, and they had one common tuck-yiard. Mrs. Rimraer was the owner of a beerhouse, and premises called "Bottle and Glass," and that property adjoined Mrs. Lord's property. He bad been tenant of one of those houses for 33 years, and during the whole of that time the waste water and sewage from Mrs. Lord's property had never gone by any other way except through Mrs. Rinnuar's property. A large reservoir was built about 24 years ago, and previous to those works by the Corporation of Liverpool, the sewage passed through Mrs. Rimmer's property into an open ditch, but after the erection of those works a covered drain was substituted for the open ditch; but the sewage ran into the same direction. About six years ago he observed the passage of the sewage through the drain was impeded, and in the drain at the end of the houses a flower-coop was found on Mrs. Lord's pro- perty. That was removed and all went on right until a month ago, when an obstrpction again was caused, and thel back-yards of the houses in eonsectdence were covered with ' house-slops and rain water, conitituting a nuisance in- jurious to health.—George Adamson.etrated Unit daring the whole of 50 years, to his knowledge, the sewage from Mrs. Lord's property had gone through Mrs. simmer's property. —John Twist, surveyor and inspector of nuisances for the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority, said the house-slops and rain water accumulated in the back-yards was a nuisance, and likely to become a much greater nuisance if permitted to exist during the warm weather. Richard Green, pavior, said he laid the drain twenty-eight years ago for Messrs. James and Robert Rimmer, by whom be was employed and paid.—Mr. Tyrer, for the defeqce, said there was a Lona-fide question of right whether Mrs. Rimmer was wrong or not in the action she had taken, and it was not for their worships to determine whether she had a right to stop the passage of the sewage at all.—Sir T. Earle said it bad gone for 28 years in the new drain, and how did Mr: Tyrer account for that.—Mr. Spencely said the summons was for a nuisance under the Public Health Act, and was entirely independent of the interests of the owners of the respective properties, and the community was not to be swept away by fever because there happened to be a quarrel between two owners of property.—The Bench said they would not go into the question of right, and made an order for the abate- ment of the nuisance. A FARM SERVANT STEALING HAY—John Leach was charged with having on Saturday, the 12th ult., stolen 22 cwt. of hay, value £4 10s., the property of John Rimmer, for whom he worked as ,servant. On that day it appeared prosecutor sent prisoner with a load of hay to Mr. Warriner, of Fairfield. Prisonerdid not. return, but sold the bay to some other person.—Prisoner, who said he was willing to pay a certain sum per week to "clear it off," was sent to prison for three months. UNAUTHORISED LODGING-HOUSES.—Mary Malone was charged with keeping her house as a common lodging-house without haging it registered.—P.S. Crawford said he visited defendant's house in Proseot, and found four lodgers sleep- there. Two of them had come from Wigan, and intended proceeding to Liverpool. The house was a very disorderly one, and in a very filthy state. He had previously cautioned defendant about keeping a disorderly house. When he I visited the house on the night hrquestion, defendant was drink.—Fined 20s. and costs.

Rana Mourn Sonoma, S. HELENS.—On Monday a miscellaneous concert was given in these scheols, with the object of raising funds for repairs and alterations. The present old fashioned windows are to be taken out, and large plate gliss windows substituted. This alteration, while giving a bold and modern, if not a picturesque appearance to the building, will also give tnore light in the rooms, and make them much more comfortable. Some excellent local talent was secured, and a good programme was gone through, the artistes giving their services gratuitously. The Excelsior glee party, consisting of Messrs. C. Grine, G. Barton (junior), linker, Dormon, F. Dennett, and Mostyn, executed several glees in such a manner as to meet with warm and deserved approbation. Miss Faram sang " Happy Dream- land' and "Kathleen Mavourneen " in very nice style con- siderable improvement being noticeable in this young lady's singing. The Misses Knowles sang two charming duets. A slight nervousness in one of the young ladies was ap- parent at the beginning of the first piece, but this was eventually overcome. Dr. Coombs, of Wigan, gave un- bounded satisfatition by his humorous songs which were executed in inimitable style and provoked rounds ,of laugh- ter. The attendance was yery good.
