div.p: DEVELOPMENT OF THE WIDNES CHEMICAL TRADE. The Railway Commission, sitting in the committee room, House of Lords, on Monday, had before them the case of the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Company, Limited, and others Y. the London and North-Western Railway Company. The commissioners were Sir Frederick Peel, Mr. Price, and Mr. Miller, Q.C. The applicants were repre- sented by Mr. Webster, Q.C., and Mr. French ; and the Solicitor-General, Mr. Moon, and Mr. Littler appeared for the railway company. Mr. Webster, in opening the case, said the applicints, besides the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Company, were the Rio Tinto Company, Messrs. Mason and Barry, Messrs. Taylor, Cameron, and Co., Messrs. Strong, Reid. and Page, Messrs. T. V. Bird and Co., Mr. Joseph Hoult, Messrs. Jos. C. Gamble, Messrs. Joseph Muspratt and Son, and Messrs. John Hutchinson and Co. The Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Company, the Rio Tinto, and Messrs. Mason and Barry were importers ef ore, which was landed in the de- fendants' dock at Garston, and intended for consumption at St. Helens, Widnes, and other places: Messrs. Taylor, Cameron and Co., Messrs. Strong, Reid, and Page, Messrs. T. V. Bird and Co., and Messrs. Joseph Hoult were, owners of steamers and sailing ships engaged in the carriage of ore at Garston ; Messrs. Joseph C. Gamble and Son. Messrs. J. Muspratt and Son, and Messrs. John Hutchinson were manufacturers occupying works, with sidings, adjoining the defendants' railway, and they were the consumers of the ore. The London and North-Western was the only conve- nient railway in the neighbourhood. By an Act passed in July, 1864, the uncle taking of the St. Helens Canal and Railway Company was vested in the defendants, this un- dertaking consisting of a line of rails from St. Helens to a dock at Widnes, with certain branches of a canal between these places and the dock to another dock at Garston. There was also a line from Warrington to Gareton. The London and North-Western Railway Company's Additional Powers Act (1365) contained clauses fixing the maximum rates which the defendants were entitled to charge for the carriage of ore from Garston Dock to St. Helens, Widnes, and other parts of the line. By virtue of another Act passed in 1867 the defendants constructed an additional dock at Garston. This Act, with regard to charges, was incor- coratecl with the Act of 1864: The railway company were ' the absolute owners of the dock at Garston, and had the exclusive control and management of it. They regulated the entry of steamers and sailing vesflels into the dock, and I:reloaded cargoes into wagons. They were' obliged by the Acts to give the traders proper accommodation and facilities for the berthing and unloading and conveyance of the im- ported ore, but they had completely failed to do this. The defendants, no doubt, would in defence urge that they did End and discharge cargoes within a reasonable time, and he gathered from the answer to the plaint note that they would urge that if any delay occurred it was under such circum- stances as justified the respondents; indeed, it would be in consequence of a •udden large demand for wagons, or other treasonable cause. The commission would be told in the course of the case that there had been an immense develop- ment of the chemical trade in the neighbourhood of Widnes and St. Helens. With regard to the actual amount of the charges, it was admitted by the respondents that the tolls they could levy in, respect to this traffic were below those for corresponding services on other parts of the line. Both the directors and the managers of the railway company gave as a reason why they had not supplied mere wagons that the trade was not r munerative. But if they wanted their tolls amended, why did they not ge to the H .use of Com- mons for more powers? He (Mr. Webst r) was sure that the commissioners would find this wee a case in which they would be satisfied that the company had not met this traffic as they should have done after seeing how it was wowing, but they had prudently—from their own point of view— subjected it to very considerable inconvenience by not pro- viding proper facilities. in 1867 so great was the trade that the c enpany found it necessary to make a new dock notable tne site oi taac The imports of ore in 1859 amounted to 26,000, and in 1880 te 280,000 ieee. There- fore the commissioners would see that it was a very large and important trade, and one that was entitled to have its grievances very carefully considered. In 1873 matters had become so bad that a number of shipowners called together a meeting, and an associatien was formed to protect the interests of the traders, and in 1874 an influential deputation waited upon the directors of the railway company and repre- sented their case. The directors made a distinct promise that they would look into the matter, and provide a larger cumber and more constant supply of wagons. That promise was carried out for a certain time but during the last few years there had on retreat and unreasonable delay. So great had it been that the shipowners in some cases had actually declined to allele their ships to go into dock. The cost really fell upon the Consumers; the shipowners saved themselves by demanding increased pay. Tbe company had frequently been told that unless ships got berths wiehout so much delay, and unless a sufficient number of wagons was supplied, the chemical trade of Widnes would come to a standstill. But there was no remedy offered, in fact there was a starvation of the traffic owing to an insufficient supply of wagons. He contended that the company should not starve tke trade, but should, if they felt that their charges were not remunerative, go' to Parliament and have their rates amended. Mr. T. V. Bird, of the firm of Messrs. Bird and Co., Liver- pool, was the first witness called. lie was examined by Mr. French. He stated that, in addition to representing Messrs. Mason, Barry, and Co., he was familiar with the trade of 'Garston, being the manager of two vessels that traded regularly between that town and other ports. The trade of Garston had very considerably increased during the last 20 years. In 1859 the imports amounted to 36.000 tons of ore, whilst last year they reached 280,000 tons. The total imports on behalf of Messrs. Mason' Barry and Co. alone amounted to 97,000 tons in 1878, to 40,000 tons odd in 1879, and to • 91,000 tons in 1880. The cargo of a vessel was taken charge of by the railway company as soon as it reached the dock, and they discharged the ship and delivered it to the con- sumers. The company had hydraulic "lifts" at each berth, and they were their own stevedores. The work was done in this way :—A stearner lay alongside her berth, two hydraulic cranes were set to work, and the ore was taken from the . ship's hold into the wagons, which were on rails alongside the ship. If no wagons were available, the vessels were dis- charged in order to save time. The result was, the cargo had to be again handled and loaded, which caused great delay and expense. An average ship's cargo was about 350 tons of ore, and that quantity would require 50 wagons if the work was to be completed in one day. That was an average day's work. He had known 80 wagons to be loaded in a day. In 1373 he was concerned in the forma- tion of an association of traders, and that association cem- tnunicated as a body with the London and North-Western Railway Company with reference to Widnes and St. Helens. Some time after the traffic was carried more satisfactorily, but speaking from general experience in the year 1879, the trade starved, and they were unable to get stocks up in their works. The witnems proceeded to give details with reference to delays which hed occurred to his own vessels, showing that in some cases the vessels were detained as long as nine (lays, a fortnight, and three weeks. If vessels in berth had had ample and sefficient wagons hie vessels would in every case have gone immediately alongside the quay, and been discharged without delay. The difficulty was not getting a berth owing to an insufficient supply of wagons. By the Sthicitor-General : Was there not in the latter part of 1879 a great revival in the chemical trade? Yes. Solicitor- 'General: I thought so; at all events, we had it on the best authority on the 9th of November, 1879. (Laughter.) During the latter part of 1879 and the beginning of 1880 was there not much more vessel tonnage than during the j corresponding period of the previous year? Yes, I think there was.—The Solicitor-General: Something like as much again, I supposei? I cannot say.--It has fallen off again? It has somewhat. The imports are about the same, I believe, but there is a falling off in the exports, which are chiefly coal.

Mr. J. S. Beaufort, member of the firm of Beaufort and Co., Liverpool, agents for the Rio Tinto Company, was then examined by Mr. French. The Rio Tinto Company were large importers of ore from Spain. In 1878 their imports at Garston amounted to 89,000 tons, in 1879, 106,000 tons; and in 1880, 139,000 tons. This was all noel in St. Heins, Widnes, and Runcorn. Mr. George Page (member of the firm of Strong, Reid and Page, shipowners, Liverpool) said they had as many as fifty or sixty vessel° engaged in the Garston trade.—Mr. French: From a shipowners' point of view tell me what your experiunce of delays is? During the last three years the delays have almost been continuous—From what cause? Solely from want of wagous.—ln consequence of those delays have you made any alteration in your terms with the charterers? We have hesitated to make contracts in advance solely on the ground that these inconveniences might be increased.—Then is it a custom of trade to contract for some periods? Two or three years, but we have declined to do it. —All owing to this delay? All owing to this delay. The witness continuing, stated that the company had frequently allowed' the Pioneer and other small steamers to appropriate berths and thus delay other vessels which might use these berths. These small steamers were eng god in importing and exporting general cargoes.—The Solicitor-General: Do you dispute that it is hardly practicable to earry on this business without having occasional delays in the wagons? They bave and can discharge 4.50 tons per day with a fair supply wagons.—Does it not depend to a great extent upon whether the tyre ns to whom these wagons are despitched return them 'a a reasonable time? It is not for uslo follow the wagons and see that they are quickly discharged and returned. (Lauahter.)—Do you think the railway company are bound to have a stock of wagons ready for you at a moment's notice? No. I say they are bound to do a good day's work, and they can do this with a sufficient number of wagons.—What you say is that, no matter how great the increase in the demand, the company are compelled to bring Into immediate existence trucks equal to the demand? I dont say that. I only ask that they shall do a good day's work.

sufficient. He knew that the accommodation was ample at such large works as those which belonged to Messrs. Mus- pratt and others. In 1879 there was an almost constant de- lay in the disch-rging of ore at Garston Dock, and the firm c,f which he was a member were greatly inconvenienced in consequence. In answer to the Solicitor-General, witness said that after the 24th December, 1879, the supplies for a time were pretty regular. It was customary to have some reserve ' stock. They did not depend altogether upon their daily supplies, but it was very inconvenient if the ore did not arrive regularly. If the company supplied a sufficient number of waggons there would be no reason to complain. Mr. James Beswick, in the employ of Messrs. Beaufort and Co., said that he looked after the arrival of ore at Gars- ton. During the years 1878, 1879, and 1880 there win a deficient supply of waggons, resulting in great inconve- nienck, to the business of the firm. In consequence of the short supply of waggons by the railway company the firm had frequently to place the ore in lighters, thereby causing additional expense. In the ordinary course of their busi- ness they would require fifty waggons a day, but at times they were only able to get fifteen. Mr. W. H. Bachanan said that be 'was out-door superin- tendent for Messrs. Strong, Reid. and Page, shipowners. His duty Was to look after the discharge of vessels at Gars- ton. He had frequently found great delay caused by an insufficient supply of waggons. Vessels had frequently been delayed in getting into berth owing to ships already alongside the quays being delayed through a want of trucks. This delay occasioned additional expense. Mr. Henry Barton, a sampler on commission, said he was employed by Messrs. Gamble and Sons, St. Helens. The firm named purchased ore from the Marais Sulphur and Copper Company. He had frequently seen the cranes at the dock idle. This was due entirely CO an insufficient supply of waggons. Occasionally, when be wanted 00 trucks he was only able to get 17. This closed the evidence on the Dart of the applicants. The Solicitor-General, who opened the case for the rail- way company, did not deny that during thy latter insuffi- cient 1879 and the early part of last year there was an nsoue fflto cient supply of waggons. This was, however, solely d the great prosperity of the chemical ototramdiessoiofn:Visidhnaeds.belonn his view the application to the c made at a time when the necessity for it had ceased. Some of the firms had actions pending against the railway com- pany. They, however, were not content with individual actions, but had set up a joint-stock claim. They stated that their trade was being crippled and injured by what WAS going on at Garston Dock, and they asked the Commissioners to remedy a system which was mischievous, but at the time they made the complaint they were able to carry on their business. He admitted that there had been delays, but be submitted that they were exceptional, owing in some instances to an exceptional increase of trade. The increase of trade was not confined to Garston, and if Garston obtained its full supply of waggons, according to its addi- tional requirements, other districts would have to be satis- fied with a diminished supply. If the company were to deal reasonably with the whole of the railway system the increase of trade in all parts must be taken into • account. Mr. Miller, one of the Commissioners, said it must not be forgotten that under the Act of 1867 the railway com- panies were compelled to supply a sufficient number of waggons with regard to the chief class of traders interested in that case. The Solicitor-General said that only applied to works ad- joining the company's line. The only people who really had works adjoining the company's line were Messrs. Mus- pratt and Son, Messrs. Gamble and Co., and Messrs. Hut- chinson; and they had not proved a single case of incon- venience. Evidence would be called to show that the com- pany honestly did their best to supply waggons for the Garston traffic. With regard to the charge of undue pre- ference to a certain line of steamers, be said that the pre- ference was given because the gobds brought were p-rishable, and that if such preference was not given the company would lose that portion of their traffic. Under the circum- stances, that was not an undue preferences and he contended there was nothing in the Act to prevent the company giving the preference in queation. Mr. Thomas Kaye, chief goods manager of the London and North-Western Railway Company, who was recalled, said that undoubtedly towards the close of 1879, and in the early part of 1880, there was a deficiency of waggons at Garston. This was owing to the revival in the chemical trade and to the spurt in the iron trade. He did his best to supply Gars- ton with waggons. It was not true that the company gave preference to other places because the rates st Garston were low. Owing to the increase of trade all the railway com- panies were busily employed. Mr. E. Braide, district goods manager of the London and North-Western Railway Company at Warrington, gave Cor- roborative evidence.
The case was again adjourned.
On Wednsday Mr. 'E. K. Muspratt, Mr. C. R. Jones, Mr. J. Cowen. Mr. C. Scotter, and Mr. M. Stevens gave evidence on behalf of the railway company, and the case was ad- journed until Saturday.

div.head: – RUNCORN COFFEE AND COCOA ROUSE
div.p: - RUNCORN COFFEE AND COCOA ROUSE
COMP ANY.

The third annual meeting of this company was held on Monday afternoon, at the rooms, in High-street, and, as was the case twelve moaths ago, great difficulty was found in securing a sufficient attendance of shareholders to form a quorum, so that the business might be transacted. Gentle- men had to be sent over the town as scouts before they could proceed. Mr. J. 0. Jackson, chairman of the company, pre- sided, and amongst those present were the Rev. Canon Barclay, Messrs. G. S. Hazlehurst, Gabriel Davies, Thomas Norman, Philip Speakman, and B. Kniveton (secretary). The report of the directors, which was taken as read, stated that they had to bring before the shareholders a more satisfactory account of the year's working. The takings during the year amount to £1,124 Is., being nearly equal to I thoce of the last twelve months, and the working expenses were £7B Bs. sd. less. After paying the deficiency of last year, amounting to £25 16s. 4d., the nett balance of profit amounted to .£3l 10s. 6d. The directors recommended that a dividend of £2 103. per cent. be paid, and the balance placed to the credit of the preliminary expense account. The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the report and balance sheet, and said that the directors, having promised to try and get the company into a better position, had done so by, first reducing the expenses; they closed the upper rooms and let them as offices. This very considerably re- duced their expenses, and their income was not much less than in the previous year. The motion was seconded by Mr. R. NORMAN. and was carried. On the motion of Mr. S. C. BEcrwrr, seconded by Mr. JAMES HIGGINS, Messrs. John Meadowcroft and R. Shaw, who retired from the directorate, were unanimously re- elected. Mr. GABRIEL P. DAVIES moved the re-appointment of Mr. James Pritchard as auditor. The motion was seconded by Mr. SPEAKMAN, and carried. Mr. Hams proposed a vote of thanks to the directors for their services during the past year. He was only sorry they could not vote them anything, as they most certainly had been put to great trouble in carrying out their duties. It was not, however, so much a question of the company being a paying concern as of it benefiting the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BECKETT seconded the motion, which was cwried. The CHAIRMAN, in respondim,t, said the object the am- pany had in view was not to make a profit so much as to find accommodation for the working classes of the town without the temptation of intoxicating liquar. They had, he theught, to a large extent been successful, and they hoped to be more so in the future. The Rev. Calton BARCLAY moved a vote of 'thanks to the chairman. He testified to the business ability and good common sense which Mr. Jackson had brought to bear on the affairs of the company during the last two years. He had tided them over many difficulties in the past, and should there be any in the future he would no doubt manage to overcome them. Much of the £1,124 the company had re- ceived during the year would doubtless have been spent in the public-house had not the cocoa rooms been erected, and although the rooms had not been made use of as freely as they had hoped, he looked upen the year's working as an earnest of coming prosperity. Mr. HAZLEHURST seconded the motion, which was adopted.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MoNDAT.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (chairman), and Mr. Thomas. THE CASE OF FURIOUS DRIVING IN BRIDGE STREET.— A respectable dressed lad named Isaac Johnson, in the em- ploy of Mr. Thomas Acton, farmer, Norton,'was summoned for furiously driving a horse and cart in Bridge-street, en the 16th ult. The case was fully considered at the previous sessions, but bad been adjourned in order that another wit- ness for the defence might be called.—Superintendent Williamson, and P.C. Hibbert gave evidence for the police, and Johnson, his master, and a lad were called for the defence. The last witness who said he was in the cart with the defendant, maintained that every effort Was made to stop the horse.—The Chairman said be was of opinion that defendant had not done what be could to stop the animal, and people's lives must not be endangered by such fellows. who were not trustworthy, and unfit to have charge of a horse. He would have to pay ss. and costs. SHAMELESS WOOLEN—Sarah Smith was convicted of having been drunk and disorderly in Cooper-street, on the 21st and 23rd Mts. The case was proved by P.C.' s Hibbei t and Person'. The Chairman said the prisoner appeared to be utterly shameless, and; she would be fined 10s. and costs Os 6d., or in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment in each case.—Sarah Ann Bailey was also fined 108. and Os. 6d. costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for a like offence in High-street, on the 23rd ult.,—Eleanor Reynolds was charged with having, on the the 24th ult., used abusive and profane language, in High-street, to the annoyance of passengers.— An officer having proved the case, and said that the woman, who now appeared very defiant and light in her behaviour, Was not drunk at the time she made use of the language, the Chairman said there was a bad list against ker, and she appeared to be utterly shameless, She would, therefore, be fined 205. and costs. In case of non-payment, she would be sent to prison one month.—Prisoner : Thank you, your

worship. ppearaedssatuol assault On on o a ec m respectably A QuEEn Lovx PIIILTER.—A powerful young fellow namedcharged ressed young lady named Mary Ellen Lovell. Com- plainant said that on the night of the 20th ult., she was Jo going to chapel, when the prisoner came up, caught hold of , whnithLeaw n is, aggravated who a her, and asked her where she was proceeding. She told him to go about his business, on which he ran after her and gave her several blows with a stick. The Deputy Magistrates' Clerk to complainant: Bare you kept company with him for some time past? Yea—Of late have you refused to have anything to do with him? Yes. —When he struck you, did he hurt you very much? Yes; there is a wound on my head.—.[Complainant uncovered her head, which had a large piece of plaister on the back part of it.]—The Chairman (to the prisoner): You appear to be a cowardly ruffian. I find that you have been charged on a previous occasion with assaulting a woman. This appears to have been an aggravated assault, and a very gross one. Now, as you are a coward and a ruffian, you probably won't like to have your pocket touched. We will try to see if we cannot make you feel in one way if not in another. You will be fined 403. and costs (163. 2d.), or one month's im- prisonment with hard labour.—The prisoner, who appeared to have made his mind up previously that he would not pay any fine, walked to the top of the stairs leading to the cells, and went down at a run. APPLICATION TO KEEP AN EXPLOSIVE STORIL—WiIEEM Edgar Lee, ironmonger, applied for permission to keep an explosive store at Weston, the quantity to be under division D of the Act, which gives permission to keep 4,000tb of gunpowder. or 2,0001 b of mixed explosives.—Superintendent Williamson, in answer to Mr. Campbell, said he had visited the premises proposed to be used for the store by Mr. use. They were situate at Weston, and belonged to Mr. Bankes. They were also the required distance from a railway or public works, and in a disused delph.—The Bench granted the application. ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM A WESTON FARMER.—William Millington, Joseph Leathwood, Joseph Rowlands, and Anne Potter were charged with stealing six ducks and one drake, the property of Mr. Joseph Lightfoot, farmer, Weston.— Prosecutor said that on the night of the 24th ult., six ducks and a drake were fastened up in a place on his farm, which was at Weston, and belonged to the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co. Between five and six o'clock on the fol- lowing morning, he found that the lock had been broken off, and six ducks and the drake taken. The four produced formed part of the stolen property.—Sergeant Walley said that on the morning after the robbery he went to the house of Thomas Potter (the husband of Anne Potter), Percival's- lane. He asked Mrs. Potter if she had bought any pigeons that morning, and she said, "No, I have not." He then id you bought any ducks, if I may ask a a qauveestion ?" She said, " No, I hays not." silleaisik‘re'dH her if anyone had brought any ducks to the house that morning, but she said not. He tUn searched, and in the pantry he found the four ducks produced. Mrs. Potter then said that a little before six o'clock some one knocked at the door. She went downstairs, undressed, and the man put the ducks through the door. She asked who had sent them, and he answered "It is all right; Tom. (meaning Mrs. Potter's husband) knows about them." The same mornins,, he appre- hended the prisoners Leathwood and Millington. On the back et the latter's coat ha found fresh blood, and inside of it two or three feathers.—P.C. Cooper apprehended the pri- noner Rowlands at the Blue Ball, in Fryer-street. As soon as the prisoner saw him, Rowlands said "It's all right: I was coming to give myself up on Monday morning."—On this statement being made by the witness Rowlands became terribly excited, and denied it in a furious manner, on which the chairman told him be had better keep his tongue still until he was asked a questien.—lnspector Rolling- worth gave evidence at great length as to statements made by the various prisoners incriminating one another.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, who appeared for the defence of Mrs. Potter, submitted that a prima facie case was not made out upon which his client could be committed for trial. There was not a tittle of evidence to show that the female prisoner knew the property had been stolem—Prisoners were each committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial.—At this point Rowlands became very indignant, and said that rather than stop in gaol until the Quarter Sessions, the last of which were only just over, he would "let it all be put on him and plead guilty." He appeared to have a great horror of staying in prison for se many weeks.—Mr. Ashton, magis- trates' clerk, said themes was now disposed of. The Bench remarked that they would grant the female prisoner bail, her husband in £2O and two sureties in £lO each. 1 POOR RATE DETADLTERS.—Mr. Sutton, assistant .over- seer, summoned 59 people for non-payment of poor rates. One was excused, and in the other cases orders were made for payment within seven or fourteen days. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick.

A WEAK CASE.—Jane Griffith was charged with stealing an apron, the property of Martha Worthington.—Com- Mainant said she lived in Parr's-court, off Church-street, and on Saturday morning she had occasion to leave her house about eleven o'clock. At that time she had an apron on a line in the kitchen, and on her return, in about ten minutes she missed it.—Mrs. Prince, a neighbour, said she saw Griffith, with whom she had been acquainted for some time, come out of a closet in the yard and go into Mrs. Worthington's house, but she could not say whether the prosecutrix was in at the time or not. She heard the prisoner call out the name of the prosecutrix, but tio answer was given. She was unable to say whether any one else went into the house during Mrs. Worthington's absence.— Inspector Hollingworth, who conducted the case, said the police had not been able to find the apron.—Mr. Chadwick did not consider the evidence sufficient to convict, and dis- charged the prisoner. A SINGULAR NIGHT ADVENTURR.—FeIix McConn, labourer, was charged with breaking into the house of John Smith, of Harper's-brow, off Water-street, and stealing a towel and other articles.—The evidence of the prosecutor was to the effect that about ten minutes to eleven at night he went out of the house and left his lad there. On his return he found that the window had bees broken open, and the prisoner, who was in a state of intoxication, was in the place.—The prosecutor's son was called, and said that soon after his father had gone out he was sitting in the house, when the prisoner pushed out the window frame' which was loose, and entered, at the same time asking "if he did not know old Conn." Witness became afraid, and ran out for the purpose of finding his father and getting a policeman. Shortly after his father came to the house, bringing an officer, on which the prisoner was found there intoxicated, and the towel missed.—Prisoner was remanded until to-day (Saturday). ALLEGED FELONY: CENSURE OF A PAWNBROKER'S Asstsrayr.—Margaret Smith, wife of the prosecutor in the last case, was charged, on remand, with stealing a chemise and a pair of drawers, the property of Elizabeth Santley, on the 26th ult.—The prosecutrix, who lives with a woman named Baker, at Harper's-brow, said she saw the articles wife on the maiden in Baker's house on Saturday morning, about eight o'clock. She and Baker went to have something to drink at Waterworth's publio-house, and on returning, about half-past nine, she missed the things. She never gave permission to pledge them, nor did she give them to the prisoner.—At the hearing of the case on the previous day, one of the assistants at Mr. Syred's pawnshop said the thirws were pledged on the 25th ult., the day before that on which the prosecutrix said they were stolen. He had dated the ticket the 25th, and the ticket on the goods had also the same date. On the WedneSday, in reply to ques- tions frnm the sitting magistrate (Mr. Chadwick), witness said he could not possibly be mistaken as to the date. On being called on Thursday, the assistant stated that the chemise was pledged at the shop on Monday, the 2Stli ult. —Mr. Chadwick severely reprimanded the witness, and said that when giving evidence he really ought to be more careful that what he was saying was the truth, and not jump at conclusions in such a manner as he seemed to have done. —Witness said that in the pawnbroking busialess it was very easy to make a mistake of the kind, as they took some hun- dreds of articles in pledge in the course of a day.—Mr. Chadwick remarked that this did not make the slightest difference, as a witness ought to exercise the greatest care as to what he swore being the truth. He hoped he would be more careful in future—P.C. Kelly proved finding the drawers in lives with ms itwh'is r Mrs. Baker, house—The who a prisoner stated ehacalled tt ie a her son t i cle and a d hs alteg,ed to he stolen were given to the boy Smith by Santley, on Saturday morning, to pawn.—Two other boys were also called, who said they were playing together in Baker's the i)eta bkoey s,thea farticles i which hff Smiththe tookmaiden ahnodusgeivaentdhtelmie them to his mother.—The magistrate did not consider the evidence sufficiently strong to convict, and discharged the Yt o saw one Santleyo f prisoner. ' THE WEATHER.

Stormy and wintry weather prevails. Railway com- munication has again been stopped in the North of Scotland ,nd in Cumberland by snowdrifts. Several shipping casual- ice are reported. A mill chimney was blown down at Church, near Accrington, last night, seriously iinjuring one i 1 the work people.

RIINCORN AMATEUR BICYCLE CLUB. The annual meeting of thi: club was held on Wednesday evening, in one of the ante rooms of the Public Hall. Mr. Thomas Norman presided. Mr. JOSEPH SALKELD read the fifth annual report, which stated that the committee were very sorry to have to record a gloomy condition of affairs. Ti was not, however, the case monetarily, as the finances wer.• ;n a flourishing condi- tion, but physically, owing to many oi the members hardly taking such an interest in the exercise of bicycling as was formerly the case. This might be due to many things on which he would express no opinion. The championship race was run on May Day last, over the Aston course, and resulted in a victory for Mr. Jesse Timmins, who now held the gold medal, and only required to win it again this year in order for it to become his property. A•good deal of dif- ference of opinion was evidenced at the meeting of the com- mittee in October, as to the advisability of giving a concert, and, by a very narrow majority, it was decided to do so. Mr. Arthur Lloyd and his company were engaged, and the concert took place on November 15th, resulting in a gain of £3 4s. sd. In December it was decided to discontinue having an annual ball. As to finances, during the year the receipts, including the profit made by the concert, had been £8 3s. 5d., and the expenditure (with the £3 108. for the championship medal) £6 Bs. 6d. The balance in hand that day was £8 195. Bd. The number of members last year was 18, as against 21 in 1879, 23 in 1878, 24 in 1877, and 17 in 1876. The meets during the year had been attended very badly, partly owing to the weather, but in a greater measure from the physical apathy to which the report had before alluded. A proposal had been to make younger members of the club office bearers during the coming official year. The CHAIRMAN asked what course the members thought they could adopt to put new life into the club. Mr. JOSEPH SALKELD said he should like to see the affairs of the club handed over to the care of younger office barer. He suggested that Mr. Jesse Timmins should be made secretary, and Mr. Norman re-elected president. He had considerable knowledge of their members, some of whom had become married men, and others quite Falstaffian in their proportions. (Laughter.) These and other such-like matters had a tendency to militate againat any strong desire to indulge in the exercise of bicycling. Doubtless they would all join with him in the opinion that it would he a very bad thing to let a well established club like that, which was in so good a position financially, go down, and so let their enemies triumph over them, and say they had been unable to carry on the association as the effect of certain things which had taken place. Let there be younger blood introduced amongst them, and the funds in hand transferred tv the new committee, and he had very little doubt as to prosperous times being in store for them. If, on the ether I hand, they were to decide to distribute the funds they had in hand, and wind up the club, they would no doubt meet with many complications, some of which might not be of the most agreeable character. He should be happy to give a subscription of a guinea to the new committee, and no doubt some who were associated with them, and had not yet taken any very active part in bicycling, might decide to do so; or they might take to tricycling. He, for one, should be glad to see their President (Mr. Norman) either on a bicycle or tricycle. Many people who did not feel equal to riding a bicycle were taking to tricycles and succeeding very well. In conclusion he proposed that Messrs. T. D. Tim- mins and W. Whittaer be elected vice-presidents. Mr. ARTHUR SALKELD, in seconding the motion, which was passed unanimously, said he was convinced that many of the older members, who were becoming rather two heavily weighed—(laughter)—for bicycling, would be glad to see some of the young men fill their places. The other officers were appointed as follows :—Committee Messrs. Alfred Norman, F. Bate, FA. Smith, and T. VV ~. Speakman; treasurer, Mr. Chorlton, manager of Parr's Bank; and auditor, Mr. J. Salkeld. Mr. JOSEPH SALKELD proposed the re-election of Mr Norman, as president. Mr..,,,,RT111712 SALHELD seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously. On the motion of Mr. Josnm SALKELD, seconded by Mr. KAY, it was agreed that the appointment of captain and sub- captain, should be left over until the first committee meeting. Mr. Airman SALKELD moved a nearly vote of thanks to Mr. Thomas Norman, for the manner in which he had carried Out his duties as president, and said the club were greatly indebted to him. Mr. MARWOOD seconded the proposition, which was carried with acclamation; and this terminated the business of the meeting.

div.head: LONDON CORNESPoNDENCE.
div.p: LONDON CORNESPoNDENCE.

The contempt with which Mr. Parnell's personal conduct at this crisis is viewed in the House was shown on Tuesday in a striking manner. Sir William Harcourt paid a tribute to the unshrinking demeanour of Mr. Dillon,. who, at least, has the courage of his opinions, and does not run Away from dangers in which his. advice has involved other people. The Home Secretary did not mention Mr. Parnell by name, but every one knew who was meant by his reference to the French captain. The House loudly cheered the point, and it was a noticeable fact that the Irish members sat silent, not even Mr. Biggar raising the defiant cheer, which has hitherto come readily to their lips when Mr. Parnell has been attacked.

For a specimen of rapid legislation, the history of the Protection Bill in the House of Lords may be cited. On Monday it was read a first time without any remark. On Tuesday it passed a second reading after what may by courtesy be called a debate extending over two hours. The committee stage was dispensed with, and on Wednesday the Lord Chancellor and two or three peers attended, when the formality of the third reading was gone through. At five o'clock in the afternoon the Royal Assent was given by commission, and shortly after daylight on Thursday Mr. Forster was in a condition of something like autocratic power in Dublin. In ladies' dress two new and singular fashions have jus commenced to set in. The Ulster has been so serviceable that it cannot be discarded. The problem has been how to vary it, and, of course, the only variance allowable would be one that would make it look even move masculine than it is. The combination of this garment with a cap of the same material makes it sometimes rather difficult to dis- tinguish a lady from a sporting man. The hood is, evidently the point most open to operation, and one development of it has made a woman look somewhat like a monk. In the matter of masculine advance, this was rather retrogressive. The latest change has taken a different line. If a lady could be made to look like a soldier all that could be desired might be obtained. And so the hood has been modified. It , is now cut square and rather oblong, so as to resemble a soldier's knapsack. The coat is grey, the binding red, and the buttons brass. This new form of the Ulster is called a Connaught. The other fashion is perhaps even more singular. Bangles have been so long in fashion that if they are to be retained they too must be modified, and the only difficulty is to know how to do it. The problem is difficult, but its solution is triumphant. They are now worn round the feet as well as round the wrists. The many-buttoned boots come in meet admirably for the new fashion; and ter house wear little bells have been hung on the bangles. Thus the e earer has music wherever she goes. But the bells are confined to the feet. The days of Queen Victoria must not be con- founded with those of Queen Elizabeth, when fools wor bells on their head-gear and not on their gaiters. The new journalistic ventures just now projected in Lon- don show how indomitable is man, and how each of us feels certain of success where others have failed. I suppose there is more money lost every year in the newspaper enterprise than in any other speculation, except, perhaps, cotton. We all know the enormous sums which were sunk in the Morning Star and the:Hsur, and irretrievably lost. But some similar ventures in the provinces have proved equally expensive luxuries. A northern daily, recently deceased, is reported to have cost its owner £50,000, although its career only extended over a few years, and its existence can scarcely be said to have been generally known. In the ad- joining county a " party " paper has cost its promoters over 00,000, and they are now able to carry it on only in a mutilated form. Not far off in the same district a more ambitious effort left its original proprietors more than £lOO,OOO to the bad,, and they were very pleased to dispose of their interest for a bagatelle, on the condition that the paper continued in the same line of polities. A commercial gentleman, not unknown in the Midlands and South Wales, indulged his fancy for journalism to the extent of over £60,000 before his efforts collapsed, while a better known personage, who took a fatherly interest in three journals, is reported to have totalled up a loss of £120,000. Even a religi MIS community who wanted an organ in the provincial press was bled to the extent of £30,000 before its- members made a free gift of the paper to a practical manager. It would thus appear that amateur journalism is not very fortu- I tunate in its results.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA- TION. The annual meeting of the general council (200) of the Warrington Liberal Association was held on Monday, in the Liberarelub, Bewsey-street, under the presidency of Alder- man John Burge.s.—Mr. F. Monks moved that Mr. Samuel Rigby be re-elected president for the ensuing year.—Mr. J. H. Gornall seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—On the motion of Mr. G. Blackhurst, se- conded by Mr. W. Brown, Messrs. John G. McMinnies, M.P., and John Burgess, J.P., were re-elected vice-presidents —Mr. .1 no. Bunnell moved that Mr. John Crosfield be re-elected hon. treasurer.—This was seconded by Mr. Ziba Armitage, and adopted unanimously.—Mr. Pluinpton moved a vote of thanks to the Liberal members on the Warrington Board of Guardians for their services during the past year.—The motion, was seconded by Mr. Richard Roberts, supported by Messrs. H. Roberts and S. Barlow and others. and carried unanimously.—Mr. Blackhurst and the Rev. John Yonge acknowledged the compliment. The following gentlemen were selected for nomination as. guardians of the poor for the ensuing year—

C. H. Cartwright. glass manufacturer, Latchford. George Blackhurst,* jeweller, Latchford. John Yonge,* Congregational minister, Wilson Patten-street. 7. Loughlin.* jeweller, Bewsey-road J. Marsh,* gentleman. Rel eaton-street. W. Longshaw,* chemical manufacturer. Sankey. John Brown,* gentleman, Wilderspool Causeway. W. Barn,* leather merchant, Arpley-street. John Greening, wire manufacturer, Bewsay-street. John Toil. baker, Museum-street.
The gentlemen with asterisks to their names are members of the present Board ot Guantans.—On the motien of Mr. Crosfield, a hearty vote or thanks was accorded to the chairman for presiding.

WARRINGTON PUBLIC RAIL COMPANY. ANNUAL MEETING. The general annual meeting of this Company was held on Monday, in the ante-room, at the Public Hall. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. Artingstall, and there were also present :—Messrs. J. Crosfield, Z. Armitage, J. Pierpoint, Chas. J. Holmes, W. Woods, H. N. Houghton, J. Marson, G. Blackhurst, T. B. Carter, J. Davies, J. T. Picton, J. White, and W. Johnson (secretary). Dr. Smith (chairman) and Mr. J. Rylauds (vice-chairman) were ab.ent through indisposition.
REPORT OF THE DIRECT'ORS. The Directors, in laying before the shareholders the state.

, . ment of 3ccounts for the past year, had pleasure in stating That the insome was larger than for several previous years. A return showed the amount received for the various pur- poses for which the hall bad been let in 1877 as 382105. 7d.; in 1878, £374 18s,; in 1879, £348 15s. 4d.; and in 1880, £4Ol 163. The total 'lncome for the past year had been £503 10s., and the expenditore £278 12s. 3d. The . _ _

' I I' • • amount avallab e or dividend was Z2OB Os. ed., out of which it was proposed to pay a dividend of £4 per cent.— Two of the directors, Dr. Bowes and Mr. Ziba Armitage, re- tired by rotation, but were eligible, and recommended for re-election.

The CILAIRMAX moved the adoption of the repert, Mr. MACKIE had great pleasme in seconding the motion. It was very gratifying to them to find, judging by the ex- tent of the dividend, that their property was 50 pit cent. more valuable now than 12 months ago. The different items of income during the year were all more or less gratifying, and he thought with the exception of thaZ re- ferring to public meetings they might reasonably calcM7ate . .

upon as good a dividend for the- coming year. He was afraid they would not have as many public meetings. Per- hatas "afraid " was the wrong word toi use, for many of the meetings arose last year from circumstances which they at present certainly did not expect, and which he should sup- pose most of them did not desire. He hoped the directors would see their way to make improvements in connection with the hall which would make it more valuable, and cer- tainly more useful, to the town in the future than it had
been in the past. 7T-k-e-r—e-w-a:s-no-ci-oai the Public Hall had

_ been of immense advantage to the town during the some- thing like a quarter of a century that it had been in existence, and he thought the general feeling of the share- holders—and he believed the directors thoroughly sympa- thised with it—was that the time had come when there might be improvements made in connection with the hall which would make it still more worthy of the town, and, he ventured to say, a more remunerative investment. The directors had seriously considered the proposition of making that enteroom a: much more comfortable room, putting in windows and a door, so that in the case of dress concerts and the like there might be a rapid and commodious means of exit for those who required cariiages to take them home. He thought the change would make the room much more likely to be let, and he fondly hoped there might be some person with sufficient speculation to make an offer to the directors to utilise the room either as a public news-room or corn exchange, or some other purpose as would make it an additional convenience to the town. 'There was one point upon which they were all agreed that would be carried out soon, and that was the erection of at least an additional stair to the galleries by which the audience might be able to get out of the building more readily. (Hear, hear.) The heating of the place was certainly not what it ought to be, and he suggested that the shareholders who might follow him should give an opinion in favour of borrowing such a sum of money on the building as would enable them to have all. the conveniences at which he had hinted and those which might have struck other shareholders or directors.
The report was adopted. THE DIVIDEND.—THE LETTING OF THE AILL.

Mr Z. ARMITAGE proposed, "That a dividend be declared for the past year at the rate of 4 per cent, free of income tax payable on and after Ist March, 1881." He said reference to the account would show that there was a sum of £2OB available for dividend, but it was thought well to retain in hand a sufficiently large balance. Of this balance 4 per cent: would take about £173 out of the £2OB, and it was thought wise that the balance of £35 should be retained to cover the cost of improvements which were necessary in the piano, and also for other matters. With regard to the scheme Mr. Mackie had referred to, it had always struck him that they must be able to see a very satisfactory offer in hand for the hire of that room before they would be justified in sacrificing

the certainty of £4O a year which they now got for the room exclusive ot what they got for it when let in con- junction with the other premises; and he had not as yet been able to see that the expense of altering that room and enlarging the hall would be remunerative to them. Of course it was a matter which had been and was still under the consideration of the directors, who were anxious and willing to do anything which would show a reasonable pros- pect of remuneration; but as the scheme lay before them at present he, personally, had not been able to see how that re- muneration would enable them to pay in future years the dividend which they were now proposing to pay. Mr. J. CROSFIELD seconded the proposition, and took the opportunity of saying that he thought one of the first things the directors should attempt to do was to see that the hall was better warmed. (Hear, hear.) During the present
• , winter he had attended several entertainments in the Public Hall when he did not think it was fit for any delicate person to sit there. He knew when Mr. Brandram gave his recita- .

tion gentlemen in dress clothes had to siCwith their top coats on, and the ladies were shivering the whole evening. If something was not done to make the hail more com- fortable as regarded warmth it would certainly affect the attendance—(bear, hear)—on those oacasions, and he ventured to suggest that the directors should warm the hall with hot air on the same principle that they warmed the large room at the Liberal Club, in Bewsey-street. That was a large room which they attempted to warm with hot water pipes. Those, however, entirely failed, and they got a firm from Manchester to come over and put it right. They did so, and as far as he remembered it cost about MO, and the room had been perfectly comfortable ever since. Speaking of the letting of the hall, he asked whether the letting of it was in the hands of the Secretary or not.. He had always understood it was, but if so he thought there ought not to be any kind of favouritism shown between the two political parties in the town. He had to complain that at the last municipal election the hall was let to the Conservative party four nights in one week, and the fourth night was Saturday night. The hall was let on these terms : that they should have the chance of refusal if they 'wished. When the Liberal party applied for he hall the Conservative party of course instantly took it. It did not much matter, as things turned out, whether the Liberals got the ball or not ; but he thought on occasions of this sort the hall should not be let four nights in one week to one of the political parties. He hoped the directors would consider this matter. The CHAIRMAN: Did the Conservatives get this hall for four nights without paying for them? Mr. CROSFIELD : That I-cannot tell you. I should like to know whether they paid for four nights. The SECRETARY: Yes. The system of letting the hall had been in vogue during the last 12 years tohis knowledge, and that he treated the Liberal party in exactly the same way at the general election in April last. Mr. Roberts came to him one morning and said he wanted the hall for certain days, and he gave Mr. Roberts the refusal of as many days as he wished, but he was to let him (Mr. Johnson) know by a certain time, on what days he required the hall. Of course if the other party had applied he would have given Mr. Roberts the privilege of saying " yes "or "no.' In the present case Mr. Thomas .Sutton came down to Mr. White's office and said "I want every vacant date you have got this week." He (the speaker) was not in at the time, and Mr. Sutton left the message, and he could not do anything beyond letting the 'hall. At that time the Saturday was not open. -

Mr. CROSFIELD: Did you not let him have the refusal of the hall on Saturday? The SECRETARY replied that he did not. At that time the ball was taken by Mr. Saunders of Liverpool. But he received a letter from Mr. Saunders saying that as it Was the election he was not coming and asking if he would let the hall. In the interval Mr. Sutton bad called at the office and said if he could have Saturday afternoon would the secretary book it to him. He got that message almost simul- taneously with Mr. Saunders letter, and just before he went out to see Mr. Sutton, Mr. Roberts came and said "I want the ball this afternoon." He said he was very sorry, Mr. Sutton had applied for it, and he must give him the refusal of it. He went to see Mr. Sutton„ and just as he was leaving, Mr. Bekaa said " does Mr. Sutton want it," and he said yes." • Mr. CROSFIELD said all he wanted was that the two parties should be fairly treated. He thought there ought to be some restriction in letting people have the refusal of the hall. A man might go and say he wanted the refusal of the Public Hall every night the next week. He did not think it right he should have it. The SECRETARY,: It was not so in this case. The CHAIRMAN : I think Mr. Crosfield's complaint has been fairly answered. Mr. Cuosnint.n : Oh, yes,.l am satisfied with the explana- tion. I hope the heating of the hall will have your atten- tion. The proposition wai, then carried. RE-ELECTION OF DIRECTORS. Alderman Hotztes moved that Dr. Bowes and Mr. Ziba Armitage be re-elected directors of the company. Mr. MACKIE seconded the motion. He remarked that Mr. Armitage was mistaken in interpreting his remark! that he intended to have a change to do away with £4O income. The only proposition was to put in a door way, and, that would just leave the £4O a year as before, Mr. ARMITAGE : As I understand these plans and the pro- posal, it would put this room in such s shape that it would not be let— Mr. MACKIE : That is a plan which has been knacked on the head months ago. I think, Mr. Armitage, yo in were not at the meeting. Alderman DAVIES, referring to the letting of the hall, said he gathered that the hall 'was-let in the interests of the shareholders for the very best sum that could' be got. It ; was a commercial company, and they must look after itshin- terests in a commercial point of view. were not supposed to recognise any partcHwealootr, heeyaerri) ItT ethey Conservative party came to take the hall, ad we prepared to pay for it, of course he would let it to them ; but he woeuar treat the Liberal party in exactly the same way. hear.) When ho heard no. director was able to sp i speak authhe ; i matter he Was rather cliauppeillted, and he thought be well for them to have a voice n the letting oftehehihmalilt. o ,If it was left with the Secretary they must t blame he, in the exercise of his judgment, did not do what was required. He concluded by supporting the motion. After it short convorntion4

div.p: wipNiZS POLICE COURT.
MovnAy._Befoe ,Z 1 r. George Pilkingtou.

A DISORMRLY Wostax.—Mar Clarke, in default of find- ing sureties for her good behaviour, was sent to gaol 14 days, for causing a disturbance in Waterloo.. -road. ^ VAGRANCY. —Sarah Ellen Johnstor):' a known to the police, was sent to gaol Jo: seven days for vagranCy. woman well

' nleton A SAD Ctn.—Harrison Turton, publicatt, of 11).7.- ' on a, who has been several times before the court lately charge of assaulting his wife, was brought up on a charge at being drunk and disorderly.—Sergeant Eastharn atated that on Saturday morning, about three o'clock, prisoner entered the police station and conducted himself in a very extraor- dinary manner. As he was under the influence of drink, he was taken into custody. The dame morning he was brorght up on the charge, and made some long rambling statements concerning some litigation with his wife and the conduct of his mother.—The magistrate remanded him, in order that he night be examined by a medical man. Dr. Cooper, of Wid- nes, now stated that ho had examined Mr. Turbo, who was at present insane. Prisoner again conducted himself in a very strange manner. He rambled into a long story absut a life assurance policy, and stated that some one intended to shoot him. He declared he would not pass another night in the cells, as on the previous one someone had presented a revolver at him through the cell window. The magistrate made an order for his committal to the County Asylum at Rainhill.
WEDNESDA.T.—Before Mr. Gibbon (chairman), and Mr. F. H. Gossage.

SCHOOL BOARD PROSECIITIONS.—A number of parents were summoned by the Widnes School Board, who were re- presented by Mr. Danby, their clerk, for not sending their children to school. The following had 55., iocluding costs, to pay in each case :—John Lynch, John McCoy, John Tarling,ton, Martin Cunningham, Joseph Twigg (two cases), and Thomas Welsh.—ln the case of a lad named Samuel Fishwick, the clerk asked their worships to make an order committing him to an industrial school. The youth was unmanageable, and he had been sent to all the schools in the town, but none of the teachers could deal with him, though he was only 12 years of age. Mr. Davies, attendance officer, was called to substantiate this statement, after which . _
the Bench made an order committing the lad to the Everton Terrace (Liverpool) Certified Industrial Scheol until he was

. , 14 years of age. ALLEGED NEW WAY OF PAYING AN ACCOUNT—WiIIiam Dwyer. coal dealer, was charged with stealing a cheque for £B, the property of Mr. John Whitfield, who was represented by Mr. Beasley. That gentleman having opened the case at some length, complainant was called, and said he was agent to Messrs. Evans, colliery proprietors, and the defen- dant Dwyer was a customer of theirs. On the 21st Feb. he owed the firm an acceunt amounting to £l4 2s. 901. On ' the :Saturday before the 19th February, he made an ap- pointment with defendant to see him, when he agreed to p.iy £B. As he was going to defendant's on the Monday morning, he met him at Appleton station. It was nearly 12 , o'clock, and at the time Walter Renshaw, a yardman in the employ of the.firm, was with witness. Dwyer asked which was the cashier, and witness told him he was. Defend int used very bad, language, pushed both of them, and told Renshaw to go back. °Renshaw returned, and witness went with defendant to his house at William-street, Appleton. Defendant then asked him what he wanted, and he told him that he knew very well what he had come about. On ask- ing him how much he was going to pay, defendant said £B. He then enquired for pen and ink, which were brought by Dwyer. He sat down by the dresser, and proceeded to make out a receipt for the amount, which he wrote upon one in his book of forms, similar to the one produced. Dwyer placed five sovereigns upon the dresser, remarking that he was not without money yet. Defendant left the coin there, and witness could easily have taken it up, but did not do so. He placed the receipt form on the account, which defendant had put upon the table. Dwyer picked the account and receipt up whilst witness was filling in the . . . .
counterfoil. Defendant hr:d.sent his wife upstairs lot the

additional three pounds. Whilst he was making out de- fendant the counterfoil, Mrs. Dwyer picked' up the £5 from the dresser. Mrs. Dwyer did not aft2rwards pay him any money, but looked at the counterfoil and told him to call at six o'clock for the cash. Dwyer went out at the back door' and witness remained in the house abo!lt a ' quarter of an hour, and then went to the corner of the street for the purpose of finding Recshaw and sending him for a policeman. Shortly after Dwyer entered the house, and asked him what he was waitiro, for. He told him he was waiting for the XS, on which defendant put him out of the house, and shut the door. After remaining some short time, he went to a Mr. Riddle's. He had not since received tue account, though he made application for it two days later to the defendant, who told hirn .he hod got the money.—ln cross-examination prosecutor stated that he laid, the infer- motion on the Monday, and on the Wednesday after again demanded the total 811111. He got the summons on the Thursday.—Walter Renshaw, yardman, corroborated the statement of the prosecutor.—Wm. Lavin, a lad employed as a carter at the Lugsdale coal yard, said that on the day of the alleged offence, he was near the house of the defen- dant and saw the complainant standing near the door. Com- plainant asked him to wait and see that neither he nor defen- dant left the place without something being done about the

money. He saw Dwyer come round the corner and go into his own house by the back door. Dwyer asked complainant what he wanted, and he replied "that £B." Complainant at this time had entered the defendant's house, and he (defen'- dant) put him out. Shortly after defendant catne out and asked him (witness) what he wanted standing there, and threatened to "shift hint with his foot" if Ile did not go away. Some further time having elapsed, thfendant came out again, and asked complainant what he wanted. He answered, "The amount of that account," on which defen-
dant replied "he wished he was as sure of the grace of God, as that Whitfield had had the money."—Mr. Husband sub- mitted that there was no case whatever against defendant.

It was apparent that from the very first the whole matter had been treated as a joke. The dispute between the parties was one which ought to be settled in the County court, as it was quite evident it was.a civil and not a criminal matter. There had been no trick tried upon the complainant; the receipt was laid down for the defendant to pick up, and he had takes it. In order to convict in such a case an animus furandi must be proved, and he quoted cases in support of this view. He maintained that there could o*t be a conviction because the receipt was giver to the defendant. Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial, and allowed bail. DISABLING A POLICEMAN WITH A POKER. Thomas Dunn, of Hebburn-on-Tyne, and formerly of Widnes, was charged with stealing a shirt, cap, and two pairs of stockings, the property of Joseph Lawley. He was also charged with unlawfully wounding P.C. Strickland. Supt. Brindle briefly stated the facts of the robbery and assault, which occurred on the 19th of June last, since which time the prisoner had been out of the way. As he had only been apprehended on the previous day at Ifebburn, tit e superinten- dent desired that the prisoner should be remanded for one week. P.C. Strickland said that on the 19th of last June, ha went to Dunn's house, and found the property which he was charged with stealing. He next took him in to custody, on whictr'a struggle took place. Dunn struck him six times on the head and she of the face with a poker, and cut through the flesh to the bone. In consequence of the assault; he was off duty for a week, and a fortnight elapsed before be was able to lift his right hand to his head.— Prisoner was remanded until that day week. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Thomas Scally was summoned for a breach of the peace. P.C. Brydges said he found de- fendant and Stephen Scally (who did not appear, and for whom a warrant was issued) yelling aid making a great noise in the street. On telling them to go away, they threw stones at him. He followed them to their own house, from which they assailed him with bottles Defendant was ordered to be bound over, himself hi £lO and two sureties in £5, to keep the peace.

Titurtsney.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. ALLEGED TxErr OF riclEorrs,—Edward Stone, aged 19. and James Hardman, 12 years of age, were charged with. stealing two pigeons, the property of John Hunt, Vine publichouse, Lugsdale. They were remanded until Wednes day next.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
TUESDAY.—BeforeMr. W. Vir.vnne Ffoulkes, Judge.

CLAIM FOR A WIFE'S MAINTENANCE.—Mr. Thos. Hough- ton, collector te the Runcorn Board of Guardians, sued Mr. Henry Hibbert for £4 10s., the cost of maintaining the wife Wm. Hibbert.—The plaintiff said he had employed Mr. W. H. Linaker to appear for him, but he had been suddenly called away to London. The action was to recover nine weeks maintenance of Wm. Hibbert's wife, at 10s. per week. He had sued the parties before, and got two verdicts, one in May and the other in March. Win. Hibbert, the husband of the woman referred to, went off to America some time ago, where he died, making a will by which he left the bulk of his property to his mother.— Mr. Husband, who defended, said there was about .£l5 in- volved in the estate. As Hibbert died abroad, probate had to be taken out in London. He hada witness there who had administered, and who could give a detailed account of how the money had been spent. If the order was made quando exciderint,no harm could be done.—Plaintiff said he believed deceased had LBO in the Trinity Building Club,—at least there was that sum there a month or two ago.—His Honour: Have you any one here from the society ?—Plaiotiff No.— His honour: Well, that witness is all important.—Mr. Husband considered it quite probable that if he was allowed to cross-examine the plaintiff, the judge would not make any order. The wife referred to in the case was Mr. Houghton's sister. She and her husband could not agree, and he/went abroad, where he died. He believed plaintiff received certain services for the money which he claimed. Plaintiff said he had a wife and no family, and his own wife WaS competent to look after the house without assistance.— In answer to His Honour, the plaintiff said that £l2 had also been paid to Mr. Joseph Griffiths, who was acting for the executors, by the Foresters' Friendly Society.— The Judge said he thought it would be well that the accounts in the case should be submitted to the Registrar, who might exan.ine them in his (the judge's) room.-7 his course was agreed to; and it was afterwards resolved that the hearing of the case should be adjourned, plaintiff paying the costs of adjournment.
